     T
         he first task of the Gamemaster is to make the strange
         and wondrous world of Charlemagne come to life. The
         characters, and the society they live in, must take shape
      and color by his descriptions. Immersion into the stories allow
      players to experience the essence of roleplaying: becoming one
      with their Player-knight.
        A good campaign depends not only on the Gamemaster
      and his description of the world, but also on the efforts of the
      players to roleplay their characters. Character identification and
      theatrical skills come in handy, both for the players as well as for
      the Gamemaster, who should set an example when incarnating
      his non-player characters.
        The Gamemaster is not the adversary of the players, but
      rather their guide. His aim must be to please the players, by giv-
      ing each sufficient time to express himself and to act, and by chal-
      lenging their capacities and rewarding their personal ambitions.
        As a source of inspiration, there is none better than the sto-
      ries of old themselves. Go to your local or university library and
      see which of the books you can get a hold of (see the Bibliography).
      To experience the imaginary world of Charlemagne, players
      should read at least The Song of Roland, and preferably some
      other epics too. It’s because the adventures of the legendary he-
      roes make us dream that we engage in roleplaying. And no other
      world, no matter how fertile the imagination of the author, can
      replace the authenticity and the infinite beauty of the literature
      — of which we are but the humble heirs.

       By cleverness you succeed when with force you fail.
           — Theodulf

ntures

  meet the major heroes, explore the lands of the empire and be-
  yond, encounter foreign peoples and cultures, and found their
  own glorious lineage.
  Campaign  Types

     Different styles of campaigns are possible. Before starting
  your campaign, it may be a good idea to ask your players which
  one they prefer.
  Classical Campaign

     Simply follow the major events listed in Chapter 15. It in-
  volves lots of travel, so the characters encounter different lands
  and peoples, and take part in many important adventures.
  Serving a powerful lord like Thierry of Ardennes, who is a per-
  sonal friend of King Charlemagne, gives the characters a reason
  to accompany him to places where adventure awaits.
  Regional Campaign
     This sort of campaign focuses on the events in a certain
  region of Charlemagne’s empire. Good choices would be the
  Saxon or Spanish frontiers. While the Player-knights miss out
  on some of the important events which take place elsewhere
  in the empire, the advantage of a regional campaign is that the
  GM and the Player-knights can dig deeper into nitty-gritty
  politics and personal objectives. Regional campaigns are gen-
  erally more down-to-earth than other styles. The canonical
  heroes come into play less often, and the Player-knights are
  usually more concerned with everyday business such as their
  households and their lands.
  Courtly Campaign
     This places the Player-knights at the court of Charlemagne,
  as ambitious young noblemen from a noble house. They may
  rise to become scarae, paladins or counts, bishops or abbots. It
  allows for major embassies to faraway lands, inspections as mis-
  si dominici, personal quests (adaptations of some of the more
  fantastic gestes), much political intriguing, and — why not? —
  romancing one of Charlemagne’s daughters.

title: Group Coherence
leftColumn:
Questing Heroes
        Finally, the most difficult type of campaign is to send all
      characters on a long-lasting quest, like Sir Astolf or Sir Lion
      of Bourges. This demands a lot of preparation, since the GM
      should at least have an idea over the over-all plot arc before he
      starts the campaign. Examples of quests are the retrieval of a
      powerful relic or enchanted item, or to accomplish a heroic feat
      worthy of paladins, like capturing an evil faerie queen or rescuing
      an important character from a far-away prison.
      Group  Coherence

        It is important to create a sense of group coherence, that
      the group of Player-knights is not simply a band of individuals
      playing the same adventures together. To build a solid group,
      the Gamemaster may require that all the knights be relatives
      in the same House, have the same lord, have the same mission,
      or all three.
      Character Histories

        A Player-knight should already have a short life story to
      tell when he is introduced into the campaign. A character his-
      tory allows the player to formulate his possible ambitions for
      the future, and to balance them with the other Player-knights.
      The Gamemaster can use it as a source of inspiration for his
      campaign, or at least find some adventure hooks to get a Player-
      knight involved in the main story.
        A special way of inserting a new character into the cam-
      paign is by giving him a goal or a mystery right from the start,
      as a sort of destiny. It may be a strange birthmark, a family oath,
      a wondrous prophecy, some sort of faerie prohibition, a curse
      from a dying enemy, or a prophetic event or dream his mother
      had the day she gave birth of a burning chapel, the flowering of
      an unusual plant on a significant place, or a fight between two
      symbolic animals.
        In return for a such a mysterious history, a Gamemaster
      may compensate the player by giving his character an appropri-
      ate blessing.
      Adventuring

       Hear me, my lords, may God grant you his aid.
       Will it please you to hear a noble tale,
       A tale which is sung with charm and grace.
           — The Coronation of Louis, I

      A
          knight’s primary duty is to serve his lord at court and
          in battle, and hunting to put food on the table is a com-
          mon occurrence. Although recurrent and routine, these
      activities are not insignificant; on the contrary, they are the
      primary focus of your character’s life. The Gamemaster can use
      these activities as recurrent components of a campaign or, with
      some additions of his own, as the basis of an adventure.
rightColumn:
Even normal, stay-at-home knights have ordinary adven-
  tures as part of their routine, without having to seek them out:
  going to tournaments, participating in battles, engaging in ro-
  mance, visiting unusual sights, and encountering unusual beings
  and foreign knights who come to plague their lands.
     Adventuring is an activity that is recognized as a legitimate
  knightly activity. Most knights do not go adventuring — for
  them the everyday activities of guard duty, tournaments, and
  battles are enough to satisfy their sense of adventure. Other
  knights, like the Player-knights, seek more, and actively look for
  adventures. Some lords send their knights to work off their en-
  ergy far, far away from home. Perhaps the sponsoring lord hopes
  that the questing knights will rouse similar feelings from his oth-
  er, less enthusiastic knights as well.
     Adventuring is the excuse for Player-knights to wander the
  roads and trails of Frankland and beyond. Adventuring is the ac-
  tivity that sets Player-knights apart from others. While knight-
  hood is the heart of Paladin, adventuring is its soul.
  Adventure  Types
     There are quite a few possible types of adventures Player-
  knights can participate in:
   n
     Participating in battles, raids, sieges and conquests.
   n
     Hunting down a rebellious vassal.
   n
     Resolving family feuds by political maneuvers and
     intrigue.
   n
     Reconciling Charlemagne with a defiant vassal.
   n
     Unmasking conspiracies against Charlemagne.
   n
     Retrieving lost paladins.
   n
     Undertaking a magical, romantic or religious quest.
   n
     Leading or accompanying an embassy to a foreign
     land.
  Quests
     All quests are adventures, but not all adventures are quests.
  A quest must include several elements to qualify as such: going
  to an unknown place, encountering something mysterious or
  unusual, facing strange dangers and — almost always — facing
  death. Quests must, by definition, occur in unknown territory.
  In strange lands awaits adventure and opportunities to test the
  ideals of the heartland of civilization.
     Knights must request leave from their lord to adventure.
  A knight, even in foreign lands, represents not just himself, but
  also his lord; so the lord sends individuals who he will not have
  to get out of trouble, and who will not bring shame or dishonor
  to himself.
     A time limit is often imposed on knights for questing. The
  proverbial “year and a day” is a good starting limit. At the end of
  that time the knight must return to court and report the results
  of his activities. Later on the time limit may be longer, indefinite,
  or until the completion of a specific task.

title: The Epics as Adventures
leftColumn:
Quest Structure
        Given below is a standard quest structure, which can also be
      used to design regular scenarios.
        Setting: You must determine where the quest takes place,
      and for how long (years or adventure sessions). You may want to
      write down the region’s main characters, its history and legends,
      and the local sites of interest.
        Hook: The quest begins when an important problem (a
      curse, a prisoner, a lost item) brings the heroes together. To get
      them more involved, it may be wise to have them experience
      some sort of personal setback, which addresses their needs, pas-
      sions or ambitions. After a first interaction with the main char-
      acters, they may head directly for adventure or, as often, they’ll
      discover some secrets and possibly a hidden, underlying cause to
      the main problem.
        Minor Villain: A false hero, or an agent of the main villain,
      may try to corrupt their quest by making interesting suggestions
      which later are revealed to be disastrous. Such an intruder may
      aim to sow discord and suspicion among the Player-knights,
      or a rival may try to steal the fruit of their labor after the
      Confrontation.
        Neutral Characters: On their way, the Player-knights
      should be invited to offer their help in an apparently unre-
      lated problem. This temporarily leads them away from their
      main goal, but by befriending such neutral characters (faeries,
      honorable enemies, creatures) the Player-knights will be giv-
      en precious aid in return (an object, some information, or a
      future favor).
        Main Villain: The main adversary should make a brief
      appearance in the beginning. This gives the players at least
      a vague idea of whom they have to deal with, and of the vil-
      lain’s potential weaknesses. As a consequence, this should
      stimulate them to carefully prepare and find additional help,
      if necessary.
        Key: By solving a mystery or defeating a minor enemy, the
      Player-knights acquire a helpful item (an enchanted sword, a rel-
      ic, a useful plant), which enables them to continue the quest and
      confront the villain on more favorable ground.
        Confrontation: In the final battle, the Player-knights ei-
      ther defeat the main villain or are defeated by him. Either way,
      the loser may flee to return later, so the previous quest phases
      may be repeated.
        Conclusion: Now is when a rival (a Minor Villain) may
      backstab the heroes and claim their rewards. A judgment or
      a test must distinguish between the true and false heroes. If
      they haven’t already, the heroes may benefit from a Neutral
      Character’s help.
        Rewards: Apart from a significant amount of Glory and
      treasure, the victorious heroes may gain the hand of a princess, a
      title, or an increase in personal capacities. Peace may be a reward
      in itself.
rightColumn:
The  Epics as Adventures

     In adapting adventures from the medieval gestes, the Player-
  knights can have different possible relations to the main heroes
  in the tales:
     Witnesses: The Player-knights are simply there when one
  of the canonical heroes does something significant. Simply hear-
  ing about these events during the Winter Phase is less exciting,
  but the Gamemaster’s objective is to keep the characters con-
  nected with the epic Carolingian background.
     Participants: The characters participate in tournaments,
  battles, feasts and other events of importance, even if they don’t
  have the starring roles.
     Followers: The characters accompany one or more heroes
  on a mission. While they aren’t the main focus of the action,
  they are also less likely to get hurt, so this may be the right role
  to choose if the group is composed of beginning characters. Even
  Roland can’t do everything himself, and he may ask his followers
  to perform some task, which could lead to Player-knights having
  some exciting adventures of their own.
     Looking for the Heroes: Knights often disappear while
  they are having adventures. Charlemagne regularly sends people
  looking for his paladins, which gives the players an opportunity

segments.text:
Quest Structure
        Given below is a standard quest structure, which can also be
      used to design regular scenarios.
        Setting: You must determine where the quest takes place,
      and for how long (years or adventure sessions). You may want to
      write down the region’s main characters, its history and legends,
      and the local sites of interest.
        Hook: The quest begins when an important problem (a
      curse, a prisoner, a lost item) brings the heroes together. To get
      them more involved, it may be wise to have them experience
      some sort of personal setback, which addresses their needs, pas-
      sions or ambitions. After a first interaction with the main char-
      acters, they may head directly for adventure or, as often, they’ll
      discover some secrets and possibly a hidden, underlying cause to
      the main problem.
        Minor Villain: A false hero, or an agent of the main villain,
      may try to corrupt their quest by making interesting suggestions
      which later are revealed to be disastrous. Such an intruder may
      aim to sow discord and suspicion among the Player-knights,
      or a rival may try to steal the fruit of their labor after the
      Confrontation.
        Neutral Characters: On their way, the Player-knights
      should be invited to offer their help in an apparently unre-
      lated problem. This temporarily leads them away from their
      main goal, but by befriending such neutral characters (faeries,
      honorable enemies, creatures) the Player-knights will be giv-
      en precious aid in return (an object, some information, or a
      future favor).
        Main Villain: The main adversary should make a brief
      appearance in the beginning. This gives the players at least
      a vague idea of whom they have to deal with, and of the vil-
      lain’s potential weaknesses. As a consequence, this should
      stimulate them to carefully prepare and find additional help,
      if necessary.
        Key: By solving a mystery or defeating a minor enemy, the
      Player-knights acquire a helpful item (an enchanted sword, a rel-
      ic, a useful plant), which enables them to continue the quest and
      confront the villain on more favorable ground.
        Confrontation: In the final battle, the Player-knights ei-
      ther defeat the main villain or are defeated by him. Either way,
      the loser may flee to return later, so the previous quest phases
      may be repeated.
        Conclusion: Now is when a rival (a Minor Villain) may
      backstab the heroes and claim their rewards. A judgment or
      a test must distinguish between the true and false heroes. If
      they haven’t already, the heroes may benefit from a Neutral
      Character’s help.
        Rewards: Apart from a significant amount of Glory and
      treasure, the victorious heroes may gain the hand of a princess, a
      title, or an increase in personal capacities. Peace may be a reward
      in itself.
The  Epics as Adventures

In adapting adventures from the medieval gestes, the Player-
  knights can have different possible relations to the main heroes
  in the tales:
     Witnesses: The Player-knights are simply there when one
  of the canonical heroes does something significant. Simply hear-
  ing about these events during the Winter Phase is less exciting,
  but the Gamemaster’s objective is to keep the characters con-
  nected with the epic Carolingian background.
     Participants: The characters participate in tournaments,
  battles, feasts and other events of importance, even if they don’t
  have the starring roles.
     Followers: The characters accompany one or more heroes
  on a mission. While they aren’t the main focus of the action,
  they are also less likely to get hurt, so this may be the right role
  to choose if the group is composed of beginning characters. Even
  Roland can’t do everything himself, and he may ask his followers
  to perform some task, which could lead to Player-knights having
  some exciting adventures of their own.
     Looking for the Heroes: Knights often disappear while
  they are having adventures. Charlemagne regularly sends people
  looking for his paladins, which gives the players an opportunity
  to live the same adventures as the canonical heroes. They may
  even have to rescue the paladin when he has, once again, been
  captured by an evil faerie.
     Heroes Themselves: Powerful Player-knights should be
  challenged by having them replace the original paladins from
  the gestes, or by adding them to the cast. In this case, they must
  confront the actual obstacles described in the epic legends. Of
  course, if one or more players know the story already, you should
  modify the plot, twist the encounters and create other possible
  solutions.
  Scenarios
  S
      cenarios are the stories of the campaign. A scenario in-
      cludes the setting, Gamemaster characters, and a poten-
      tial plot to challenge or beguile the knights. Scenarios
  supply the interface between your imagination, your character,
  the setting, and the game. The word “scenario” is the general
  word used for any kind of game event that can be experienced
  by players. This section introduces the basic concepts, types, and
  terms used in the creation of Paladin scenarios.
  Writing Scenarios
     When creating a scenario, keep in mind the following six
  golden rules:

1. Involve the Players: What sort of games have they
     played before? What do your players expect from you
     as a Gamemaster and from Paladin as a game? What
     sort of adventures do they prefer?

title: Chapter Nineteen: Adventures
leftColumn:
2. Create Interesting Characters: Player-knights and
        important non-player characters should have solid
        backgrounds and colorful, well-defined personali-
        ties. Adventures often appeal more to players if they
        made the effort of creating an interesting character.
        Add a mystery, a special ability, or the promise of
        future greatness and the players will indulge in your
        campaign more freely.
       3. Make the Setting Come to Life: The world in which
        the players live should not be too black-and-white.
        Good and evil exist everywhere, sometimes in unex-
        pected places. A convincingly-narrated setting stim-
        ulates overall player participation, especially when
        it is linked to their character histories. Gamemasters
        will find it easier to invent captivating intrigues,
        or provoke naturally conflicting passions for their
        Player-knights.
rightColumn:
4. Present Real Challenges: An adven-
             ture should not be too simple, nor too
             complex. Players should know what is
             expected of them, and their charac-
             ters should have an idea of what they
             are doing. Present them with a clear
             introduction, a coherent main event
             in which you alternate scenes based
             on personality and skills, court en-
             counters, and combat. A good scenario
             rhythm is important.
              To resolve a problem, the Player-
             knights must not only act, but also
             think of clever solutions. This in-
             creases both player involvement and
             suspense. Ideally, there should always
             be more than one solution to every
             problem, which avoids players getting
             blocked because of a bad idea or some
             failed die rolls.
             5. Create Interesting Enemies: A wor-
             thy opponent is more attractive and
             motivating for players. He should have
             a name and a complete personality,
             comprehensible motives for his ac-
             tions, awesome strengths and hidden
             weaknesses.
             6. Avoid Frivolous Combat Encounters:
             The best combats in Paladin are those
             with purpose, particularly in battle or
             adventure. Knights fight for reasons
             that go far beyond the crude con-
             cerns of unscrupulous mercenaries
             and plundering Saxons. Knights may
             even refuse combat on rare occasions,
     should loyalty dictate. Pomp and circumstance are a
     part of combat, although blood may be drawn with-
     out ritual or preamble when characters are angry or
     impassioned.
     More important is the purpose behind the appearance of
  combatants in the scenario: a secret they hide, the sorceress they
  guard, or the magical riddle that they’ll reveal to you if they are
  vanquished and spared. If such underlying mysteries are handled
  well by characters, in addition to simply defeating the creature,
  the Gamemaster should award additional Glory.
     For an example of how combat could be directly affected
  by roleplaying concerns, imagine meeting a young knight whose
  father is the hated enemy of your father. Do you challenge the
  knight or leave him be, knowing that his only crime is to be the
  son of his father? If you do fight, is it a combat to the death or a
  fight “for love”? Once combat is joined and you are victorious,
  do you accept the lad’s surrender chivalrously, or mock his hu-
  miliation before slaying him?

title: The Adventure of the Jewel
leftColumn:
The  Adventure

     T
         his short introductory adventure for squire characters
         presents the world of the Franks, anno 766. While play-
         ing the adventure, the Gamemaster and the players may
      familiarize themselves with both the game mechanics and the
      world of Paladin. The Player-knights experience the game’s
      fundamental concepts: some major passions and standings will
      play a significant role, as will combat and non-combat skills.
      The players learn about the concept of knighthood, instituted
      by King Pepin at his coronation, and the new attitude of chivalry
      promoted by the young Prince Charlemagne. They see the del-
      icate role played by knights in wielding power and maintaining
      justice, which — untempered by forgiveness and compassion for
      the weak — can sometimes lead to the cruelest oppression.
        Accompanied by a tutor, chaplain Jerome, the squires are
      presented with choices as to what kind of knights they want to
      become. The players must show their understanding of the laws
      of hospitality, the concept of Honor (which distinguishes no-
      bles from commoners), and the ambitious ideal of chivalry. The
      events call on their sense of justice and the Christian virtues of
      mercy and forgiveness. Finally, their relations with the peasants
      and the Church will be put to the test.
      Synopsis
        In the year 766, while Prince Charlemagne orders all knights
      of the Ardennes to hunt down a robber knight with a jewel set in
      his shield, the player squires are sent to the bishop in Liege. On
      the way back, they meet a pilgrim and are attacked by a band of
      desperate brigands. In a nearby village, they’ll be confronted with
      the suffering of the poor peasants. The local lord, Sir Eingar, is ar-
      rogant, cruel, and secretly a robber knight. He is not the one who
      has the jewel, but he does own a magic wolf-skin cape that allows
      him to take on the form of a wolf at night. Do the player squires
      take sides with the lord, the peasants, or with no one at all? And
      can they uncover the mystery of the Wolf Cloak?
      The Quest of the Jewel
        Monday, the 15th day of the month of April, anno 766.
      While King Pepin has called on the army to continue his war
      against Aquitaine, Prince Charlemagne comes to the castle of La
      Roche to hold his spring court. He is welcomed by his friend,
      Lord Thierry, who tells him of a mysterious robber knight hid-
      ing somewhere in the Ardennes Forest, who can be identified by
      a priceless jewel set in his shield.
        Hearing this news, the prince calls the bravest men from the
      duchy together, and bids them sally forth separately, with only a
      page as escort, in quest of the knight. Once found, they are to
      challenge him in true knightly fashion, and win the jewel he so
      arrogantly wears. Successful or not, the courtiers are to return in
      a month to give a truthful account of their adventures while on
      the quest.
        All the knights depart and scour the Ardennes Forest, each
      hoping to meet the robber knight and win the jewel. Among
rightColumn:
ure of the Jewel

  them is Prince Charlemagne’s brother-in-law, Sir Milo, accom-
  panied by his 16 year-old son, Roland, who serves as his squire.
  The  Squire’s Mission

     While the Ardennes knights are roaming the forest in search
  of the robber knight and his fabled jewel, the Player-knights are
  commanded by Lord Thierry — who is now desperately short of
  household knights — to accompany their old chaplain, Jerome,
  to Liege, to pick up the reliquary of Saint Marcian, which Bishop
  Fulcaire of Liege has agreed to loan him.
     A successful Religion roll allows the players to know more
  about Saint Marcian (see the nearby box), while Intrigue gives
  them a hint about why Lord Thierry wants this particular relic:
  to end the plague of wolves in the Ardennes. On a critical suc-
  cess, the character has spoken to a forester who says he wounded
  an unusually large wolf last month (this was Sir Eingar in wolf
  shape; the knight still bears the unhealed scars on his left arm).
     Have the players make a list of the things they carry, the
  horses they have taken, the money and food supplies they have
  with them. They should describe the route they plan on taking,
  as well as their travel speed and possibly other routines (camp
  procedures, marching order).
     The adventure begins after they have retrieved the reliquary
  from Liege, and are on their way back.
  A  Strange Pilgrim
     The player squires travel on a forest track in the northern
  part of the Ardennes Forest, near where the Ourthe joins the
  Amblève. It’s only half a day since they left Liege; they are still on
  the lands of the prince-bishop. They meet a dirty pilgrim com-
  ing from the opposite direction. He has a walking a stick and
  carries a small bag on his back. He politely asks the gentle sirs
  for alms, and tells them he is waiting for a friend, with whom he
  wishes to visit the abbey of Saint Hubert.

           Saint Marcian’s Relic

      Saint Marcian was a fugitive Visigoth who lived at the
   abbey of Merille near Auxerre. He had a strange power over
   animals: birds flocked to his hands, bears and wolves departed
   at his command, and once a boar fled to him for protection
   from hunters. His feast day is April 20th.
      The relic the players are carrying consists of some hair
   and a finger bone set in a golden necklace, which is itself kept
   in a small silver reliquary box studded with small gems (total
   worth approximately 20 £.).
      Anyone praying to Saint Marcian’s relic to pacify wild
   animals may do so at +5 to their Love [Charlemagne]. In this
   particular adventure, a successful prayer gives Sir Eingar a –5
   to all actions against the Player-knights.

segments.text:
T
         his short introductory adventure for squire characters
         presents the world of the Franks, anno 766. While play-
         ing the adventure, the Gamemaster and the players may
      familiarize themselves with both the game mechanics and the
      world of Paladin. The Player-knights experience the game’s
      fundamental concepts: some major passions and standings will
      play a significant role, as will combat and non-combat skills.
      The players learn about the concept of knighthood, instituted
      by King Pepin at his coronation, and the new attitude of chivalry
      promoted by the young Prince Charlemagne. They see the del-
      icate role played by knights in wielding power and maintaining
      justice, which — untempered by forgiveness and compassion for
      the weak — can sometimes lead to the cruelest oppression.
        Accompanied by a tutor, chaplain Jerome, the squires are
      presented with choices as to what kind of knights they want to
      become. The players must show their understanding of the laws
      of hospitality, the concept of Honor (which distinguishes no-
      bles from commoners), and the ambitious ideal of chivalry. The
      events call on their sense of justice and the Christian virtues of
      mercy and forgiveness. Finally, their relations with the peasants
      and the Church will be put to the test.
      Synopsis
        In the year 766, while Prince Charlemagne orders all knights
      of the Ardennes to hunt down a robber knight with a jewel set in
      his shield, the player squires are sent to the bishop in Liege. On
      the way back, they meet a pilgrim and are attacked by a band of
      desperate brigands. In a nearby village, they’ll be confronted with
      the suffering of the poor peasants. The local lord, Sir Eingar, is ar-
      rogant, cruel, and secretly a robber knight. He is not the one who
      has the jewel, but he does own a magic wolf-skin cape that allows
      him to take on the form of a wolf at night. Do the player squires
      take sides with the lord, the peasants, or with no one at all? And
      can they uncover the mystery of the Wolf Cloak?
      The Quest of the Jewel
        Monday, the 15th day of the month of April, anno 766.
      While King Pepin has called on the army to continue his war
      against Aquitaine, Prince Charlemagne comes to the castle of La
      Roche to hold his spring court. He is welcomed by his friend,
      Lord Thierry, who tells him of a mysterious robber knight hid-
      ing somewhere in the Ardennes Forest, who can be identified by
      a priceless jewel set in his shield.
        Hearing this news, the prince calls the bravest men from the
      duchy together, and bids them sally forth separately, with only a
      page as escort, in quest of the knight. Once found, they are to
      challenge him in true knightly fashion, and win the jewel he so
      arrogantly wears. Successful or not, the courtiers are to return in
      a month to give a truthful account of their adventures while on
      the quest.
        All the knights depart and scour the Ardennes Forest, each
      hoping to meet the robber knight and win the jewel. Among

them is Prince Charlemagne’s brother-in-law, Sir Milo, accom-
  panied by his 16 year-old son, Roland, who serves as his squire.
  The  Squire’s Mission

While the Ardennes knights are roaming the forest in search
  of the robber knight and his fabled jewel, the Player-knights are
  commanded by Lord Thierry — who is now desperately short of
  household knights — to accompany their old chaplain, Jerome,
  to Liege, to pick up the reliquary of Saint Marcian, which Bishop
  Fulcaire of Liege has agreed to loan him.
     A successful Religion roll allows the players to know more
  about Saint Marcian (see the nearby box), while Intrigue gives
  them a hint about why Lord Thierry wants this particular relic:
  to end the plague of wolves in the Ardennes. On a critical suc-
  cess, the character has spoken to a forester who says he wounded
  an unusually large wolf last month (this was Sir Eingar in wolf
  shape; the knight still bears the unhealed scars on his left arm).
     Have the players make a list of the things they carry, the
  horses they have taken, the money and food supplies they have
  with them. They should describe the route they plan on taking,
  as well as their travel speed and possibly other routines (camp
  procedures, marching order).
     The adventure begins after they have retrieved the reliquary
  from Liege, and are on their way back.
  A  Strange Pilgrim
     The player squires travel on a forest track in the northern
  part of the Ardennes Forest, near where the Ourthe joins the
  Amblève. It’s only half a day since they left Liege; they are still on
  the lands of the prince-bishop. They meet a dirty pilgrim com-
  ing from the opposite direction. He has a walking a stick and
  carries a small bag on his back. He politely asks the gentle sirs
  for alms, and tells them he is waiting for a friend, with whom he
  wishes to visit the abbey of Saint Hubert.
Saint Marcian’s Relic

Saint Marcian was a fugitive Visigoth who lived at the
   abbey of Merille near Auxerre. He had a strange power over
   animals: birds flocked to his hands, bears and wolves departed
   at his command, and once a boar fled to him for protection
   from hunters. His feast day is April 20th.
      The relic the players are carrying consists of some hair
   and a finger bone set in a golden necklace, which is itself kept
   in a small silver reliquary box studded with small gems (total
   worth approximately 20 £.).
      Anyone praying to Saint Marcian’s relic to pacify wild
   animals may do so at +5 to their Love [Charlemagne]. In this
   particular adventure, a successful prayer gives Sir Eingar a –5
   to all actions against the Player-knights.

leftColumn:
After receiving his alms (the players must all check Selfish
      if no-one gives anything), he thanks the Player-knights and vol-
      untarily shares some information about a small hunting cabin
      where they can spend the night, as he did. It is situated near the
      village of Esneux. Then he sits down in the grass and bids the
      Player-knights farewell.
      Brigands!

        An hour after the encounter with the pilgrim, the track
      on the east bank of the Ourthe leads away from the river into
      the dense forest. The squires may dismount and look for a bet-
      ter track, or try to determine which way to continue east (roll
      Hunting). If they do so, they discover some unusual tracks from
      a big lone wolf.
        All of a sudden, they are ambushed by a band of poor brig-
      ands armed with knives and clubs (they are exiled peasants, and
      the false pilgrim is among them).
        Half of the brigands pretend to attack from the front, while
      two or three others sneak up from the back (roll Awareness to see
      if anyone spots them). Their aim is not to fight, but to create con-
      fusion and steal a horse or some luggage before fleeing under the
      cover of arrows fired by their comrades hidden in the trees on the
      other side of the river. As soon as any brigand is seriously wounded
      (i.e. when he takes a Major Wound, or loses half or more of his Hit
      Points), they all flee, crossing the river at a nearby ford.
        The Player-knights have no trouble in following their
      tracks leading to the ford, but once inside the forest a normal
      hunt must be played out, should the Player-knights pursue the
      brigands.
        After the brigands’ attack, the Player-knights may continue
      their way, either by the eastern forest track or by following the
      river north (roll once on the Hunting Obstacles table). Either way,
      they find themselves blocked by a large stretch of flooded forest

  and six feet deep in the middle. A bit further downstream is a
  large single oak standing on a small bushy island. Roll Awareness
  to see if the Player-knights spot the bearded man who is hiding
  in the bushes.
     The Player-knights may either continue to the island, or try
  to find their way to Esneux through the forest.
  The  Hermit of the Isle

     If the characters decide to go to the island, they are wel-
  comed by a soft-voiced hermit (who may be a canon character
  in disguise, if the Gamemaster so wishes). As he shows them to
  his humble wooden hut, they pass a dolmen (an ancient stone
  structure). He shares his meager vegetarian meal with them (and
  their prisoners, if any) and can talk about any religious, spiritual
  or poetic subject (roll for the appropriate skill). He refuses to
  give any information about himself, not even his name, but he is
  very interested in the player squires’ stories.
     If asked, he will pray for them (they may roll Love [God] to
  benefit from his prayers) and try his healing skills (First Aid and
  Chirurgery 15) on any wounded character.
     All he can say about the brigands is that, if they attacked a
  band of armed squires in broad daylight, those poor men must
  have been pretty desperate. He prays for their souls, especially
  for the dead, if any. Any character who spontaneously suggested
  this to the hermit earns a Love [God] check.
     At nightfall, he invites his guests to lie down inside, while
  he himself insists on sleeping in a muddy hole near the dolmen.
     Any respectful efforts to please the hermit, like sharing
  some hearty food, giving him warm dry clothes, or proposing
  to let him sleep in the hut in the character’s stead, should be re-
  warded with an appropriate trait check, but are refused.
  The  Dream of the Desperate Sheep
     During the night, Player-knights who roll Love
  [Charlemagne] have a very weird dream: they are shepherd dogs
  keeping guard over a flock of sheep in a light forest. Suddenly,
  one large black dog goes mad and attacks the grazing sheep, bit-
  ing them until they bleed heavily. The shepherd is standing with
  his back to the flock, fighting off a pack of wolves. The dream
  ends abruptly.

  hermit of sorcery. They claim the hermit has cursed the river: it is
  running dry a few miles downstream, depriving the mill of water.

  either flee (if the Player-knights behave aggressively), or calm
  down (if they take the hermit’s defense and propose to sort
  things out).

  leave, cursing the sorcerer and his devil-men! Only the village

title: The Beaver Dam
leftColumn:
priest, Father Aigulf, stays to talk to the Player-knights, but he
      obstinately refuses to wade to the island — he makes a cross over
      his chest as he talks about the little island.
        If the characters have not yet met the hermit, the villagers
      lead them to the island, where they prudently post themselves
      on the eastern bank to “back up the heroes” while they confront
      the “sorcerer.”
      The Beaver  Dam

        After a short investigation, the characters find that the
      cause of the down-stream drought is a newly-constructed bea-
      ver dam. The characters can easily destroy it. If a player wonders
      about possible negative consequences, he will realize the resul-
      tant flood may be dangerous to those who live near the river
      downstream. A successful Siege roll allows them to take down
      the dam without releasing a flood.
        The Player-knights are invited to the village.
      The Village of Esneux

        The village, a part of the holdings of the Bishopric of Liege,
      lies at the foot of a small hill in a bend of the river Ourthe. A
      manor on the hilltop is the home of Sir Eingar. The largest
      building in town is the water mill. If the squires released a flood
      when they destroyed the dam, it is currently in bad shape.
        The characters can learn several things here, some of which
      may need a successful Standing [commoners] roll to find out
      (+5 if the squires showed themselves particularly helpful, –5 if
      they hold any prisoners). Let the players ask the questions them-
      selves and answer accordingly, either as an appropriate villager or
      Father Aigulf, the local priest.
       n
        Sir Eingar: A vicious, cruel, unjust and savage man.
        If he were to die tomorrow, no one in the village
        would mourn him. Some villagers say he has a pact
        with the devil, even if he does occasionally attend
        mass. Strangely, he dislikes hunting and has no hunt-
        ing dogs. Critical: A few peasants accuse their lord of
        being a robber knight, who often goes out on noctur-
        nal escapades to who-knows-where.
       n
        A Jewel: Sir Eingar does not possess such a thing. Or if he
        does, nobody has ever seen it, nor heard about it. Eingar
        is unmarried and wears no jewelry, only simple clothes
        and his stinking black wolf cloak, even in summer.
       n
        Father Aigulf: A very wise and peaceful man; broth-
        er-in-law to, and hated by, Sir Eingar.
       n
        The Mill: The lord’s mill is the only one they’re al-
        lowed to use. Last year Sir Eingar had the local miller
        hanged and replaced with one of his own men.
       n
        The Brigands: Silence. There are no brigands here.
        Critical: They are exiled peasants from Esneux, most
        of them relatives of their hosts, actively sought by
        Sir Eingar.
rightColumn:
n
     The Hermit of the Isle: A strange and secretive char-
     acter, suspected by the priest of worshiping pagan
     gods on the ancient stone altar. The hermit is accused
     of witchcraft and animal sacrifices. Critical: Some vil-
     lagers sometimes pay him a visit and give him small
     gifts. In return he reads the stars (tells their future),
     cures children and blesses them.
   n
     Special Mass: If the Player-knights speak of Saint
     Marcian’s relic, Father Aigulf insists on celebrating
     a special mass for Saint Marcian. Afterwards, the
     guests are modestly feasted inside the church. On a
     successful Love [Charlemagne] roll, Sir Eingar is at
     –5 to all his rolls when trying to oppose or hurt that
     Player-knight.
   n
     The Wolves: The village itself has not suffered any
     wolf attacks, but some of the neighboring ham-
     lets were not so lucky. A newly-wed peasant from
     Ternières brought his two cows with him to Esneux,
     and they still bear the wounds of a wolf attack a
     month ago. If a player squire shows an interest, he is
     shown the cows. On a successful Hunting roll he real-
     izes that the wounds are from a particularly big wolf.
   n
     The Newly-Wed Servants: They were married last
     week, against the will of Sir Eingar. The man comes
     from a neighboring village called Ternières. Father
     Aigulf assured the village that “what is united by God
     cannot be separated by man.”
  Unwanted   Visitors
     A group of shouting men-at-arms come to claim a toll of
  2d per horsemen for crossing the river at the ford. If the players
  released a flood when they destroyed the beaver dam, they also
  demand 40d to pay for the mill; the wheel broke when the flash
  flood hit it. Since the peasants can’t pay, the knight’s men turn to
  the Player-knights.
     If the player squires pay for the mill, the peasants are most
  relieved. If not, the player squires lose their friendship: all subse-
  quent Standing [Commoners] rolls are temporarily at –5.
              Men-at-arms
      Four time the number of player squires.
      The soldiers are equipped with leather armor, a spear
   and a dagger. They serve their lord without asking questions.
   Their presence is usually enough to get what they want, and so
   they barely have any real combat skills.

priest, Father Aigulf, stays to talk to the Player-knights, but he
      obstinately refuses to wade to the island — he makes a cross over
      his chest as he talks about the little island.
        If the characters have not yet met the hermit, the villagers
      lead them to the island, where they prudently post themselves
      on the eastern bank to “back up the heroes” while they confront
      the “sorcerer.”
      The Beaver  Dam

After a short investigation, the characters find that the
      cause of the down-stream drought is a newly-constructed bea-
      ver dam. The characters can easily destroy it. If a player wonders
      about possible negative consequences, he will realize the resul-
      tant flood may be dangerous to those who live near the river
      downstream. A successful Siege roll allows them to take down
      the dam without releasing a flood.
        The Player-knights are invited to the village.
      The Village of Esneux

The village, a part of the holdings of the Bishopric of Liege,
      lies at the foot of a small hill in a bend of the river Ourthe. A
      manor on the hilltop is the home of Sir Eingar. The largest
      building in town is the water mill. If the squires released a flood
      when they destroyed the dam, it is currently in bad shape.
        The characters can learn several things here, some of which
      may need a successful Standing [commoners] roll to find out
      (+5 if the squires showed themselves particularly helpful, –5 if
      they hold any prisoners). Let the players ask the questions them-
      selves and answer accordingly, either as an appropriate villager or
      Father Aigulf, the local priest.
       n
        Sir Eingar: A vicious, cruel, unjust and savage man.
        If he were to die tomorrow, no one in the village
        would mourn him. Some villagers say he has a pact
        with the devil, even if he does occasionally attend
        mass. Strangely, he dislikes hunting and has no hunt-
        ing dogs. Critical: A few peasants accuse their lord of
        being a robber knight, who often goes out on noctur-
        nal escapades to who-knows-where.

     week, against the will of Sir Eingar. The man comes
     from a neighboring village called Ternières. Father
     Aigulf assured the village that “what is united by God
     cannot be separated by man.”
  Unwanted   Visitors
     A group of shouting men-at-arms come to claim a toll of
  2d per horsemen for crossing the river at the ford. If the players
  released a flood when they destroyed the beaver dam, they also
  demand 40d to pay for the mill; the wheel broke when the flash
  flood hit it. Since the peasants can’t pay, the knight’s men turn to
  the Player-knights.
     If the player squires pay for the mill, the peasants are most
  relieved. If not, the player squires lose their friendship: all subse-
  quent Standing [Commoners] rolls are temporarily at –5.

   and a dagger. They serve their lord without asking questions.
   Their presence is usually enough to get what they want, and so
   they barely have any real combat skills.

title: Manor Eingarstein
leftColumn:
As they leave, the soldiers roughly take a small pig from
      a peasant girl while the peasants stand by with clenched fists,
      grinding their teeth.
        The crowd in the village square suddenly turns silent as
      Sir Eingar himself arrives, wearing his black wolf-fur cloak. He
      enters the small wooden church. Even through the shut door,
      the characters can hear an argument between Eingar and Father
      Aigulf about the newlywed peasants.
        Coming out of the Church, Sir Eingar loudly vows never to
      separate the couple, even if the marriage took place against his
      will. He leaves the church and takes the servant couple with him.
      He invites the Player-knights to dine at the castle tonight, as the
      custom of hospitality dictates.
        If Sir Eingar spots any captured brigands, he thanks the
      squires for capturing “that filthy vermin.” He orders his men to
      seize them and immediately pronounces their sentence: they will
      be flayed alive tomorrow. He adds, with a nasty grin, that he will
      personally nail the brigands’ skins to the chapel door to set an
      example.

               Sir Eingar of Esneux
         Sir Eingar is a violent brute. He lives for his own sin-
       ful pleasures and delights in abusing his power and needless
       cruelty.
       Heraldry: A golden wolf’s head, with a red tongue and teeth,
         on a black field.
       Appearance: Tall and fat, with long dark hair and beard, an
         ugly face, and stinking breath. He always wears a black fur
         cloak (see “the Wolf Cloak”, below).
       SIZ 17, DEX 8, STR 13, CON 11, APP 6
       Damage: 5d6; Armor: 8 (wolf cloak) +6 (shield); Move 2
       Hit Points: 28, Major Wound 11, Unconscious 7, Knockdown
         17, Healing Rate 2
       Combat Skills: Axe 14, Dagger 12, Unarmed Combat 9
       Skills: Horsemanship 14
       Traits & Passions: Valorous 14; Arbitrary 16, Cruel 16,
         Deceitful 16, Proud 16, Suspicious 16, Vengeful 16
                 The Wolf Cloak
         Once per night, this magic wolf skin allows the wearer
       to take on the shape of a large wolf. As a wolf he may com-
       mand a pack of 20 wolves and communicate with them using
       very basic barks and howls. Thus changed, the wearer must
       return to human form before dawn, and may not laugh while
       in wolf shape [i.e. if a player laughs during the gaming session
       while his character is transformed], otherwise the wearer has
       to spend an entire moon cycle as a wolf.
       wolf statistics
       SIZ 10, DEX 22, STR 18, CON 14
       Damage: 3d6; Armor: 5; Move 8
       Hit Points: 24, Major Wound 14, Unconscious 6, Knockdown 10
       Combat Skills: Bite 20
rightColumn:
Manor   Eingarstein

     If the Player-knights accept his invitation, Sir Eingar wel-
  comes them at his castle as the noble members of famous fam-
  ilies they are. The food is ordinary but plenty, the two young
  serving wenches are evasive and silent.
     If they ask to see the newly-wed servant couple, Sir Eingar
  burst out in laughter. He takes them to a field just outside the
  castle and shows them two halves of a tree trunk tied together,
  lying in a freshly dug grave. The couple is bound in between the
  two hollowed-out logs, both apparently dead. If the characters
  untie the tree they find the man still breathing, but the woman
  is dead. Sir Eingar just laughs about his own cruel joke: he didn’t
  separate the young couple, quite on the contrary!
  Peasant  Revolt
     While the Player-knights are examining the grave, a mob
  of about 50 angry peasants wielding farm tools arrive. As soon
  as they see what has happened, the priest and his wife run to the
  semi-conscious servant and his dead spouse. He yells insults at
  Sir Eingar, who is still laughing.
     The male serf regains consciousness. He immediately gets
  up and tries to attack Sir Eingar, but is stabbed to death by a
  soldier. The peasants scream and hurl insults, but none move,
  thinking the Player-knights are on Sir Eingar’s side. The players
  may roll Folk Lore to realize this.
     Unless the Player-knights make it very clear that they aren’t
  supporting Sir Eingar, the peasants take the woman’s dead body
  and accompany their priest back to the village in grieving silence.
     On the other hand, if the Player-knights stand up for jus-
  tice, then a bunch of strong peasants move up to their unjust and
  cruel lord and menace him with their sickles and scythes. The
  player squires may now fight Sir Eingar. His footmen hold back
  the peasants and pay little attention to the player squires un-
  less directly challenged. Sir Eingar fights to the death. Though
  it may be more efficient, if the player squires band together to
  attack a single knight, this costs all involved 1 point of Honor.
     If the Player-knights defeat Sir Eingar, the remaining sol-
  diers flee and the peasants storm the castle to plunder it, unless
  the Player-knights prevent this.
     Sir Eingar’s treasury contains some beautiful but old tapes-
  tries (£6), skins and furs (£3), clothes (£3), weapons and armor
  (6 good swords, 10 daggers, 20 spears, 3 axes, 1 mace, 5 bows
  and arrows, 12 leather hauberks, 2 ring mail hauberks, a scale
  hauberk, for a total value of £5), a chest with silver coins (£10), a
  golden ring (£1) and some silver cutlery (£2).
     The peasants want to burn the dead body of their hated
  lord — and his wolf cloak with him.
  Conclusion

     Back at the castle of La Roche, Charlemagne, seated on his
  throne, bids all knights to appear before him and relate their ad-
  ventures. One knight after another strides up the hall, followed

title: Epilogue
leftColumn:
Glory Awards
       Per killed or wounded brigand: 1.
       Per captured brigand: 2.
       Successfully interpreted the dream: 10.
       Blessed by Saint Marcian’s relic: 20.

       Per defeated man-at-arms: 10.
       Defeated Sir Eingar: 50.
       Treasure donated to their lord: 1 per £.
       Gained the Wolf cloak: 50.
       Eloquent at court: Double all Glory gained in this adventure!
         Glory should be awarded for other actions which helped
       to advance the plot or which contributed to the fun during
       the game.
               Experience Awards
         Just: If the player accused Sir Eingar of being an un-
       worthy lord and challenged him to a duel, raise his score by
       a point. If he fought against Sir Eingar with the peasants, he
       gets a check.
         Merciful: If the Player-knight spares Sir Eingar when he
       could have killed him, he earns a check.
         Prudent: If a player prevented the flash flood, he gains
       a check.
         Honor: If a player appealed to this passion to justify his
       acts, check Honor. If he was Inspired by it, raise his score by
       one.
         Standing [commoners]: If the Player-knight chose the
       peasant’s side and paid for the mill, raise this score by one. If
       he did only one of the two, he earns a check.
         Standing [Church]: If he supported the priest in his
       action against Sir Eingar, and made a donation to the local
       church, a check is earned.
         Folk Lore: All player squires automatically gain a check.
         Hunting: For any useful piece of information gained by
       a successful Hunting roll, a player gains a check.
         Eloquence: Each Player-knight who captured Prince
       Charlemagne’s attention deserves a check.
         Intrigue: If they got useful information from the farm-
       ers of Esneux, they earn a check.

     Last of all comes Sir Milo. Roland is walking close behind
  him, proudly holding his father’s shield, in the center of which
  the jewel shines radiantly. Milo relates his search, and reports
  that he, too, found the giant knight slain and the jewel gone.
  Shouts of incredulity make him turn his head.
     When Milo sees the jewel blazing on his shield, he ap-
  pears so amazed that Prince Charlemagne questions Roland,
  who tells the court how he himself obtained it in a fair com-
  bat. Charlemagne and Duke Thierry are delighted, and praise
  Roland for his outstanding skill and bravery.
     Now is time for the player squires to tell their story. Each
  player must roll Eloquence to draw the crowd’s attention, as
  most knights present are now talking about Roland’s exploits.
     Depending on their adventure’s outcome, Prince Charlemagne
  and Lord Thierry congratulate or rebuke the player squires.
  Epilogue

     Now what happens? What are the possible consequences of
  this adventure?
     If Sir Eingar was defeated and killed by the Player-knights,
  a new Lord of Esnaux must be installed (if Eingar survived, he is
  sent to the monastery of Lobbes to finish his days in the service
  of God). If the character who slew Sir Eingar successfully rolls
  Standing [lord], one of his older family knights will be granted
  the manor and castle of Esneux. Otherwise, Duke Thierry sim-
  ply rewards one of his faithful household knights. In either case,
  Bishop Fulcaire objects and wants to “recover” what he consid-
  ers to be an ecclesiastical manor.
     Less easy to mollify are Sir Eingar’s family members, who
  will certainly seek vengeance, demanding a compensation equal
  to his heribannum, or even start a feud against the killer’s family.
  The total family strength of Eingar’s clan is 15 knights. They are
  friends with the clan of Mayence and descend indirectly from
  Prince Grifo, Charles Martel’s illegitimate brother.
     Remind the players that they should donate half of their
  treasure to their lord. Otherwise, lower their Honor and their
  Standing [lord] scores by one point immediately.

title: The Adventure of the Humble Squires
headings: The Adventure of the Humble Squires
leftColumn:
The   Adventure    of th

      W
          itness the birth of the chivalric order of paladins!
             This scenario is meant to be the first important
          adventure in the world of Charlemagne — maybe after
      some shorter adventures, such as the Adventure of the Jewel, in
      which the characters were introduced to the rules and the game
      world. The scenario is written to help you to get your campaign
      going and see the player characters knighted.
        The story contains all sorts of knightly events: a journey
      across the Alps, a short hunt, battles and skirmishes, some court-
      ly encounters, and a fair bit of intriguing and romancing. All
      in all, it will probably take two sessions to complete the whole
      adventure.
      Gamemaster   Goals
        This first major adventure should be used in the first place
      to introduce the main characters: Charlemagne himself, his
      court, Duke Naymo and Archbishop Turpin, and future pala-
      dins like Ogier, Roland (age 17), Oliver (age 17) and Renaud
      (age 14), who are all yet but squires at the royal court.
        The basic passions and ideals such as Love [Charlemagne],
      Honor, and Love [God] will be illustrated. Much of what it is
      to behave in a knightly, chivalric and courteous fashion will be
      shown — not only by the Frankish characters, but also by their
      main antagonists, the Saracens and Persians.
        The paragons of chivalry are the paladins, but who are they
      really? The players will personally witness the creation of the
      chivalric order by Prince Charlemagne himself. At the same cer-
      emony, the attending player squires will be dubbed as knights.
        As a Gamemaster, you should familiarize yourself with the
      most important rules, specifically the hunting and skirmish sys-
      tems. After a short hunt at the beginning of the adventure, you
      will have to run a small battle — one of the major events in any
      knight’s career!
        Finally, this adventure contains a minimum of subtle reli-
      gious magic, like the white deer sent by God, prophetic dreams,
      and divine signs during the battle.
      Synopsis

        Anno 767. After the death of Pope Paul I, Rome is besieged
      by an alliance of Duke Toto of Nepi, the Saracen Emir Agolant
      and his son Aumont, and a Danish pirate called Danemont.
      Sultan Corsuble sends his son, Balan, to demand fealty from
      Charlemagne, who naturally refuses. To prevent the infidels
      from capturing Rome, Charlemagne travels across the Alps with
      his army and joins his Lombard allies.
        In a first battle near Rome (the Battle of the Humble Squires),
      the Lombards flee and Charlemagne’s army is almost routed.
      But some valorous Frankish squires, led by Ogier the Dane, seize
      the Oriflamme and turn the tide of battle. The Saracens flee in
      panic and Duke Toto is killed. A new Pope is elected, and the
rightColumn:
the Humble    Squires

  heroic squires are knighted by prince Charlemagne, who creates
  the Order of Paladins at the same time.
     Gerard of Vienne and Prince Carloman arrive at the Eternal
  City. Eager to prove themselves and to accumulate Glory, they
  give pursuit to the retreating Saracens. In a second battle near
  Mount Bitter they defeat Aumont, who refuses to call for help.
  Roland kills him and claims his equipment, including Durendal,
  Veillantif, and Oliphant.
     A week later, a courteous Persian emir named Carahue, dis-
  guised as a herald, comes to the Frankish court at Rome and issues
  chivalric challenges against the Franks. Ogier accepts Carahue’s
  challenge, while Carloman will fight Sadon. Unfortunately, the
  treacherous Danemont interferes and Ogier gets captured while
  Carloman escapes. Ogier is imprisoned in Aumont’s Tower and
  guarded by the gentle Princess Floripas.
     Duke Naymo attempts to climb Mount Bitter with a small
  band of knights, in an foolhardy attempt to deliver Ogier from
  the Saracens, but his mission fails miserably.
     An outraged Carahue offers himself as a hostage to
  Charlemagne to be exchanged for Ogier, whose liberation he
  ardently desires. Finally, both parties agree to settle the issue of
  the prisoners by a duel, in which Ogier kills his rival Danemont.
  The pagans leave Rome.
  Crossing  the Alps
     Your lord, Duke Thierry of Ardennes, receives the annual
  call to arms, so you travel to the May Field in Burgundy. While
  King Pepin takes his army to the south on a campaign against the
  Aquitainians, Lord Thierry has been ordered to stay with Prince
  Charlemagne and Prince Carloman’s men.
     A debate is raging in the royal council: some want to exe-
  cute the half-giant, Ogier the Dane, a hostage for his treacher-
  ous father. His guardian, Count Ganelon of Ponthieu, insists on
  implacable retaliation, for the Danes apparently insulted some
  royal messengers and renounced their oaths of fealty.
     Just as the passionate discussion between counts and
  dukes threatens to get out of hand, two exhausted messengers,
  a Lombard and a Roman, arrive at the Frankish camp, shouting
  the horrible news of what is going on in Rome:
    “The Duke of Nepi has allied with the Saracens. The pa-
    gans have landed near Rome and occupy Mount Janicu-
    lum, and these dogs prepare to cross the Tiber and carry
    fire and sword into the capital of the Christian world
    as we speak! They have even installed a false Pope! To
    arms! Liberate the Eternal City from these foul infidels
    and honorless renegades!”
     You may ask for Intrigue rolls to see who realizes that Pepin
  and his sons, Charlemagne and Carloman, are official Patriarchs
  of Rome, and are therefore compelled to assist the Pope.

title: The Adventure of the Humble Squires
leftColumn:
The Pagans
         Agolant: The emir of Babylon is a cruel but valorous
       warrior, though slightly naive. He is the father of Aumont,
       Troiano, and Galaciella (the mother of Rogero and Marfisa).
       He commands the Saracen troops at the Battle of Aspremont,
       where he dies at his son’s side.
         Aumont: Agolant’s son is a noble and chivalrous
       prince, but fatally proud. He is killed by Roland at the Battle
       of Aspremont, who takes his horn, his helmet, the horse
       Veillantif, and the sword Durendal.
         Balan: Corsuble’s son is a an honorable and even chiv-
       alrous prince. His war banner is “de pourpre aux trois lions
       d’or” (three golden lions on a purple field). The handsome,
       eloquent Balan is a very tall and strong warrior.
         Carahue: A chivalrous emir from Persia, engaged to
       Princess Gloriande. This skilled and agile knight possesses a
       magic sword, Courtain, which he gives to Ogier as a sign of his
       high esteem. To satisfy his curiosity (he wants to see the reput-
       ed Frankish court), he even disguises himself as a messenger.
         Corsuble: The old, wily Sultan of Babylon is the father
       of Prince Balan and Princess Gloriande. He is said to eat ser-
       pents fried in oil, and to occasionally kill foreign messengers.
         Danemont: This proud Danish half-giant prince is a
       wicked man. Exiled from Denmark, and Ogier’s rival for
       the Danish throne, he has become an ally of the Saracens,
       whom he furnishes with fast ships. Danemont is the owner of
       Broiefort, a large, strong warhorse, which Sir Ogier acquires
       after defeating him in a duel.
         Floripas: Balan’s daughter is an extremely beautiful and
       willful young princess. Her heart is set on Guy of Burgundy.
         Gloriande: Corsuble’s daughter is a gorgeous and cour-
       teous princess. She engaged to the courteous Carahue of
       Persia, but the evil Danemont dreams of marrying her.
         Gorhant: Balan’s son acts as Agolant’s seneschal. The
       handsome youth is generous and valorous, and secretly in love

  [God]. The most successful player squire sees a white deer

title: The Lombard Alliance
leftColumn:
The White Deer
       Movement 10
       Skills: Avoidance 39
         This magic animal is sent by God to put Charlemagne’s
       men back on track and guide them safely through the Alps.

        The character who first finds the White Deer, but doesn’t
      attack it, realizes that he is gazing over a green plain below him:
      he found a hidden pass through the mountains! If no character
      succeeds in this mini-quest, a major character does so in their
      stead. It is relatively easy to find the tracks back to the army
      (Hunting +12) and to clearly mark the precious path.
      “Where have you been, wretched knaves?”

        Once they get back to the main army, they are hailed by a
      furious Lord Thierry:
        “You miserable and honorless rats! My men are looking for
      you everywhere! Where have you been, wretched knaves — by the
      bones of Saint Boniface, tell me why I shouldn’t hang deserters like
      you!” Let the characters explain where they have been, but don’t
rightColumn:

  lord. When it finally dawns on Thierry that his squires discov-

title: The Battle of the Humble Squires
headings: The Battle of the Humble Squires
leftColumn:
table 19–2: ruMors
      1d6 Result Rumor
        1   The Enemy: The wicked Duke Toto of Nepi and his
            Saracen ally, the savage Sultan Corsuble, have been fight-
            ing Duke Gregory of Campania, who was cruelly execut-
            ed after a disastrous battle. The evil Sultan is known to
            eat fried serpents, and to serve his prisoners to his men
            for dinner!
        2   The Siege of Rome: The pagans have already plundered
            the city and taken the holy relics from the cathedral: the
            crown of thorns, the nails from the cross and the holy oil!
            Their army, including a fearsome giant, surrounds the
            Lateran Palace, where the last defenders have retreated.
        3   The new Pope: He is an illiterate imposter put on the
            Holy See by his own brother, the renegade Duke Toto!
        4   Prince Carloman: Where is Charlemagne’s brother?
            He was supposed to come along, wasn’t he? He probably
            got stuck in the Alps. Or did his tutor Gerard take the
            northern road?
        5   The Lombards: King Desiderius is actively trying
            to find a suitable husband for two of his gorgeous
            daughters, Desideria and Gerberga. Apparently, Prince
            Carloman and Ogier the Dane are both very interested!
        6   The Lombard Army: The allied Lombards are led by
            Sir Alory of Biterna, a cousin of the late Pope. God is
            on our side!
      The Calm Before the Storm
        Apart from gaining information, the Player-squires may
      try to heal (on Sunday, the last day of their stay), or engage in a
      courtly activity if they came through the Alps unscathed.
        The next day, a Lombard and a Frankish herald make the
      following announcement:
        “Hear, hear, soldiers of the True Faith, defenders of
      Christianity! The pagans have killed the Pope and plundered the
      Papal Palace. We march in haste against the sacrilegious hounds!”
      Without waiting for Prince Carloman and his Burgundian
      troops, Charlemagne’s army marches to Rome and camps on the
      hills just outside the city. From there, one may observe a Saracen
      camp on a hill south of the city. Both sides prepare for battle.
        Maybe some squires will be knighted tomorrow on the field
      of honor, who knows?
      The Battle of the Humble Squires
        The next day, as the early mists dissipate and the battlefield
      in the valley becomes visible, so does the Saracen camp on the
      opposite hills with its numerous waving green banners. Roll
      Battle to see how the characters evaluate the military situation.
      Critical: The pagan baggage camp is virtually undefended. A
      sweeping attack from the hills behind Mount Janiculum would
      be devastating! Success: The Saracens have a large numerical su-
      periority, so it is going to be a tough battle. Much depends on
      which side is able to maintain itself on the hilltops. Failure: Why
      do we need the Lombards to kill off this pagan rabble? Fumble:
      Their camp is impossible to conquer with the small army we
      have. It would be wiser to retreat and negotiate!
rightColumn:
During a short religious ceremony, Archbishop Turpin
  blesses the army. All characters who succeed with a Love [God]
  roll are at +1 to all die rolls for the duration of the battle (+2
  on a critical; –1 on a fumble). If a player remarks that his char-
  acter isn’t going to benefit from this battle bonus, since his
  character is unlikely to participate in the battle at all, comfort
  him in this idea.
     Prince Charlemagne gives the honor of carrying the
  Frankish battle standard, the Oriflamme, to Sir Alory, the leader
  of the Lombards.
  May the Best Army Win
     Lord Thierry raises his black and white banner and moves
  to the front of the vanguard, led by Duke Naymo. The squires
  are sent back to guard the baggage train. Tell the players: “You
  can hear the battle cries (“Monjoie! Saint Denis!”) as you retire
  to the wooded hill where Charlemagne’s camp is situated, and
  you actually have quite a good view of the battlefield.”
     On the first charge the Saracens use devastating lance
  charges, a relatively new technique!
     Quite a lot of other noble squires are hanging around (Ogier,
  Roland, Renaud, Oliver, and Guy, for example), commenting
  the battle, cheering every successful Frankish or Lombard charge
  and cursing at each counter-attack. The giant Ogier is grum-
  bling, very displeased at not being allowed to participate.
     Let the players roll Battle or Intrigue to catch specific news
  about how the fight is going, or how their lord is doing (make
  this news up as you go). At some point, Duke Thierry comes
  riding into the camp. While they take care of him — he urgently
  needs a new shield (roll Awareness) and medical care (roll First
  Aid) — he gives some disconcerting news: Count Anquetin of
  Normandy and Count Guydelon the Elder have both been cap-
  tured by an unknown demi-giant knight. Roll Heraldry at –5 to
  recognize Danemont’s banner.
  Alory the Coward
     The battle has been going on for a few hours; it is now
  early in the afternoon. The squires can see how all of a sudden
  the Frankish standard (the Oriflamme) turns around and flees
  from the field, together with a large part of the Lombard army!
  A few minutes later Charlemagne’s personal banner falls to the
  ground, as does the Frankish prince himself. He is almost en-
  tirely surrounded by Saracen warriors — only Duke Naymo and
  Archbishop Turpin are by his side (roll Heraldry +10 to identify
  them). Give the players some time to react individually before
  continuing.
     The squires, and Ogier especially, hurl insults at the faith-
  less and cowardly Lombards, whom they can see coming their
  way as they return to the camp. The huge Alory — still holding
  the Oriflamme — addresses the squires in a panicked voice:
     “Alas! King Charlemagne has fallen and most of his men are
  dead — it would be better to retire and negotiate a treaty, while we
  still have the chance to do so!” This is too much for Ogier, who
  seizes a wooden club and runs towards Alory, whom he insults
