table 19–2: ruMors
      1d6 Result Rumor
        1   The Enemy: The wicked Duke Toto of Nepi and his
            Saracen ally, the savage Sultan Corsuble, have been fight-
            ing Duke Gregory of Campania, who was cruelly execut-
            ed after a disastrous battle. The evil Sultan is known to
            eat fried serpents, and to serve his prisoners to his men
            for dinner!
        2   The Siege of Rome: The pagans have already plundered
            the city and taken the holy relics from the cathedral: the
            crown of thorns, the nails from the cross and the holy oil!
            Their army, including a fearsome giant, surrounds the
            Lateran Palace, where the last defenders have retreated.
        3   The new Pope: He is an illiterate imposter put on the
            Holy See by his own brother, the renegade Duke Toto!
        4   Prince Carloman: Where is Charlemagne’s brother?
            He was supposed to come along, wasn’t he? He probably
            got stuck in the Alps. Or did his tutor Gerard take the
            northern road?
        5   The Lombards: King Desiderius is actively trying
            to find a suitable husband for two of his gorgeous
            daughters, Desideria and Gerberga. Apparently, Prince
            Carloman and Ogier the Dane are both very interested!
        6   The Lombard Army: The allied Lombards are led by
            Sir Alory of Biterna, a cousin of the late Pope. God is
            on our side!
      The Calm Before the Storm
        Apart from gaining information, the Player-squires may
      try to heal (on Sunday, the last day of their stay), or engage in a
      courtly activity if they came through the Alps unscathed.
        The next day, a Lombard and a Frankish herald make the
      following announcement:
        “Hear, hear, soldiers of the True Faith, defenders of
      Christianity! The pagans have killed the Pope and plundered the
      Papal Palace. We march in haste against the sacrilegious hounds!”
      Without waiting for Prince Carloman and his Burgundian
      troops, Charlemagne’s army marches to Rome and camps on the
      hills just outside the city. From there, one may observe a Saracen
      camp on a hill south of the city. Both sides prepare for battle.
        Maybe some squires will be knighted tomorrow on the field
      of honor, who knows?
      The Battle of the Humble Squires
        The next day, as the early mists dissipate and the battlefield
      in the valley becomes visible, so does the Saracen camp on the
      opposite hills with its numerous waving green banners. Roll
      Battle to see how the characters evaluate the military situation.
      Critical: The pagan baggage camp is virtually undefended. A
      sweeping attack from the hills behind Mount Janiculum would
      be devastating! Success: The Saracens have a large numerical su-
      periority, so it is going to be a tough battle. Much depends on
      which side is able to maintain itself on the hilltops. Failure: Why
      do we need the Lombards to kill off this pagan rabble? Fumble:
      Their camp is impossible to conquer with the small army we
      have. It would be wiser to retreat and negotiate!

During a short religious ceremony, Archbishop Turpin
  blesses the army. All characters who succeed with a Love [God]
  roll are at +1 to all die rolls for the duration of the battle (+2
  on a critical; –1 on a fumble). If a player remarks that his char-
  acter isn’t going to benefit from this battle bonus, since his
  character is unlikely to participate in the battle at all, comfort
  him in this idea.
     Prince Charlemagne gives the honor of carrying the
  Frankish battle standard, the Oriflamme, to Sir Alory, the leader
  of the Lombards.
  May the Best Army Win
     Lord Thierry raises his black and white banner and moves
  to the front of the vanguard, led by Duke Naymo. The squires
  are sent back to guard the baggage train. Tell the players: “You
  can hear the battle cries (“Monjoie! Saint Denis!”) as you retire
  to the wooded hill where Charlemagne’s camp is situated, and
  you actually have quite a good view of the battlefield.”
     On the first charge the Saracens use devastating lance
  charges, a relatively new technique!
     Quite a lot of other noble squires are hanging around (Ogier,
  Roland, Renaud, Oliver, and Guy, for example), commenting
  the battle, cheering every successful Frankish or Lombard charge
  and cursing at each counter-attack. The giant Ogier is grum-
  bling, very displeased at not being allowed to participate.
     Let the players roll Battle or Intrigue to catch specific news
  about how the fight is going, or how their lord is doing (make
  this news up as you go). At some point, Duke Thierry comes
  riding into the camp. While they take care of him — he urgently
  needs a new shield (roll Awareness) and medical care (roll First
  Aid) — he gives some disconcerting news: Count Anquetin of
  Normandy and Count Guydelon the Elder have both been cap-
  tured by an unknown demi-giant knight. Roll Heraldry at –5 to
  recognize Danemont’s banner.
  Alory the Coward
     The battle has been going on for a few hours; it is now
  early in the afternoon. The squires can see how all of a sudden
  the Frankish standard (the Oriflamme) turns around and flees
  from the field, together with a large part of the Lombard army!
  A few minutes later Charlemagne’s personal banner falls to the
  ground, as does the Frankish prince himself. He is almost en-
  tirely surrounded by Saracen warriors — only Duke Naymo and
  Archbishop Turpin are by his side (roll Heraldry +10 to identify
  them). Give the players some time to react individually before
  continuing.
     The squires, and Ogier especially, hurl insults at the faith-
  less and cowardly Lombards, whom they can see coming their
  way as they return to the camp. The huge Alory — still holding
  the Oriflamme — addresses the squires in a panicked voice:
     “Alas! King Charlemagne has fallen and most of his men are
  dead — it would be better to retire and negotiate a treaty, while we
  still have the chance to do so!” This is too much for Ogier, who
  seizes a wooden club and runs towards Alory, whom he insults

table 19–3: raNdo
            1d20 Result Opponent(s) Skill
              1–4   Wounded Saracens Spear 5
              5–8   Wounded Danes Axe 5
             9–12   Fleeing Saracens Sword 10

             13–14  Berserker Danes 2-Handed Axe 30
             15–18  Saracen knights Sword 15, Lance
              19    A Saracen giant Tree trunk 20
              20    A Saracen leader Lance 22, Sword

      before unhorsing him with a single blow. He takes the royal stan-
      dard and Alory’s armor, gets onto a horse, and in a loud ringing
      voice he urges all squires to follow him:
        “We must prepare for battle in this hour of need, for our
      prince has fallen and is surrounded by enemies. We shall have but
      one thing in mind: hit hard on the pagans and redden our arms
      up to our shoulders in their blood! Follow me! Never shall we let
      Charlemagne fall into the hands of these Infidels. Monjoie!” Most
      of the squires look at each other in surprise. No one dares to stop
      the massive Dane, and a few [Recognize: Roland, Renaud and
      Oliver are among them] even arm themselves in found armor
      and get on their horses as well!
      The Squires Attack
        What do the player squires do? Some players may wish to
      roll Honor against Love [Charlemagne], or some other traits
      or passions. Players who enter combat without hesitation get
      Valorous and Reckless checks. Those who think of putting on
      appropriate armor first receive checks in Valorous and Prudent.
        Remind the players that squires are not allowed to fight
      with swords. Inform them that doing so warrants the loss of a
      point of Honor. Ogier, for example, has taken a huge club.
        Some player squires may wish not to participate in the
      fight, as they might be afraid to stain their Honor by disobeying
      military orders (they were ordered to defend the camp and take
      care of knights returning from the field). These squires won’t be
      knighted after the battle, but will receive their swords and spurs
      at a later date, at the Gamemaster’s discretion. Alternatively, you
      may have them roll Love [God] and, if successful, give them a
      divine sign which makes it clear that God himself desires them
      to follow Ogier and fight the pagans.
        All Player-squires entering the battle should now choose a
      standard bearer for their unit, probably best if it’s the character
      with the highest Battle skill. This leader should try to rally as
      many squires to his banner as possible: roll Eloquence and, if
      successful, add the number rolled as followers.
        Ogier acts as the squires’ battalion commander — and since
      he is holding the Oriflamme, he automatically succeeds at all his
      Battle rolls. Play out 5 battle rounds using the system on page 140.
      The unit leader’s Battle roll is at +5 (surprise bonus) for the first
      round, plus any follower bonuses. Use Table 19–3: Random Battle
      Enemy, above, to determine the opponents’ skill and group size.

  squire’s battle rouNd 1 (+5 battle)
     The Player-squires’ unit enters the fray, taking the Saracens
  by surprise. Take some time, though, to describe the deafening
  sound of whinnying horses, screaming and crying men; the odor
  of sweat and blood; the sight of chaos and slaughter; the feeling
  of excitement and fear as they strike left and right, and maybe get
  hurt themselves as well.
  squire’s battle rouNd 2 (+0 battle)

     The Player-squires’ unit has approached the center of the
  battle field, near to where Prince Charlemagne has remounted
  and is desperately resisting the Saracen hordes. They arrive at the
  flank and penetrate the thick of the melee. To effectively come to
  the Prince’s help, the player squires’ unit leader must successfully
  roll Battle. If he fails, only individual characters may help their
  prince (check Reckless and Valorous).
     Any character defending Lord Charlemagne may roll
  Awareness. If successful, he sees a Saracen trying to slay
  Charlemagne’s warhorse with a dagger, while another is at-
  tempting to stab the prince in the back. The Player-squire may
  now chose to ignore his own opponent and attack one of the
  treacherous Saracens. Preventing a Saracen from stabbing the
  king gains the successful Player-squire 100 Glory, a check to
  Love [Charlemagne] and +1 Standing [Charlemagne]. If a sec-
  ond player manages to save Charlemagne’s horse, it is worth 50
  Glory and a check to Standing [Charlemagne].
     Despite their help, Lord Charlemagne is in a bad position.
  He falls from his horse and is calling out for a new one. Only
  superior chargers can carry the huge prince. To offer him such
  a steed, an unengaged character (or a character ignoring his op-
  ponent and thus granting the enemy an unopposed attack roll)
  needs successful rolls in Awareness and Horsemanship. This
  act earns 100 Glory, a check to Love [Charlemagne] and +1 to
  Standing [Charlemagne].
     Prince Charlemagne has also dropped his sword, Joyeuse.
  A successful Awareness roll reveals its location. Again, to in-
  tervene a player squire must ignore his opponent, if any, and
  then roll DEX and Horsemanship to pick up the sacred sword
  from the ground. Handing Joyeuse back to Charlemagne earns
  50 Glory, and checks to Love [Charlemagne] and Standing
  [Charlemagne].

  non-combat rolls for the next week.

  half their Hit Points or with a Major Wound.

title: Chivalric Challenges
tables: Table 19-5: Battle of Mount Bitter Events
leftColumn:
The next morning, the young men are brought before the
      Frankish barons and Prince Charlemagne, wielding the blessed
      blade, Joyeuse. The knightings take place in reverse order of Glory
      precedence, so the player squires are probably asked to step forward
      first. Play out the knighting ceremony described in Chapter 1.
        The last squires to be knighted are Roland, Ogier (who re-
      ceives Alory’s white armor), and Oliver of Vienne.
        All new knights receive rich gifts from their sponsors: the
      new Player-knights each get one free roll on the Frankish Birth
      Gifts table (page 39).
      The Order of Paladins
        Then, to everybody’s surprise, Charlemagne announces the
      creation of the Chivalric Order of Paladins:
       One day King Charlemagne was sitting in his great hall
       amidst his vassals, and he told them: “By the grace of
       God, and if you agree to it, I would like to choose twelve
       worthy men to lead my palace guards in battle to con-
       front the pagans with courage.” They all replied favorably
       and asked him to accomplish his wish.
         So the prince declared: “I will name as paladins first
       my kinsman Roland, then Oliver, thirdly Turpin. (...) I
       place them at the head of my army to fight the pagans,
       in memory of the order God gave his twelve apostles to
       spread His word all around the world; and likewise shall
       each one of you bring aid and strength when danger is
       highest, as if you were all blood-brothers.” All accepted
       this mission gladly.
           — Karlamagnus Saga, 1.LIX
        The first generation of twelve peers are: Roland, Oliver,
      Turpin, Ogier, Guy of Burgundy, Odo of Lengres, Berenger the
      Gascon, Warin of Vergy, Samson of Brittany, Anseïs the Proud,
      Ivory the Foundling, and Yvo the Black.
        Briefly explain the ins and outs of paladinhood, possibly
      reading the paragraph dedicated to paladins in Chapter 13:
      Frankish Society.
      The Battle of Mount  Bitter

        After the victory ceremonies and numerous festivities,
      the army of Prince Carloman arrives at Rome. A surprised
      Charlemagne gently taunts his younger brother, who has the
      nerve to show up only after the Franks have already defeated
      the pagans! This mockery thoroughly vexes Count Gerard of
      Vienne, who came with Prince Carloman. The haughty count
      immediately decides to launch his men in the pursuit of the pa-
      gans, who have retreated and set up their camp in a stronghold
      on the other side of the Tiber, behind a snow-covered mountain
      called Mount Bitter.
        Together with a few others, Roland declares he will join this
      adventure, but most other Franks take leave of the army and pre-
      pare their homeward voyage.
        If the player squires wish to follow the hot-headed Gerard of
      Vienne on his punitive expedition, they need to get permission
rightColumn:
from Duke Thierry: Roll Standing [Lord] at –5; –10 if they
  are wounded. They may roll Battle to realize the reduced pagan
  army is fighting on favorable terrain (defending a hill fortress)
  and is at an advantage due to its capacity to move troops by boat
  along the coast.
     If necessary, play out the Battle of Mount Bitter using the
  Random Battle Enemy table above. However, the disadvanta-
  geous battlefield confers a –5 penalty to all unit commanders’
  Battle rolls.
   table 19–5: battle of MouNt bitter eveNts
   Round Events
    1  The Franks endure a volley of the Saracen archery: each
       knight receives 3 bow attacks at 15, doing 3d6 damage per
       arrow.
    2  The Saracens carry out a lance charge.
    3  Prince Carloman gets seriously injured by a Saracen giant.
       The Player-knight’s unit must cover the prince’s retreat while
       fighting the great Saracen leader, Agolant himself (treat as an
       automatic result of 20 on the Random Battle Enemy table).
    4  The Player-knights’ unit routs. All Player-knights must fight
       their opponents individually!
    5  Young Sir Roland slays the second Saracen leader, Aumont,
       and captures his sword (Durendal), horse (Veillantif) and
       horn (Oliphant).
     Roland’s glorious feat of arms brings the Franks an indeci-
  sive victory. They honorably retire from the field and return to
  Charlemagne’s camp.
  Chivalric Challenges
     Everything has been calm in Rome for a week or so, when a
  richly dressed herald arrives at the Frankish court. On a successful
  Recognize roll, a Player-knight realizes that the messenger wears
  Persian garb, not Saracen. In the name of the Saracen King Carahue
  of Mauritania (himself, actually!), the herald politely presents his
  lord’s glove to challenge the Frankish nobles to a courtly combat, as
  “my master wishes to prove his love for the lady of his heart.”
     Prince Charlemagne announces that: “Never does a knight
  of the Frankish court refuse a challenge on equal terms!” and asks
  who among his barons would like to defend Frankish honor.
     The young Carloman and Sir Ogier start bickering about who
  has the right to accept this challenge. The Dane first claims the
  fight with Sir Carahue, but Carloman officially states he will fight
  the Persian prince to defend the honor of Princess Gerberga. Roll
  Intrigue to see if a Player-knight is aware of the intense rivalry be-
  tween the two men, who are both courting the Lombard princess.
     At the end of the delicate negotiations, the following court-
  ly challenges are arranged: Prince Carahue of Mauritania to
  fight Sir Ogier, while Carahue’s nephew, Sir Sadon, fights Prince
  Carloman. Sir Sadon vows to fight without a shield, to compen-
  sate for Prince Carloman’s youth and inexperience.
     If some Player-knights wish to accept a challenge, they may
  confront a random Saracen or Persian knight. They should first
  ask their lord’s permission (roll Standing [lord]).

      adventure, but most other Franks take leave of the army and pre-
      pare their homeward voyage.
        If the player squires wish to follow the hot-headed Gerard of
      Vienne on his punitive expedition, they need to get permission

from Duke Thierry: Roll Standing [Lord] at –5; –10 if they
  are wounded. They may roll Battle to realize the reduced pagan
  army is fighting on favorable terrain (defending a hill fortress)
  and is at an advantage due to its capacity to move troops by boat
  along the coast.
     If necessary, play out the Battle of Mount Bitter using the
  Random Battle Enemy table above. However, the disadvanta-
  geous battlefield confers a –5 penalty to all unit commanders’
  Battle rolls.
   table 19–5: battle of MouNt bitter eveNts
   Round Events
    1  The Franks endure a volley of the Saracen archery: each
       knight receives 3 bow attacks at 15, doing 3d6 damage per
       arrow.
    2  The Saracens carry out a lance charge.
    3  Prince Carloman gets seriously injured by a Saracen giant.
       The Player-knight’s unit must cover the prince’s retreat while
       fighting the great Saracen leader, Agolant himself (treat as an
       automatic result of 20 on the Random Battle Enemy table).
    4  The Player-knights’ unit routs. All Player-knights must fight
       their opponents individually!
    5  Young Sir Roland slays the second Saracen leader, Aumont,
       and captures his sword (Durendal), horse (Veillantif) and
       horn (Oliphant).
     Roland’s glorious feat of arms brings the Franks an indeci-
  sive victory. They honorably retire from the field and return to
  Charlemagne’s camp.
  Chivalric Challenges
     Everything has been calm in Rome for a week or so, when a
  richly dressed herald arrives at the Frankish court. On a successful
  Recognize roll, a Player-knight realizes that the messenger wears
  Persian garb, not Saracen. In the name of the Saracen King Carahue
  of Mauritania (himself, actually!), the herald politely presents his
  lord’s glove to challenge the Frankish nobles to a courtly combat, as
  “my master wishes to prove his love for the lady of his heart.”
     Prince Charlemagne announces that: “Never does a knight
  of the Frankish court refuse a challenge on equal terms!” and asks
  who among his barons would like to defend Frankish honor.
     The young Carloman and Sir Ogier start bickering about who
  has the right to accept this challenge. The Dane first claims the
  fight with Sir Carahue, but Carloman officially states he will fight
  the Persian prince to defend the honor of Princess Gerberga. Roll
  Intrigue to see if a Player-knight is aware of the intense rivalry be-
  tween the two men, who are both courting the Lombard princess.
     At the end of the delicate negotiations, the following court-
  ly challenges are arranged: Prince Carahue of Mauritania to
  fight Sir Ogier, while Carahue’s nephew, Sir Sadon, fights Prince
  Carloman. Sir Sadon vows to fight without a shield, to compen-
  sate for Prince Carloman’s youth and inexperience.
     If some Player-knights wish to accept a challenge, they may
  confront a random Saracen or Persian knight. They should first
  ask their lord’s permission (roll Standing [lord]).

title: A Dishonorable Ambush
leftColumn:
All duels are to be held on an island in the Tiber River,
      which serves as the frontier between the two camps. The Saracen
      herald smiles with satisfaction. He swears an oath of chivalry on
      his master’s behalf, and then returns to whence he came. Roll
      Religion to notice that the herald’s religion is not the Saracen
      one, but Persian.
      A Dishonorable  Ambush

        Roll Intrigue at –5 to see if the Player-knights find out
      the following pieces of information. Success: Prince Carloman
      is buying black horses. Critical: Prince Carloman has come to
      claim some black hauberks for his own men, because his baggage
      train suffered great losses in the Alps.
        Prince Carloman secretly gives the black steeds and the
      black armor to some of his knights, for he is preparing an am-
      bush. On a successful Love [God] roll, a Player-knight has the
      following prophetic dream on the night before the duels: “You
      are at a noble feast, dancing with other young knights, when you
      accidentally step on a black snake who bites your ankle.”
        As is the military custom, both sides exchange hostages to
      ensure the truce for the duration of the challenges. While the “mi-
      nor” duels take place, Sir Ogier and Sir Carahue themselves fulfill
      the role of hostage. Both champions then fight the final duel, for
      which the Player-knights are appointed as peace hostages. Note
      that it has been arranged that their lives are only forfeit if their side
      is treacherous, not if their champion is defeated or killed.
        If the Player-knights did not accept any challenge, they
      are tasked with being messengers and bringing Carloman’s
      and Ogier’s gloves to the Saracen camp to confirm the duels.
      Suspicious Player-knights may scout to see if the Saracens have
      prepared an ambush. Roll Hunting, but unless a Player-knight
      obtains a critical success or explicitly states he is searching the
      Frankish side of the Tiber, he won’t spot a band of black-ar-
      mored knights hiding in a small grove. However, a success in
      Battle reveals that it’s possible for the Saracens to use their boats
      in a surprise attack.
        In the afternoon, quite a few Saracen ladies have installed
      themselves on the opposite bank of the Tiber to witness their
      champions. Roll Recognize to spot a beautiful Saracen princess
      (Gloriande) attaching a flower to Prince Carahue’s crown. A
      second success identifies Carahue as the messenger who came
      to court yesterday!
        Small boats take the contenders to the small island, where
      a Saracen and a Frankish herald are waiting. The four (or more)
      knights courteously greet each other.
       The perfidious [Carloman] meditated the blackest trea-
       son. During the night he collected some knights unworthy
       of the name, and like himself in their ferocious manners;
       he made them swear to avenge his injuries, armed them
       in black armor, and sent them to lie in ambush in the
       wood, with orders to make a pretended attack upon the
       whole party, but in fact to lay heavy hands upon Ogier
       and the two Saracens.
           — Bulfinch, XXIV
rightColumn:
When all is set for the duels, a number of knights armed
  all in black come out of the forest on flat barges to ambush
  the knights on the isle. A furious Sir Ogier ardently defends
  the Saracen challengers against the anonymous black knights.
  Charlemagne sends his men to aid his brother and liberate Sir
  Ogier. Roll Awareness (at –5) to notice that several knights from
  Prince Carloman’s court are nowhere to be seen. On the Saracen
  side of the river many knights, led by Danemont, spur across to
  the island.
     The relief units must cross the River Tiber, either by wad-
  ing it (roll the horses’ DEX and STR) or by finding a barge or
  another vessel (roll Awareness at –5). Play out a small three-way
  skirmish between the Franks, black knights, and pagans (Danes
  and Saracens), using the Early Knights table on page 149: Prince
  Carahue is a Rich Knight (line “21+”), Sir Sadon is a Rich
  Knight (line “17”), Sir Danemont is a Mounted Jarl (Line “18”
  on the Saxons and Danes table, page 152).
     After a few rounds of combat the black traitors retreat,
  while Prince Carloman swims to safety to the Frankish shore.
  Ogier is carried off by his rival, Danemont, against the protests
  of Carahue.
  Rescue  Attempts
     Spies report that Ogier is held prisoner at Aumont’s Tower,
  behind Mount Bitter. Charlemagne wonders if the Franks
  should attack the pagan camp in order to obtain Ogier’s libera-
  tion, but finally the prince accepts Duke Naymo’s plan: a discrete
  mission, consisting of a few knights and the duke himself, will
  scale the flanks of Mount Bitter and try to seize Aumont’s Tower
  and its prisoners by surprise. The Player-knights may volunteer
  for the mission (check Honor and Standing [Charlemagne]). If
  they don’t volunteer, Duke Thierry orders them to participate
  anyway, unless they are seriously wounded.
  Mount Bitter
     Cold winds and hailstorms sweep the steep and rocky
  mountain flanks, marked by many trackless ravines, wild
  streams without bridges, and caves inhabited by bears and
  leopards (use panther statistics). The summit is inhabited by
  a fearsome griffin.
     Each player should roll once on the following table:
   1d6 Result Test On a failed roll:
     1   Swimming Washed downstream and bashed on rocks.
               Take 2d6 damage (no armor).
     2   Climbing The character takes 3d6 damage (no ar-
               mor) from a violent fall.
     3   CON   The character takes a violent chill from the
               cold. Roll on the Table 10–2: Attributes
               Lost and check Chirurgery Required.
     4   STR   The character discards his armor and
               shield, going forward with only his sword.
     5   Energetic Attacked by a bear (use the stats on page
               380).
     6   Temperate Attacked by a leopard (use the Panther stats
               on page 382).

title: The Final Duel
leftColumn:
Duke Naymo is attacked and severely wounded by a griffin,
      barely managing to drive it off. A Player-knight that has succeed-
      ed at his own test may help the Duke in this combat.
        The expedition is doomed to fail. Even if the Player-knights
      manage to pull themselves through, the severely wounded Duke
      Naymo ultimately abandons his quest.
        If the Gamemaster wishes, the expedition may be captured
      by Saracens (tipped off by Carloman!). In that case, the Player-
      knights find themselves prisoner at Aumont’s Tower together
      with Sir Ogier. Their warden is the Saracen Princess Floripas,
      who is secretly in love with a Frankish paladin, Sir Guy of
      Burgundy. Play through the Aumont’s Tower section, below.
      Sir Carahue
        The Saracens refuse to exchange Ogier for Sadon and the
      other Saracen captives. They send a messenger (possibly the
      Player-knights) to announce that they will shortly execute the
      Dane. When the noble Sir Carahue hears this, he immediately
      rides to the Frankish court and makes himself prisoner as a guar-
      antee for Ogier’s life!
      Aumont’s Tower

        This tall strong tower, situated on a small island in
      Aspremont Bay, guards a pass from the coast to the plain of the
      Tiber. A causeway with a drawbridge connects the tower to the
      slopes of Mount Bitter in the north, and another leads to a natu-
      ral harbor in the south, where the Danish and Saracen ships have
      cast their anchor.
        Meanwhile, the romantic Princess Floripas tests the court-
      liness of her noble captives (note that she has a Amor [Sir Guy]
      of 19, and won’t form an attachment for a Player-knight). Each
      Player-knight may try to prove his worth as a true gentleman by
      trying to perform three tests of his choice. Romantic knights are
      at +5 to all required rolls:
       n
        Please her by demonstrating exquisitely refined table
        manners and conversation (Courtesy).
       n
        Teach her a new Frankish dance (Dancing).
       n
        Captivate her by telling a known tale of two lovers,
        like the story of Floris and Blancheflour (Eloquence).
       n
        Compose her an original love poem which makes her
        blush (Languages).
       n
        Play her a romantic tune that makes her weep (Play
        Instruments).
       n
        Respond correctly and with delicacy to the lady’s
        varying moods and her profound emotional needs
        (Romance).
       n
        Sing her a heart-felt serenade (Singing).
        If a Player-knight succeeds with all of his three romantic
      tests, Princess Floripas throws her governess (who might betray
      her passion to her father, the Sultan) out of a high window,
      then slays the jailor on the accusation of treason. Once these
rightColumn:
Glory Awards
   The Battle of Mount Bitter, for each successful battle round:
      50.
   The skirmish on the island, per successful battle round: 20.
   Per defeated creature on the flanks of Mount Bitter: bear 10,
      leopard 75.
   Helping Duke Naymo fight the griffin: 100
   Succeeding in Princess Floripas’ romantic trials, per test: 25.
   Heroically resisting a siege inside Aumont’s Tower: 100.

  two obstacles are removed, she secretly liberates Sir Ogier and
  the other prisoners in exchange for their promise to bring her
  Sir Guy of Burgundy, whom she wishes to marry (after being
  baptized, of course). Thus, the Franks are able to take com-
  mand of Aumont’s Tower.
     However, soon afterwards Prince Balan comes to besiege
  them. Use the Siege rules (page 156), pitting Sir Balan’s modified
  Siege skill of 26 against the best Player-knight’s score (Aumont’s
  Tower has DV 10, but only one set of defenses). If the Siege
  result would have the Saracens seize Aumont’s Tower, Princess
  Floripas holds them back by throwing an enormous quantity
  of gold out of the windows. The Saracen soldiery abandon the
  siege and collect the loot, giving the Franks the chance to escape.
  However, Sir Ogier refuses to flee, “for the noble Carahue’s and
  Gloriande’s sake!” And he can’t swim, anyway...
     If the Player-knights remain in their besieged tower, they
  just have to make the best of it. Food and drink are abundant, and
  they even have time to court one of Gloriande’s ladies-in-wait-
  ing, or otherwise indulge in courtly activities. But if they stay,
  their adventure ends here.
  The  Final Duel
     After a week of intense negotiations, Franks and pagans fi-
  nally agree to settle the affair of the prisoners by a duel between
  the besieged Sir Ogier and Sir Danemont — not Carahue, who is
  now considered a traitor by the Saracens. Sultan Corsuble prom-
  ises Danemont the hand of his daughter, Gloriande, should he
  defeat his rival. On the other hand, Sir Carahue sends Ogier his
  sword Courtain to help him in his fight against Danemont.
     In the final duel, Sir Ogier (wielding Courtain) defeats
  Danemont (riding Broiefort) in a short but violent confron-
  tation. The pagans retire in dismay and release all remaining
  Frankish prisoners, if any.
     As for the Franks, they release the courteous Sir Carahue,
  who pledges his eternal respect and friendship to Sir Ogier.
  Afterwards, he claims the hand of the beautiful Gloriande. All
  other Saracen prisoners are either baptized or executed; Prince
  Carloman insists.

Duke Naymo is attacked and severely wounded by a griffin,
      barely managing to drive it off. A Player-knight that has succeed-
      ed at his own test may help the Duke in this combat.
        The expedition is doomed to fail. Even if the Player-knights
      manage to pull themselves through, the severely wounded Duke
      Naymo ultimately abandons his quest.
        If the Gamemaster wishes, the expedition may be captured
      by Saracens (tipped off by Carloman!). In that case, the Player-
      knights find themselves prisoner at Aumont’s Tower together
      with Sir Ogier. Their warden is the Saracen Princess Floripas,
      who is secretly in love with a Frankish paladin, Sir Guy of
      Burgundy. Play through the Aumont’s Tower section, below.
      Sir Carahue
        The Saracens refuse to exchange Ogier for Sadon and the
      other Saracen captives. They send a messenger (possibly the
      Player-knights) to announce that they will shortly execute the
      Dane. When the noble Sir Carahue hears this, he immediately
      rides to the Frankish court and makes himself prisoner as a guar-
      antee for Ogier’s life!

This tall strong tower, situated on a small island in
      Aspremont Bay, guards a pass from the coast to the plain of the
      Tiber. A causeway with a drawbridge connects the tower to the
      slopes of Mount Bitter in the north, and another leads to a natu-
      ral harbor in the south, where the Danish and Saracen ships have
      cast their anchor.

     After a week of intense negotiations, Franks and pagans fi-
  nally agree to settle the affair of the prisoners by a duel between
  the besieged Sir Ogier and Sir Danemont — not Carahue, who is
  now considered a traitor by the Saracens. Sultan Corsuble prom-
  ises Danemont the hand of his daughter, Gloriande, should he
  defeat his rival. On the other hand, Sir Carahue sends Ogier his
  sword Courtain to help him in his fight against Danemont.

  Danemont (riding Broiefort) in a short but violent confron-
  tation. The pagans retire in dismay and release all remaining
  Frankish prisoners, if any.
     As for the Franks, they release the courteous Sir Carahue,
  who pledges his eternal respect and friendship to Sir Ogier.
  Afterwards, he claims the hand of the beautiful Gloriande. All
  other Saracen prisoners are either baptized or executed; Prince
  Carloman insists.

title: Short Form Scenarios
leftColumn:
Short   Form

       He had an innate urge to witness or hear of any new
       adventure
           — Orlando Furioso, XLII
     T
         o build their own scenarios, Gamemasters should look to
         the events listed in Chapter 15: The Future and the epics
         themselves. Below we present 18 short forms: scenario
      examples of different types and scopes.
      Adventure: The Adulterous Spouse

        A married Player-knight returns home after a long period of
      absence (campaign, foreign embassy, pilgrimage or solo adven-
      ture) to find his wife accused of adultery.
        Setting: The knight’s manor.
        Characters: The accused wife (Valorous 10, STR 8, CON
      12, Hit Points 20); the accuser; the accuser’s champion.
        Problem: Several witnesses support the claim of the ac-
      cuser. The pretended lover was executed immediately after his
      discovery, so he can no longer tell his story. Unless the Player-
      knights establish her innocence, the wife will be condemned.
        Secrets: Is the wife really innocent? Was there just an
      awkward conjunction of circumstances for which no one is to
      blame? Or are the heinous accusations part of a set-up from a
      jealous rival?
        Actions: To establish the wife’s innocence or guilt, the
      Player-knight will first want to hear the story from the accuser
      and to interrogate his witnesses. In short, this is what they all
      say: “That night, around midnight, [the accuser] heard noises in
      the manor hall. He warned [the witnesses], lit a torch and went in.
      There he found the couple. He dragged them out of the manor into
      the court yard, both as naked as the day they were born!”
        The wife contradicts this accusation: “When I woke up in
      the dark, I felt someone lying next to me in our bed. Before I had
      time to realize who it was, or even yell, [the accuser] came storming
      in with a burning torch and he dragged me out of my bed, naked,
      to the court yard, where [the witnesses] saw me. I swear I had never
      seen [the lover] before in my life.”
        Solutions: Resorting to the use of torture while interro-
      gating the witnesses causes an immediate loss of points in Just,
      Merciful and Standings [retinue, Church, and commoners].
      The tortured witness tells the Player-knight whatever he wants
      to hear. If he succumbs to his injuries (roll greater than his CON
      of 10), his accusation is no longer valid, and the Player-knight
      loses another point of Honor.
        The Player-knight’s wife may be forced to prove her inno-
      cence by submitting to an ordeal (see the boxed text). All Player-
      knights who agree to this solution must check Cruel. If the wife is
      truly innocent, she may benefit from the Player-knight’s prayers
      and a Just roll (see Judicial Combats and Ordeals in Chapter 9).
rightColumn:
m  Scenarios

                Ordeals
      Hot Iron/Boiling Water: Roll Valorous. On a failed
   roll, the character faints and is declared guilty. On a success,
   roll 4d6 damage. If he survives, roll against CON. He will re-
   gain as many Hit Points as indicated by a successful roll (dou-
   ble Hit Points on a critical; none on a failure; on a fumble he
   dies of his wounds). The character is considered innocent if,
   at the end of three days, he has still more than half his Total
   Hit Points.
      Proof of the Cross: Roll STR. A successful roll indicates
   the number of minutes he was capable of holding the weights
   up. To be proven innocent, a woman must hold them for at
   least 3 minutes; a man must hold them for at least 6.
     Instead of an ordeal, the Player-knight may challenge the
  accuser to a duel. For this, he gains checks in Valorous, Trusting,
  and Love [spouse]. Both the knight and the accuser have to put
  up hostages — whose lives are forfeit if their champion is killed!
     The problem is that the accuser is not a nobleman, so he
  must find a champion to fight in his place within 40 days, or
  retract his accusations. Surely, a rival knight will accept the chal-
  lenge to defend the law and the besmirched honor of manhood.
     If the wife is truly innocent, her champion may roll Just
  and, if successful, add half the value of the die roll to his armor
  (see Judicial Combats and Ordeals).
     Conclusion: The law is very strict with adulterous noble-
  women. If the wife is condemned, she will be executed — hanged
  after having been strangled (or, if she is pregnant, banished).
     If a Player-knight loses the trial by combat, he is at the mer-
  cy of his opponent, who is within his rights to slay him.
     If the wife’s innocence is proven, the wrongful accusers and
  his witnesses (and his champion, if any) must be punished as if
  he himself had committed the crime. If the Player-knight wants
  to forgive the deluded accusers, he needs to roll Forgiving. If he
  succeeds, he gains checks in Forgiving, Merciful and Standing
  [commoners].
     Glory: 50 for establishing the wife’s innocence; 75 for de-
  feating the champion in a trial by combat.
  Adventure:  The  Angry Merchant

     The Player-knights are enjoying the hospitality of a count
  for some reason (envoys of their lord, visiting a relative, on their
  way back from war, or on a pilgrimage).
     Setting: A count’s castle.
     Characters: An uncouth count (Arbitrary, Selfish; Love
  [Charlemagne] 10); Sigulf, a corrupt household knight (SIZ 17,
  DEX 9, STR 15, CON 13, Hit Points 30, Damage 5d6, Cruel,
  Deceitful, Selfish); a huge merchant (Charlemagne in disguise).

title: Adventure:
leftColumn:
Problem: The knights are staying at a count’s castle while
      he holds his annual court of justice. It soon becomes apparent
      that the greedy count does as he pleases, caring little about the
      truth and ignoring the knights’ advice. He clearly values money
      more than justice. All commoners mutter and complain about
      the count’s “very unorthodox sense of the law.”
        The last plaintiff is a tall, bold Frankish merchant. In a cold
      and angry voice, he claims to have been robbed of his horses by
      a knight from the count’s retinue. The count laughingly asks
      the knights for aid “in rapidly settling this difficult case.” The
      Player-knights are in an unpleasant situation. Especially chival-
      ric knights probably want to help the oppressed population and
      teach the selfish count a lesson, but the laws of hospitality (and
      thus their honor) prevent them from any direct accusations or
      actions against their host.
        Secrets: The merchant is no other than Charlemagne
      himself, who has come here anonymously to inspect his greedy
      count.
        Actions: If the Player-knights want to investigate the
      merchant’s case, they may ask him questions about the robber
      knight’s identity, what exactly happened where and when, etc.
      The merchant’s detailed and convincing descriptions all lead to
      the same conclusion: the thief is Sigulf, a household knight of
      the Count. He hid the stolen horses, so a quick tour around his
      manor proves fruitless.
        The Player-knights may be intrigued by the eloquent and
      valorous merchant. To discover his true identity, they should try
      to ask questions accordingly, or otherwise succeed in Intrigue
      and Recognize rolls (for these rolls, do not add Charlemagne’s
      Glory/1,000!).
        Solutions: The knights must show the count the capi-
      tal importance of justice. Blunt threats only have the opposite
      effect. Treat him as someone who is Melancholic after a failed
      Love [Charlemagne] test. To get the count back on the path of
      peace, rolls in Just, Honest, Eloquence and even Religion may be
      helpful (i.e. provide bonuses), but the ultimate resolution is the
      clash between the count’s Love [Charlemagne] and a relevant
      Player-knight’s passion.
        Alternately, if they discover the merchant’s true iden-
      tity, they may inform their incredulous host, who will need
      convincing.
        Conclusion: If the Player-knights refuse to judge the case,
      or if they unscrupulously choose the Count’s side and send
      the merchant away without compensation, they’ll have to face
      Charlemagne’s wrath. The King reveals his identity and strips
      the Count and his knights of their titles. As the Player-knights
      do not belong to the Count’s retinue, Charlemagne merely con-
      demns them to pay heavy fines, typically a number of £ equal to
      their Selfish or Arbitrary score. They get an immediate +1 to
      Arbitrary.
        If the knights try but fail to sway the count, Charlemagne
      reveals himself and does as above, but without condemning the
      Player-knights.
rightColumn:
If the Player-knights accuse the bandit-knight, Sigulf im-
  mediately challenges an accusing knight to a duel. The count
  will be very displeased with his guests, whom he will first try to
  bribe (£5). If the Player-knights refuse, a combat is inevitable.
  The angry count states conditions to the judicial combat which
  clearly favor his knight. On the other hand, the “merchant” will
  pray for the Player-knight’s success. On a successful Love [God]
  roll, they receive the value of the roll as a bonus to an Inspiration
  roll.
     If the Player-knights succeed in convincing the Count to
  let justice prevail, the Count will reluctantly punish his knight.
  The king reveals his identity; he admonishes the count, confis-
  cates the punished knight’s manor and grants it to one of the
  Player-knights.
     Glory: 100 for allowing justice to prevail in the presence of
  Charlemagne; 50 for defeating Sir Sigulf.
  Adventure:
  Children of the Blue Heaven

     Riots broke out in a city a few days ago. An angry mob
  lynched a Jewish merchant just outside town, accusing him of
  stealing Christian children for “their demonic sabbaths.” The
  Player-knight are sent to assist the viscount in restoring peace
  and order.
     Setting: An episcopal trading city where the Player-knights
  are respected, and preferably have some authority (this adven-
  ture is particularly suited for player missi dominici).
     Characters: Agobard, the corrupt and ruthless bishop
  (Cruel, Deceitful, Selfish); Milo, the respectable magister of
  Jews (Religion 19); Odalric, the obedient viscount (Lazy);
  Donatio, the sly Lombard wine merchant (and slave trader),
  owner of a trading vessel called The Blue Heaven (Deceitful;
  Light Crossbow 12).

segments.text:
Problem: The knights are staying at a count’s castle while
      he holds his annual court of justice. It soon becomes apparent
      that the greedy count does as he pleases, caring little about the
      truth and ignoring the knights’ advice. He clearly values money
      more than justice. All commoners mutter and complain about
      the count’s “very unorthodox sense of the law.”
        The last plaintiff is a tall, bold Frankish merchant. In a cold
      and angry voice, he claims to have been robbed of his horses by
      a knight from the count’s retinue. The count laughingly asks
      the knights for aid “in rapidly settling this difficult case.” The
      Player-knights are in an unpleasant situation. Especially chival-
      ric knights probably want to help the oppressed population and
      teach the selfish count a lesson, but the laws of hospitality (and
      thus their honor) prevent them from any direct accusations or
      actions against their host.
        Secrets: The merchant is no other than Charlemagne
      himself, who has come here anonymously to inspect his greedy
      count.
        Actions: If the Player-knights want to investigate the
      merchant’s case, they may ask him questions about the robber
      knight’s identity, what exactly happened where and when, etc.
      The merchant’s detailed and convincing descriptions all lead to
      the same conclusion: the thief is Sigulf, a household knight of
      the Count. He hid the stolen horses, so a quick tour around his
      manor proves fruitless.
        The Player-knights may be intrigued by the eloquent and
      valorous merchant. To discover his true identity, they should try
      to ask questions accordingly, or otherwise succeed in Intrigue
      and Recognize rolls (for these rolls, do not add Charlemagne’s
      Glory/1,000!).
        Solutions: The knights must show the count the capi-
      tal importance of justice. Blunt threats only have the opposite
      effect. Treat him as someone who is Melancholic after a failed
      Love [Charlemagne] test. To get the count back on the path of
      peace, rolls in Just, Honest, Eloquence and even Religion may be
      helpful (i.e. provide bonuses), but the ultimate resolution is the
      clash between the count’s Love [Charlemagne] and a relevant
      Player-knight’s passion.
        Alternately, if they discover the merchant’s true iden-
      tity, they may inform their incredulous host, who will need
      convincing.
        Conclusion: If the Player-knights refuse to judge the case,
      or if they unscrupulously choose the Count’s side and send
      the merchant away without compensation, they’ll have to face
      Charlemagne’s wrath. The King reveals his identity and strips
      the Count and his knights of their titles. As the Player-knights
      do not belong to the Count’s retinue, Charlemagne merely con-
      demns them to pay heavy fines, typically a number of £ equal to
      their Selfish or Arbitrary score. They get an immediate +1 to
      Arbitrary.
        If the knights try but fail to sway the count, Charlemagne
      reveals himself and does as above, but without condemning the
      Player-knights.

title: Adventure: The Devil’s Bridge
leftColumn:
notice that the magister is a pious and learned man, who cites
      his Bible and seems to know it better than the bishop himself!
        Successful Intrigue rolls reveal the reputation and the nota-
      ble character traits of the main characters.
        A success in Folk Lore is useful, for it informs the Player-
      knights of a popular rumor: that the souls of the poor missing
      boys can be heard wailing in the cathedral at night. Spending
      a vigil in the cathedral reveals traces of sacramental wine near
      the altar (as you might expect) but also near the now hermeti-
      cally-locked crypt (where the children were kept prisoner before
      they were put in wine barrels and sold to Donatio).
        If the Player-knights think of speaking to the poor boys’
      parents (artisans living in the suburbs outside the city walls),
      they describe their missing boys. A successful Recognize roll lets
      a Player-knight remember having seen a boy on the cathedral
      square playing with a puppet described by a bereaved parent.
      Finding the boy is easy, and he says that he found the puppet in
      an alley just behind the cathedral.
        If the Player-knights are explicitly interested in the chronol-
      ogy of the past events, roll Stewardship. Success indicates they
      realize that each time some boys disappeared, it was always just
      before the monthly wine market.
        On a successful Indulgent roll, they notice how the bishop
      serves the very same wine as that which the merchant Donatio
      pretends to have sold in Spain. If they go and check out Donatio’s
      wine barrels, they find them smelling not of wine, but distinctly
      of sweat and blood.
        For answers to questions, the players may roll Awareness or
      another suitable skill, trait or standing.
        Solutions: After a thorough investigation, the Player-
      knights should find out how Donatio sells children as slaves for
      the bishop. If they confront Donatio, he will not hesitate to use
      his crossbow. If captured, he accuses the bishop and only con-
      fesses his crimes under duress.
        If at some point the Player-knights share their suspicions
      about Donatio with the ruthless bishop, he has his accomplice
      arrested and executed. He thanks the Player-knights and de-
      clares the case closed.
        If the Player-knights get too close to discovering the truth,
      strange “accidents” happen. The suspicious or desperate bishop,
      who knows his city well, may even organize an ambush with a
      few palace guards!
        Conclusion: If the Player-knights suspect the bishop, they
      should warn Charlemagne, who will send some paladins or mis-
      si dominici. They’ll confirm the bishop’s guilt and execute him.
      The disappearance of boys abruptly comes to an end.
        If the Player-knights are unable to identify the roots of evil,
      boys begin to disappear again in half a year, this time attributed
      to the Frisians.
        After this adventure, pious Player-knights may vow to buy
      back Christian children on the slave markets of Toledo.
        Glory: 50 for condemning Donatio; 100 for the bishop.
rightColumn:
Adventure:  The  Devil’s Bridge

     The Player-knights accompany their lord on the annual
  campaign when they are trapped between a chasm and a pagan
  army.
     Setting: The lord’s men are trapped in a mountainous re-
  gion. Before them lies a wide, deep chasm; behind them the pa-
  gans have blocked the road.
     Characters: The Player-knight’s lord; a pagan Giant
  (Honor 9); a demon (vice attacks; illusions).
     Problem: The Player-knights must either fight a pagan
  champion, or aid in the construction of a bridge across the
  chasm.
     Secrets: The chasm is the home of a demon, who destroys
  the construction works each night.
     Actions: The Player-knights are sent out as scouts to evalu-
  ate the situation on the pagan side. Roll Battle. A critical success
  reveals the superiority of the pagan position: high up the rocky
  cliffs and their superior numbers (evaluation: the Franks will
  be at –15 in battle); a success reveals only one of these elements
  (evaluation: –10 in battle); a failure indicates the Player-knight
  cannot see any decisive advantages for the pagans (evaluation:
  –5 in battle); on a fumble, he considers the pagans to be inferior
  in equipment and in numbers (evaluation: +5 in battle).
     The Gamemaster may want to stage a short skirmish with
  some patrolling pagans to show the danger the Franks are re-
  ally in. All skirmish Battle rolls are at –10, unless a successful
  Awareness roll draws the Player-knight’s attention to their op-
  ponent’s presence before the two patrolling groups meet (Battle
  rolls +10 for a critical, +5 for a success; –10 for a failure and –15
  on a fumble).
     The lord’s army has water and food rations for about a
  month. Unless the Player-knights advise against it, the lord
  much prefers constructing a bridge to risking a confrontation.
     During the day, diligent workers begin the construction of
  a wooden bridge. However, each morning, they invariably find
  the bridge collapsed into the chasm. A Player-knight who sug-
  gests a possible supernatural cause may roll Faerie Lore to obtain
  some vague information about the demon of the chasm.
     Once they have realized their situation is desperate, the
  Player-knights may want to pray for divine aid. Independently of
  their possibly successful prayers, Player-knights who successful-
  ly roll Love [Charlemagne] have one of the following prophetic
  dreams (both on a critical):
   1. The Player-knight dreams of an imperturbable smil-
     ing virgin who stands singing outside in the dark,
     surrounded by candles, while a biting black hound
     dog tears at her flesh. The dream ends with a sunrise,
     at the exact moment of the actual sunrise outside. A
     Player-knight may roll Religion to recognize the vir-
     gin’s song as the Litany of the Saints, which is sung
     during the Easter night vigil.

        knight rides out of the castle and slays the beast.
        Solutions: If the Player-knights decide to spend the night
      praying on the newly built bridge, the demon comes to harass
      them with attacks against their souls. These tests of virtue all
      necessitate a successful roll in a Christian trait. For example, he
      will try to lure a knight away with the Lustful calls from a wom-
      an (opposed Chaste and Lustful), or he tries to incite hatred and
      the desire of Vengeance against a Player-knight’s rival sleeping in
      the Frankish camp “Why is he not risking his life on the bridge, the
      filthy coward!” (Opposed Forgiving and Vengeful).
        If at least one player remains on the bridge at the end of
      the night, the demon creates the illusion of a rising sun. On a
      successful Awareness roll the Player-knight notices that the “sun”
      is rising slightly to the north and that the mass candles have not
      yet completely burnt. If the players leave the bridge, the demon
      leaps forward and destroys it. This time, the workers categorical-
      ly refuse to rebuild it.
        If the Player-knights fail the test of the bridge, the only solu-
      tion left is to take on the challenge of a pagan giant. It is up to
      the Gamemaster if this will be a single combat, or if the haughty
      giant agrees to fight more than one opponent at a time.
        Each combat round against the giant represents an hour of
      exchanged blows, retreats, periods of rest, the exchange of insults
      or attempts to convert the giant. If the Player-knight keeps up
      the fight for 5 rounds, the giant becomes tired in round 6 (–5 to
      all actions), even more so in round 7 (–10 to actions) and finally
      falls asleep before the beginning of round 8.
        Conclusion: If the Player-knights succeed in protecting
      the bridge, they can escape the pagan trap. The Player-knights
      might participate in a rear-guard action to destroy the bridge.
        If the Player-knights succeed in defeating the “invincible”
      giant, the incredulous pagans retreat.
        If the Player-knights fail against both the demon and the
      giant, the Franks are forced to engage in a desperate battle (with
      a –15 Battle modifier, which probably results in the Player-
      knights being captured).
        Glory: 250 for vanquishing the demon of the chasm; 250
      for defeating a pagan giant in combat.
      Adventure: The  Faerie Castle
        This encounter occurs when the Player-knights are lost in,
      hunting in, or exploring a dark forest.
        Setting: An un-tracked and primeval forest, like
      Broceliande or the Black Forest.
        Characters: A faerie lady.
        Problem: How to leave the enchanted castle?
        Secrets: None.
rightColumn:
Actions: While roaming in the forest, the Player-knights
  discover a path leading to some abandoned ruins. Once inside
  these ruins, the Player-knights may roll Awareness; on a success
  they notice they have lost their shadows. A further success in
  Faerie Lore makes them realize that they have entered the en-
  chanted realm of Faerie.
     Enchanted, the ruins transform into a splendid castle sur-
  rounded by lush gardens. A moment later a beautiful lady in
  flowery garments walks up from behind them and welcomes her
  guests with heart-warming enthusiasm. The faerie queen is po-
  lite and does everything to please the knights.
     Inside the castle, knights are unable to attack anyone, they
  do not recognize anyone, nor can they leave the faerie realm.
     Solutions: The Player-knights are magically trapped inside
  the faerie castle. The only way out is to resist all six of its en-
  chantments. A knight must earn the privilege to resist each test
  by beating a faerie host in a random skill test:
         table 19–6: faerie skill test
   1d6 Result Invitation Tested Skill
     1   Elegant Flattery Courtesy or Eloquence
     2   Faerie Chess Gaming or Siege

     3   Family Tales Heraldry or Recognize
     4   Grand Feast Dancing or Singing
     5   Wild Hunt Horsemanship or Hunting
     6   Wondrous Tales Faerie Lore or Folk Lore
     If the Player-knight fails his skill roll, his faerie opponent
  wins and the knight spends the next month indulging in his favor-
  ite sins. It is important to keep track of time, as the Player-knights
  can easily remain captive at the faerie castle for several years!
     If the knight wins the skill contest, the faerie queen applauds
  and gives him a precious gift, such as an imperishable flower, a gold-
  en ring, a potion of healing, a faerie horse, an enchanted sword, or a
  cap of invisibility. She then puts the Player-knight’s virtue to the test
  (roll on Table 19–7: Faerie Temptation).
     Each time a character fails to resist a temptation (he fails a
  virtuous trait roll), he proves himself unable to escape the faerie
  enchantment, and must win another skill test to obtain the next
  chance to resist a temptation.
     Once a character has resisted all six temptations the illusory
  castle transforms back into the abandoned ruins in the forest.
  The Player-knight may now either try to find back the path out
  of the forest, or stay and try to help a friend who is still under the
  faerie spell by making skill or virtue rolls on his behalf.
     A liberated Player-knight may leave the ruins at will. He
  may roll Recognize to see if he recognizes any of the captured
  knights inside the castle (apart from his friends). On a critical
  success, one of them is a paladin!
     Conclusion: For every “year” spent inside the faerie ru-
  ins, a Player-knight ages one year, as normal. He makes normal
  aging rolls (if any) and resolves experience checks. However,
  time in the real world will have progressed by any time span the
  Gamemaster decides — days, weeks, or even years.

leftColumn:
table 19–7: faerie teMPtatioN
      Temptation Tested Virtue Description
      Envy   Trusting A lovely faerie lady, who has been
                     pleasantly attentive to you, spends
                     time with another knight. What are
                     they doing? She says: “nothing.”
      Gluttony Temperate The food is excellent and fine wines
                     keep being served endlessly!
      Greed  Generous The faerie queen asks you whom she
                     should bless with the gift of strength/
                     courage/longevity. “Myself” is cer-
                     tainly a possibility.
      Lust   Chaste  The faerie damsels are exquisite crea-
                     tures and not at all shy!
      Pride  Modest  All the faerie court demands you to
                     tell them of your astonishing capac-
                     ities, your legendary deeds and your
                     imperishable glory, encouraging you
                     to exaggerate!
      Sloth  Energetic The beds are soft and warm, the lush
                     landscape is so beautiful to behold!
      Wrath  Forgiving The faerie queen asks you which
                     knight in the outside world you
                     would like her to curse.
        All the gifts the faerie queen gave to the Player-knight for
      their successes in the skill tests turn out to be worthless unless he
      obtains a critical success in Faerie Lore (one roll per object, no
      Inspiration or prayers possible).
        Glory: 100 for having spent a year inside a faerie castle; 100
      for helping to liberate a paladin.
      Adventure:

      For the Love of Bayard

        A few peasants bring in a seriously injured Sir Renaud
      of Montauban. The semiconscious paladin needs his gaping
      wounds looked after, but that’s not what worries him most. Just
      before he passes out, Renaud asks that someone takes care of
      his beloved horse, which the peasants left in the nearby clearing
      where they found his master.
        Setting: A Player-knight’s manor; before the year 771.
        Characters: Renaud of Montauban; Bayard (see stats on
      page 378).
        Problem: Sir Renaud was traveling alone, so there is no one
      to take care of Bayard. The Player-knights’ squires are incapa-
      ble of handling this mighty and dangerous steed, so the knights
      should obviously do it themselves. Renaud is unconscious most
      of the adventure, but during occasional feverish bouts of de-
      lirium his only understandable words are “care” and “Bayard.”
      Bayard does not abandon his master, but dealing with his haugh-
      ty and quirky nature is an adventure in itself.
rightColumn:
Secrets: None really, but the knights must find out how to
  deal with the capricious faerie horse: his habits, demands, and
  whims. Faerie Lore gives some hints as to Bayard’s needs and
  wants. Note that though Bayard is capable of understanding hu-
  man speech, this doesn’t mean he agrees to do what he is told!
     Actions: Taking care of Bayard for an entire week is both
  difficult and dangerous. The main tasks are feeding, brushing,
  shoeing, exercising and boxing the horse. Orders from anyone
  but his master irritate Bayard. An angry Bayard always attacks
  the nearest person. Trying to ride Bayard without Renaud’s per-
  mission makes him go berserk, unless he is subdued by force first
  (i.e. a successful Knockdown in unarmed combat).
     Feed: Bayard eats only the best of grains (cost: £1 per
  month). Trying to feed him common horse fodder (hay or grass)
  is an insult. Bayard simply refuses to eat that sort of fodder. If
  pressed, he will kick and bite. Failing to correctly feed Bayard
  makes him irritable, giving a –5 to all subsequent Horsemanship
  rolls for that day.
     Grooming: Bayard needs daily brushing and washing. To
  do this, one must obviously approach Bayard, gain his confi-
  dence and then touch him. Each of these three steps needs a suc-
  cessful Horsemanship roll. Any indelicacy is punished as usual.
  Failing to groom Bayard results in a –5 on all subsequent rolls in
  dealing with the horse.
     Shoeing: Probably the most difficult task is to shoe Bayard,
  though this feat needs to be performed only once. To succeed, a
  farrier must first groom Bayard before putting on the four steel
  shoes (iron shoes simply break the next day), without the help
  of a travis (a framework to hold a horse immobile while it is
  worked on). If forced inside such a wooden frame, Bayard pro-
  tests violently!
     Entertainment: If left alone during the day, Bayard will not
  just amble around the domain, but strays into the forest. To pre-
  vent this, Bayard needs to be convinced to stay around, either
  with very special food, or better, by presenting him with some
  clever challenges (roll Gaming, Hunting, or Swimming).
     Sleeping: At the end of each day, Bayard wants to sleep
  somewhere inside, near a fire if possible. Trying to put him in a
  stable provokes the usual irritated reaction. If locked up, Bayard
  breaks down his prison with his powerful hooves and gallops
  away to freedom.
     Conclusion: If the knights manage to take good care of
  Bayard and hand him back over to his master in good health,
  Renaud rewards them with the promise of a future favor.
     If they lose Bayard, Renaud curses them and leaves at once
  in search of his horse, despite his unhealed wounds.
     After Bayard survives the drowning into the Meuse (772),
  the fabulous horse escapes into the Ardennes Forest. Player-
  knights may take on the quest of finding and capturing Bayard,
  which should be impossible to everyone except knights who
  know the horse and took good care of him one day. They receive
  +5 to Hunting for Bayard.
     Glory: 50 for taking good care of Bayard.

A few peasants bring in a seriously injured Sir Renaud
      of Montauban. The semiconscious paladin needs his gaping
      wounds looked after, but that’s not what worries him most. Just
      before he passes out, Renaud asks that someone takes care of
      his beloved horse, which the peasants left in the nearby clearing
      where they found his master.
        Setting: A Player-knight’s manor; before the year 771.
        Characters: Renaud of Montauban; Bayard (see stats on
      page 378).
        Problem: Sir Renaud was traveling alone, so there is no one
      to take care of Bayard. The Player-knights’ squires are incapa-
      ble of handling this mighty and dangerous steed, so the knights
      should obviously do it themselves. Renaud is unconscious most
      of the adventure, but during occasional feverish bouts of de-
      lirium his only understandable words are “care” and “Bayard.”
      Bayard does not abandon his master, but dealing with his haugh-
      ty and quirky nature is an adventure in itself.

Secrets: None really, but the knights must find out how to
  deal with the capricious faerie horse: his habits, demands, and
  whims. Faerie Lore gives some hints as to Bayard’s needs and
  wants. Note that though Bayard is capable of understanding hu-
  man speech, this doesn’t mean he agrees to do what he is told!
     Actions: Taking care of Bayard for an entire week is both
  difficult and dangerous. The main tasks are feeding, brushing,
  shoeing, exercising and boxing the horse. Orders from anyone
  but his master irritate Bayard. An angry Bayard always attacks
  the nearest person. Trying to ride Bayard without Renaud’s per-
  mission makes him go berserk, unless he is subdued by force first
  (i.e. a successful Knockdown in unarmed combat).
     Feed: Bayard eats only the best of grains (cost: £1 per
  month). Trying to feed him common horse fodder (hay or grass)
  is an insult. Bayard simply refuses to eat that sort of fodder. If
  pressed, he will kick and bite. Failing to correctly feed Bayard
  makes him irritable, giving a –5 to all subsequent Horsemanship
  rolls for that day.
     Grooming: Bayard needs daily brushing and washing. To
  do this, one must obviously approach Bayard, gain his confi-
  dence and then touch him. Each of these three steps needs a suc-
  cessful Horsemanship roll. Any indelicacy is punished as usual.
  Failing to groom Bayard results in a –5 on all subsequent rolls in
  dealing with the horse.
     Shoeing: Probably the most difficult task is to shoe Bayard,
  though this feat needs to be performed only once. To succeed, a
  farrier must first groom Bayard before putting on the four steel
  shoes (iron shoes simply break the next day), without the help
  of a travis (a framework to hold a horse immobile while it is
  worked on). If forced inside such a wooden frame, Bayard pro-
  tests violently!
     Entertainment: If left alone during the day, Bayard will not
  just amble around the domain, but strays into the forest. To pre-
  vent this, Bayard needs to be convinced to stay around, either
  with very special food, or better, by presenting him with some
  clever challenges (roll Gaming, Hunting, or Swimming).
     Sleeping: At the end of each day, Bayard wants to sleep
  somewhere inside, near a fire if possible. Trying to put him in a
  stable provokes the usual irritated reaction. If locked up, Bayard
  breaks down his prison with his powerful hooves and gallops
  away to freedom.
     Conclusion: If the knights manage to take good care of
  Bayard and hand him back over to his master in good health,
  Renaud rewards them with the promise of a future favor.
     If they lose Bayard, Renaud curses them and leaves at once
  in search of his horse, despite his unhealed wounds.
     After Bayard survives the drowning into the Meuse (772),
  the fabulous horse escapes into the Ardennes Forest. Player-
  knights may take on the quest of finding and capturing Bayard,
  which should be impossible to everyone except knights who
  know the horse and took good care of him one day. They receive
  +5 to Hunting for Bayard.
     Glory: 50 for taking good care of Bayard.

title: Adventure: The Foreign Embassy
leftColumn:
Adventure: The Foreign Embassy

        The Player-knights are sent (by their lord, their bishop, a
      paladin, a lover, a princess, or even by Charlemagne himself)
      on an embassy to some foreign court: Byzantium, Baghdad,
      Babylon, Jerusalem, Cordoba or Denmark. Such missions are
      generally made up of one or more clergy members (a palace
      monk, bishop, or abbot), a count, and some knights.
        Setting: Foreign lands; foreign court.
        Characters: The foreign lord (Honor 15); his resentful son
      (any appropriate negative trait at 16); his charming daughter
      (Honor 15, Chaste 15).
        Problem: The mission may have any number of goals to
      achieve:
       n
        Bring or exchange royal letters and expensive gifts.
       n
        Conclude a peace treaty.
       n
        Exchange or bring back valuable books.
       n
        Find medicinal herbs for a lady or lord suffering from
        an illness.
       n
        Arrange a peace marriage or escort a princess to her
        future husband.
       n
        Negotiate a ransom for an imprisoned friend or lord
        and escort him back to Frankland.
       n
        Go relic hunting (secretly).
       n
        Convert the local pagans.
        The main challenge of a delicate embassy is to not insult
      the host and his court, and to avoid conflicts in a place where
      support is non-existent.
        Secrets: None.
        Actions and Solutions: The first step is to get to the for-
      eign court, which generally means a long journey. If the trip leads
      through hostile territory or, worse, to a hostile court, then the
      Frankish embassy would be wise to demand an exchange of hos-
      tages as guarantees for their own safety.
        The voyage itself can be as eventful as the Gamemaster
      wishes, but may require successful rolls in Awareness (to detect
      possible ambushes), Folk Lore and Languages (to get reliable
      information from foreign locals), Horsemanship (to avoid inju-
      ries to the riding horse), Stewardship (to manage the expenses
      for lodging, transport and food). For a long sea voyage, CON
      rolls for men and mounts may be in order to check for sickness
      or disease. You might use the Holy Lands solo adventure as
      inspiration.
        Once they arrive at their destination, the Player-knights are
      welcomed by their host and treated with all due honors, unless
      the court is openly hostile, in which case they may be provoked
      or treated with contempt (no one bows to them, they receive
      little or bad food, their squires are imprisoned, etc.).
        Roll Heraldry or Recognize to see if any known enemies are
      present. A successful Modest roll is needed to keep one’s cool,

The Tale of the Insulted Host
   Hear the very instructive story of a Frankish envoy in
   Constantinople: “The king then summoned him to his banquet
   and sat him down amidst his nobles. Among these people a law
   had been established whereby no one at the king’s table, whether
   a native or a foreigner, should turn over any animal or piece of
   meat on its other side. He was to eat from the top part. A spicy
   river fish was brought in and put on his dish. The guest, ignorant
   of the custom, turned that fish over, and everybody jumped up
   and shouted to the king, ‘Lord, you have been dishonored as none
   of your ancestors were.’ The king let out a groan and said to the
   envoy, ‘I cannot stand in their way, and I must hand you over to
   death right away. But first ask for something, whatever you like,
   and I will do it. But I cannot grant you your life against the law
   of the Byzantines.’ The envoy thought for a while, and then, in the
   hearing of all, he came out with these words: ‘Here is the request
   of the man who is about to die: let anyone who saw me turn over
   that fish be deprived of his eyes.’ Although dumbstruck at such
   a proposition, the king swore in Christ’s name that he had not
   seen this, but that he had merely believed those who said it was
   so. Right away the queen began to make excuses for herself. Then
   the rest of the nobles, one after another, wishing to get themselves
   out of such a dangerous predicament, tried to absolve themselves.”
      — Notker, 6
  positively modified for provident Player-knights, like those who
  recognized any hostile court members.
     The Franks are challenged to test their courtly and/or mar-
  tial skills, depending of the host’s culture (for example: Dancing,
  Eloquence, Falconry, Gaming, Play Instruments, Singing, a me-
  lee weapon skill, or Bow). If a hostile or a particularly proud host
  himself is participating in any of these court events, it may be
  wise for the Player-knights to lose such a contest on purpose (roll
  Prudent to realize this). If not, they may be accused of cheating,
  which is invariably taken as an insult.
     If a Player-knight willingly or unwillingly insult their host
  (by inappropriate reaction to a provocation, publicly winning
  a contest from their host, or fumbling a courtly skill), or if he
  fails a Courtesy roll, he’ll be accused of the terrible crime of
  lese-majesty (grave disrespect to the host). Unless he comes up
  with very convincing excuses or some clever answer (see The
  Tale of the Insulted Host in the boxed text), a local champion
  challenges him, to wash away the stain on his lord’s honor. The
  Gamemaster should make sure that the duel conditions are not
  in the Player-knight’s favor. Several challenges may be made
  against the party…
     If even one Player-knight loses such a combat, they’ll all be
  stripped of all their possessions and sent back to Frankland with-
  out any further ado. They each lose a point of Honor.
     Once the Player-knights have shown sufficient skill to be
  accepted at court, they must explain their mission to their host.
  This requires a roll in Eloquence, and Deceitful if the Player-
  knight is lying. A failed roll indicates the host’s displeasure
  (or his wrath, on a fumble!), which means that whatever the
