title: Adventure: The Greedy Abbot
leftColumn:
Player-knights propose or demand is refused. If the host recog-
      nizes their mission as just and fair, the Player-knights may still
      try to achieve their objectives.
        On a successful Intrigue roll, a Player-knights gets another
      opportunity to advance one of the embassy’s goals. Depending
      on the nature of the objective, another roll is needed for it to
      materialize. For example, proposing a peace marriage may need a
      final roll in Romance or Honor.
        Conclusion: Unless the Gamemaster wishes to use it as an
      introduction to the next adventure, the return voyage should be
      a formality. At their safe return, the hostages (if any) are released,
      and the Player-knights must relate their adventure to the per-
      son who sent them on their perilous mission. If they have been
      particularly successful, the Player-knights may gain points in
      Honor, Amor, Love, and/or Standing [lord], as appropriate.
        Glory: 50 per goal obtained.
      Adventure: The  Greedy  Abbot

        A local abbot enrolls the Player-knights in his service to
      protect the church treasures of his abbey, which are displayed on
      the church altar next to the local saint’s relics during the yearly
      market.
        Setting: A rich abbey, its church, and the market grounds.
        Characters: Abbot Nortgaud (Deceitful, Selfish, Suspicious);
      a band of three thieves (use bandit statistics, page 374).
        Problem: Anticipate the plans of the thieves, recognize
      their preparations and catch them red-handed.
        Secrets: The “miracle” at the saint’s relics is a hoax orga-
      nized by the monks for the enrichment of their abbey.
        Actions and Solutions: To effectively prevent thieves
      from stealing the exposed church treasure, the Player-knights
      should first examine the surroundings, evaluate the risks and
      take their precautions. To gain bonuses on future rolls, a Player-
      knight must either come up with some clever ideas or succeed
      in an appropriate skill roll (+2 per critical, +1 per success, –2
      per fumble), such as Awareness (to spot a construction weak-
      ness), Hunting (to determine possible escape routes for thieves),
      Recognize (to see if anyone reported the presence of a notorious
      robber band), or Religion (to be aware of the exact procedures
      during the religious processions and the veneration of relics).
        The market fair lasts for a whole week. Sometime during the
      first three days the thieves make their first attempt. Their plan is
      for two of them to start pushing the crowd, creating a dangerous
      mass movement forwards. As the crowd reaches the altar, one of
      the thieves snatches a treasure away, while his accomplice puts a
      valuable object in an innocent pilgrim’s mantle, whom the third
      thief loudly accuses, while the first thief sneaks away.
        Unless the Player-knights anticipated such a plan and
      therefore have a good chance of foiling it, the thieves will suc-
      ceed. However, a vigilant Player-knight (roll Awareness) may
rightColumn:
Recognize the real thief and try to catch him before he reaches
  the narrow streets of the town (where horses are at a disadvan-
  tage) or the nearby forest.
     Some days later, men and women praying at the tomb of the
  local saint inside the church are suddenly seized with epilepsy.
  Many pilgrims present at the site panic, and try to calm the anger
  of their saint by gifts of gold, silver and cattle.
     This is not another thieves’ trick. If the Player-knights in-
  terrogate the “victims,” they may Recognize some monks from
  the abbey. If they confront the abbot with this fact, he arrests
  the monks (per church law) and promises painful chastisement
  for the “depraved sinners.” Only if the Player-knights insist will
  the abbot make a public announcement and return some of the
  pilgrim’s money.
     The last night of the fair, the thieves make their second at-
  tempt, if the first one failed or if none of them were caught the
  first time. Alternatively, a second band of robbers has a go at the
  treasure. At night, the thieves actually try to pierce the church
  walls! Once more, unless the players anticipated this, the thieves
  succeed, though vigilant Player-knights (roll Awareness) may be
  attracted by suspicious noise and get a bonus to their chase roll
  or, on a critical, catch the thieves red-handed.
     If the players keep a permanent watch over the altar and the
  relics, the thieves will try to drug the guard’s drinking cup or his
  food (oppose his Energetic to Poison 15), or create a small fire at
  the main entrance to divert the guard’s attention.
     If all else fails, the thieves shoot arrows from a hidden posi-
  tion first, then attack the guard with daggers (swords and other
  melee weapons are at –5 due to lack of combat space) and try to
  take the treasure by force.
     If the thieves succeed, they take the treasure out through
  the freshly-dug hole and run for it.
     If the thieves manage to get the treasure in either attempt,
  the Player-knights have one last chance to catch them by chas-
  ing them down. The Gamemaster should run a small Chase (see
  The Hunt, below). Influencing factors are the horses’ Movement
  Rates, and the Player-knights’ skills in Hunting (to correctly fol-
  low the thieves’ tracks), Horsemanship (for extra speed), Folk
  Lore or Standing [commoners] (to get correct hints about what
  way the thieves went).
     Conclusion: If the treasure got stolen from under the
  Player-knights’ noses, or if the Player-knights catch the thieves
  but fail to find back the treasure, the abbot will be furious. They
  lose a point in both Honor and Standing [Church].
     If nothing gets stolen, or if the thieves are caught and their
  loot is retrieved, the abbot thanks the Player-knights and gives
  them an appropriate reward (worth a number of £ equal to
  each knight’s Glory/1,000). They gain a point in Honor and
  Standing [Church].
     Glory: 50 for protecting the treasure; 50 for catching the
  thieves; 25 for unmasking the hoax miracle.

Player-knights propose or demand is refused. If the host recog-
      nizes their mission as just and fair, the Player-knights may still
      try to achieve their objectives.
        On a successful Intrigue roll, a Player-knights gets another
      opportunity to advance one of the embassy’s goals. Depending
      on the nature of the objective, another roll is needed for it to
      materialize. For example, proposing a peace marriage may need a
      final roll in Romance or Honor.
        Conclusion: Unless the Gamemaster wishes to use it as an
      introduction to the next adventure, the return voyage should be
      a formality. At their safe return, the hostages (if any) are released,
      and the Player-knights must relate their adventure to the per-
      son who sent them on their perilous mission. If they have been
      particularly successful, the Player-knights may gain points in
      Honor, Amor, Love, and/or Standing [lord], as appropriate.
        Glory: 50 per goal obtained.
      Adventure: The  Greedy  Abbot

A local abbot enrolls the Player-knights in his service to
      protect the church treasures of his abbey, which are displayed on
      the church altar next to the local saint’s relics during the yearly
      market.
        Setting: A rich abbey, its church, and the market grounds.
        Characters: Abbot Nortgaud (Deceitful, Selfish, Suspicious);
      a band of three thieves (use bandit statistics, page 374).
        Problem: Anticipate the plans of the thieves, recognize
      their preparations and catch them red-handed.
        Secrets: The “miracle” at the saint’s relics is a hoax orga-
      nized by the monks for the enrichment of their abbey.
        Actions and Solutions: To effectively prevent thieves
      from stealing the exposed church treasure, the Player-knights
      should first examine the surroundings, evaluate the risks and
      take their precautions. To gain bonuses on future rolls, a Player-
      knight must either come up with some clever ideas or succeed
      in an appropriate skill roll (+2 per critical, +1 per success, –2
      per fumble), such as Awareness (to spot a construction weak-
      ness), Hunting (to determine possible escape routes for thieves),
      Recognize (to see if anyone reported the presence of a notorious
      robber band), or Religion (to be aware of the exact procedures
      during the religious processions and the veneration of relics).
        The market fair lasts for a whole week. Sometime during the
      first three days the thieves make their first attempt. Their plan is
      for two of them to start pushing the crowd, creating a dangerous
      mass movement forwards. As the crowd reaches the altar, one of
      the thieves snatches a treasure away, while his accomplice puts a
      valuable object in an innocent pilgrim’s mantle, whom the third
      thief loudly accuses, while the first thief sneaks away.
        Unless the Player-knights anticipated such a plan and
      therefore have a good chance of foiling it, the thieves will suc-
      ceed. However, a vigilant Player-knight (roll Awareness) may

Recognize the real thief and try to catch him before he reaches
  the narrow streets of the town (where horses are at a disadvan-
  tage) or the nearby forest.
     Some days later, men and women praying at the tomb of the
  local saint inside the church are suddenly seized with epilepsy.
  Many pilgrims present at the site panic, and try to calm the anger
  of their saint by gifts of gold, silver and cattle.
     This is not another thieves’ trick. If the Player-knights in-
  terrogate the “victims,” they may Recognize some monks from
  the abbey. If they confront the abbot with this fact, he arrests
  the monks (per church law) and promises painful chastisement
  for the “depraved sinners.” Only if the Player-knights insist will
  the abbot make a public announcement and return some of the
  pilgrim’s money.
     The last night of the fair, the thieves make their second at-
  tempt, if the first one failed or if none of them were caught the
  first time. Alternatively, a second band of robbers has a go at the
  treasure. At night, the thieves actually try to pierce the church
  walls! Once more, unless the players anticipated this, the thieves
  succeed, though vigilant Player-knights (roll Awareness) may be
  attracted by suspicious noise and get a bonus to their chase roll
  or, on a critical, catch the thieves red-handed.
     If the players keep a permanent watch over the altar and the
  relics, the thieves will try to drug the guard’s drinking cup or his
  food (oppose his Energetic to Poison 15), or create a small fire at
  the main entrance to divert the guard’s attention.
     If all else fails, the thieves shoot arrows from a hidden posi-
  tion first, then attack the guard with daggers (swords and other
  melee weapons are at –5 due to lack of combat space) and try to
  take the treasure by force.
     If the thieves succeed, they take the treasure out through
  the freshly-dug hole and run for it.
     If the thieves manage to get the treasure in either attempt,
  the Player-knights have one last chance to catch them by chas-
  ing them down. The Gamemaster should run a small Chase (see
  The Hunt, below). Influencing factors are the horses’ Movement
  Rates, and the Player-knights’ skills in Hunting (to correctly fol-
  low the thieves’ tracks), Horsemanship (for extra speed), Folk
  Lore or Standing [commoners] (to get correct hints about what
  way the thieves went).
     Conclusion: If the treasure got stolen from under the
  Player-knights’ noses, or if the Player-knights catch the thieves
  but fail to find back the treasure, the abbot will be furious. They
  lose a point in both Honor and Standing [Church].
     If nothing gets stolen, or if the thieves are caught and their
  loot is retrieved, the abbot thanks the Player-knights and gives
  them an appropriate reward (worth a number of £ equal to
  each knight’s Glory/1,000). They gain a point in Honor and
  Standing [Church].
     Glory: 50 for protecting the treasure; 50 for catching the
  thieves; 25 for unmasking the hoax miracle.

Adventure: Guarding  Maugis

        The Player-knights’ lord brings them a prisoner to guard:
      the noted sorcerer-knight, Sir Maugis. The lord himself will be
      absent for the rest of the adventure, leaving the Player-knights
      in charge.
        Setting: The lord’s castle, before the year 772, or after 795.
        Characters: Sir Maugis. Even in prison, he is always coop-
      erative, polite and quite at ease.
        Problem: They must not hurt their prisoner (unless they
      want to attract the undying hatred of the House of Clermont),
      and the resourceful magician has many cards up his sleeve. He
      will undoubtedly escape, unless the Player-knights come up with
      some clever ideas.
        Secrets: Maugis can use herbs and powders to send peo-
      ple to sleep. He has the power to cast less-powerful spells, which
      may untie knots, open doors, and work any other subtle form
      magic the Gamemaster desires.
        Actions: The first thing the Player-knights need to decide
      are the imprisonment conditions of Sir Maugis:
        Where do they keep him? The stone cellar under the castle
      is a strong prison, but it makes it easier for Maugis to predict
      where he is exactly.
        Do they bind Maugis’ hands and feet? If so, this causes
      some problems for the daily routines.
        Do they put a gag in his mouth to prevent him from speak-
      ing? This is considered an unknightly and degrading treatment,
      which costs a point of Honor. If they do put something in his
      mouth, Sir Maugis goes all red in the face and actually faints
      from suffocation (this is a trick to scare the Player-knights into
      removing the gag).
        Where do they keep Maugis’ personal effects, including his
      sword, but especially his potions and powders? Simply handling
      the latter exposes a Player-knight to the following adverse effects
      (roll 1d6):
             Magical Powder effects
      1d6 Result Powder Effect
         1   Magical sleep for [Lazy] hours.

         2   A violent rash causing a –5 to all actions for [Indulgent]
             days.
         3   Can’t speak for [Deceitful] days.
         4   Deafness or blindness for [Lustful] hours.
         5   An impenetrable mist or darkness fills the castle for
             [Arbitrary] hours.
         6   Inability to use weapons for [Cowardly] hours.
        Note: None of these magical effects can be used against
      Maugis himself.
        The next step is to establish the daily routine. Sir Maugis
      needs to go to the lavatory and eat. To perform these actions,
      Sir Maugis needs his feet, hands or mouth free. If the Player-
      knights agree to liberate his hands or remove his gag, the wizard
rightColumn:
discretely performs or whispers a magic formula, the effect of
  which will not be immediately visible, but allows him to escape
  later. Possibilities include turning a stone into bread or trans-
  forming a small object into a key.
     The Player-knights probably keep Maugis under strict sur-
  veillance. If a knight stands guard alone during the night, he
  must roll Energetic to stay permanently vigilant. On a failed roll,
  Maugis finds a way to escape; a powder hidden inside one of the
  buttons of his shirt allows Maugis to create an illusion (a call for
  help, an angel, a fire) to divert his guard’s attention. This gives
  him time to perform sufficient magic to escape.
     If Maugis escapes, the Player-knights should have a chance
  to capture him again and return him to his cell. Success depends
  on the Player-knights’ precautions and the means Maugis uses
  to carry out his escape; equipment, magic items, a horse, suffi-
  cient geographic knowledge, external aid, etc. Along with care-
  ful planning and clever ideas, opposed rolls in Awareness (notice
  traces of Maugis’ recent or current activities), Hunting (where
  is he heading?), Recognize (Maugis is probably disguised!), or
  Intrigue (find a helpful witness), may all be appropriate.
     Solutions: Taking away Maugis’ equipment (herbs and
  powders) is essential. Note that Maugis won’t reveal the power
  or use of any of his possessions under any circumstances. Next,
  he must be guarded day and night, and preferably bound tightly
  with a gag in his mouth. Even this cannot prevent Maugis from
  escaping; anticipating his subsequent actions gives the Player-
  knights a chance to keep their troublesome prisoner in their
  power.
     Conclusion: If the Player-knights fail their delicate mission,
  they lose a point of Honor and Standing [lord]. If they somehow
  hurt Sir Maugis, they lose a point of Honor and the entire house
  of Clermont (Aymon, Renaud and his brothers, Bradamant, and
  all their relatives) develop a Hate [Player-knights]. Shortly after
  the adventure, they solemnly declare a feud to avenge the insult
  and harm done to their kinsman.
     Glory: 50 for successfully keeping Sir Maugis in prison un-
  til the lord’s return.
  Adventure:  Love Conquers   All
     In this adventure the Player-knights must help one of their
  own in an accelerated wooing of his lady (especially a foreign
  lady in a far-away land), following the rules of fin’amor.
     Setting: Any court. Phase 2 or after (or during Phase 1 at
  the royal court).
     Characters: The Player-knight’s amor (Awareness 8); the
  lady’s husband (or father) (Suspicious 10); some romantic rivals
  (notable or famous knights).
     Problem: Conquer the lady’s heart before a rival does!
     Secrets: Is the lady sincerely in love with the Player-knight,
  or is she just playing a cruel game with him?
     Actions and Solutions: If the Player-knight has not yet
  done so, he must meet the lady alone in a secret place and declare
  his love for her in an appropriate manner. The Player-knights

title: Adventure:
leftColumn:
may make a cunning plan to get the husband away from the
      knight’s lady-love, or simply make a Romance roll (any one
      Player-knight) opposed to the husband’s Suspicious or Romance
      to see if the lovers get caught or not. On a fumbled Romance, the
      husband catches a Player-knight (not necessarily the one in love)
      participating in the stealthy maneuver, and accuses him of mess-
      ing around with his wife. Resolve this either by a challenge to
      first blood, or by the payment of a fine (half the knight’s herib-
      annum value) and the loss of a point of Honor.
        Once they can meet, generate an Amor value for the knight,
      and a Potential Amor for the lady.
        If the knight rolls 16 or more for his Amor, he is truly in
      love with the lady, and will do his best to win her. If he rolls lower
      than 16, he can decide to not follow up on the passion, flirting
      with her only for the romance of it. But if he decides to keep the
      Amor, he must stick it out!
        Once the meeting takes place, the Player-knight must find
      an elegant way to declare his ardor. Roll Amor [lady]. After a
      successful declaration the lady virtuously rejects her suitor, but
      later sends him a message demanding that he confirm his love
      in public. If the Amor roll fails, the lady is not convinced and
      she will ignore the Player-knight until he proves his love in some
      other spectacular way.
        To confirm his love, the Player-knight must state his pas-
      sion in public, using a coded message. Any Player-knight may
      roll Romance and any one of: Eloquence, Play instruments,
      or Singing (player’s choice). On a failed Performance roll, the
      knight nervously failed in his presentation and didn’t manage to
      pass on the message; on a failed Romance roll the lady misunder-
      stood the message and possibly mistakes the identity of her ad-
      mirer (the Player-knights should try again). A fumbled Romance
      roll indicates that one of the other knights present (not the hus-
      band) becomes suspicious of one of the Player-knights (again,
      not necessarily the one in love), and will watch him closely from
      now on (sending spies, popping up at inconvenient moments, or
      hindering him at delicate tasks).
        Various rivals, or their representatives, also address their
      messages of love. A critical success in Romance is needed to
      discern their identity, while a normal success gives the player
      just a hint. If a Player-knight confronts a rival, he challenges the
      Player-knight to a duel (to first blood) for the right to court the
      lady. A knight who loses such a combat goes mad with frustra-
      tion and flees into the forest (see Madness on page 431).
        The lady requires multiple tests of her suitors (see Table 19–
      28: Lover’s Tasks from the Romance solo scenario). Remember
      that at any stage of the romance there is always the danger of the

        Once they can meet, generate an Amor value for the knight,

        If the knight rolls 16 or more for his Amor, he is truly in
      love with the lady, and will do his best to win her. If he rolls lower
      than 16, he can decide to not follow up on the passion, flirting
      with her only for the romance of it. But if he decides to keep the
      Amor, he must stick it out!
        Once the meeting takes place, the Player-knight must find
      an elegant way to declare his ardor. Roll Amor [lady]. After a
      successful declaration the lady virtuously rejects her suitor, but
      later sends him a message demanding that he confirm his love
      in public. If the Amor roll fails, the lady is not convinced and
      she will ignore the Player-knight until he proves his love in some
      other spectacular way.

      sion in public, using a coded message. Any Player-knight may
      roll Romance and any one of: Eloquence, Play instruments,
      or Singing (player’s choice). On a failed Performance roll, the
      knight nervously failed in his presentation and didn’t manage to
      pass on the message; on a failed Romance roll the lady misunder-
      stood the message and possibly mistakes the identity of her ad-
      mirer (the Player-knights should try again). A fumbled Romance
      roll indicates that one of the other knights present (not the hus-
      band) becomes suspicious of one of the Player-knights (again,
      not necessarily the one in love), and will watch him closely from
      now on (sending spies, popping up at inconvenient moments, or
      hindering him at delicate tasks).

      discern their identity, while a normal success gives the player

leftColumn:
nor of other arms, to do wonderful things. His prodigious
       strength sufficed. At the first wrench of his mighty arm
       he tore up a pine-tree by the roots. Oaks, beeches, ma-
       ples, whatever he met in his path, yielded in like manner.
       The ancient forest soon became as bare as the borders of
       a morass, where the fowler has cleared away the bushes
       to spread his nets. The shepherds, hearing the horrible
       crashing in the forest, abandoned their flocks to run and
       see the cause of this unwonted uproar. By their evil star,
       or for their sins, they were led thither. When they saw the
       furious state the count was in, and his incredible force,
       they would fain have fled out of his reach, but in their
       fears lost their presence of mind. The madman pursued
       them, seized one and rent him limb from limb, as easily
       as one would pull ripe apples from a tree. He took another
       by the feet, and used him as a club to knock down a third.
       The shepherds fled; but it would have been hard for any
       to escape, if he had not at that moment left them to throw
       himself with the same fury upon their flocks. The peas-
       ants, abandoning their plows and harrows, mounted on
       the roofs of buildings and pinnacles of the rocks, afraid to
       trust themselves even to the oaks and pines. From such
       heights they looked on, trembling at the raging fury of the
       unhappy Orlando. His fists, his teeth, his nails, his feet,
       seize, break, and tear cattle, sheep, and swine; the most
       swift in flight alone being able to escape him. When at
       last terror had scattered everything before him, he en-
       tered a cottage which was abandoned by its inhabitants,
       and there found that which served for food. His long fast
       had caused him to feel the most ravenous hunger. Seiz-
       ing whatever he found that was eatable, whether roots,
       acorns, or bread, raw meat or cooked, he gorged it indis-
       criminately. Issuing thence again, the frantic Orlando
       gave chase to whatever living thing he saw, whether men
       or animals. Sometimes he pursued the deer and hind,
       sometimes he attacked bears and wolves, and with his
       naked hands killed and tore them, and devoured their
       flesh. Thus he wandered, from place to place.
           — Orlando Furioso, VIII
        To put a bit of pressure on the Player-knights, they are not
      the only ones who have accepted the mission of bringing back
      the paladin. One of their rivals is on his track and trying to com-
      plete this mission before the Player-knights do.
        When the knight find their “prey,” the savage paladin has
      obviously gone temporarily Melancholic for one reason or an-
      other (see Passions in Chapter 3). Whether he is unarmed or not,
      to take the paladin back to court the knights should subdue him
      without physically harming him.
        Solutions: Once the paladin has been captured, the knights
      should seek to bring him back to his senses. To achieve this, they
      need to know what caused the paladin’s Melancholy and then at-
      tempt the dangerous task of healing him. If they fail, the paladin
      attacks them and flees into the woods again.
rightColumn:
Conclusion: If the Player-knights bring back the paladin
  in good physical and mental health, the king is very pleased and
  grant them a favor or a gift. If not, he thanks them all the same
  and sends others to continue the search.
     Glory: 100 for bringing back the Melancholic paladin to
  court.
  Adventure:  The  Miracle of Truth

     The bishop demands the Player-knights accompany and
  protect a missionary into Saxon territory, where the holy man
  will sanctify a pagan site, baptize the local population, and build
  a church where he can display his relics.
     Setting: A village of Frankish settlers in the Saxon border
  land.
     Characters: A missionary (Love [God] 18, Deceitful 16);
  a “blind” Saxon; a Frankish village chief.
     Problem: Seemingly, the hostile Saxon population can
  only be converted when threatened by fire and sword. The mis-
  sionary, however, thinks he can sway them by showing them
  some fake miracles.
     Secrets: The pious missionary is a fraud. He unscrupulous-
  ly stages tricks to convince the local Saxons to believe in God’s
  superiority.
     Actions: At the village, the missionary pretends to have
  an angelic vision, confirmed by a (fake) letter which falls from
  heaven. The next day, he demands the Player-knights accompa-
  ny him into the woods, where he freely distributes good white
  clothes to all Saxons. The priest then sets out to prove the power
  of God by miraculously curing a “blind” Saxon accomplice (who
  leaves on a “pilgrimage” the next day). He voluntarily submits to
  a trial of boiling water. In fact, he fools the spectators by “retriev-
  ing” a white stone which he placed in his sleeve beforehand. Roll
  Awareness –5 to spot this.
     If they spot his tricks, the knights may either unmask the
  priest as a fraud or let him manipulate the Saxons freely. If con-
  fronted with his trickery in private, the holy man admits to the
  fakery, but tries to convince the knights that it’s the only way
  to stay alive and to bring these savage Saxons onto the path of
  salvation. To him, the ends justify the means. Will the knights
  tell the people, or not?
     Meanwhile, the knights should mobilize the villagers to
  build a suitable church for the relics and to raise some defenses.
  A steward, masons or other Frankish specialist personnel will
  reduce the time to finish these works, but they demand double
  their normal pay due to the danger.
     Rumors of an imminent Saxon attack grow stronger and
  stronger. Unless the knights take precautions, the missionary
  abandons the village and disappears, leaving his precious reli-
  quary behind. When the Saxons launch their massive raid, they
  particularly aim to destroy the church and its reliquary.
     Solutions: A true miracle convinces the Saxons to genu-
  inely convert and accept the True Faith. In that case, the new

      to take the paladin back to court the knights should subdue him
      without physically harming him.
        Solutions: Once the paladin has been captured, the knights
      should seek to bring him back to his senses. To achieve this, they
      need to know what caused the paladin’s Melancholy and then at-
      tempt the dangerous task of healing him. If they fail, the paladin
      attacks them and flees into the woods again.

Conclusion: If the Player-knights bring back the paladin
  in good physical and mental health, the king is very pleased and
  grant them a favor or a gift. If not, he thanks them all the same
  and sends others to continue the search.
     Glory: 100 for bringing back the Melancholic paladin to
  court.
  Adventure:  The  Miracle of Truth

The bishop demands the Player-knights accompany and
  protect a missionary into Saxon territory, where the holy man
  will sanctify a pagan site, baptize the local population, and build
  a church where he can display his relics.
     Setting: A village of Frankish settlers in the Saxon border
  land.
     Characters: A missionary (Love [God] 18, Deceitful 16);
  a “blind” Saxon; a Frankish village chief.
     Problem: Seemingly, the hostile Saxon population can
  only be converted when threatened by fire and sword. The mis-
  sionary, however, thinks he can sway them by showing them
  some fake miracles.
     Secrets: The pious missionary is a fraud. He unscrupulous-
  ly stages tricks to convince the local Saxons to believe in God’s
  superiority.
     Actions: At the village, the missionary pretends to have
  an angelic vision, confirmed by a (fake) letter which falls from
  heaven. The next day, he demands the Player-knights accompa-
  ny him into the woods, where he freely distributes good white
  clothes to all Saxons. The priest then sets out to prove the power
  of God by miraculously curing a “blind” Saxon accomplice (who
  leaves on a “pilgrimage” the next day). He voluntarily submits to
  a trial of boiling water. In fact, he fools the spectators by “retriev-
  ing” a white stone which he placed in his sleeve beforehand. Roll
  Awareness –5 to spot this.
     If they spot his tricks, the knights may either unmask the
  priest as a fraud or let him manipulate the Saxons freely. If con-
  fronted with his trickery in private, the holy man admits to the
  fakery, but tries to convince the knights that it’s the only way
  to stay alive and to bring these savage Saxons onto the path of
  salvation. To him, the ends justify the means. Will the knights
  tell the people, or not?
     Meanwhile, the knights should mobilize the villagers to
  build a suitable church for the relics and to raise some defenses.
  A steward, masons or other Frankish specialist personnel will
  reduce the time to finish these works, but they demand double
  their normal pay due to the danger.
     Rumors of an imminent Saxon attack grow stronger and
  stronger. Unless the knights take precautions, the missionary
  abandons the village and disappears, leaving his precious reli-
  quary behind. When the Saxons launch their massive raid, they
  particularly aim to destroy the church and its reliquary.
     Solutions: A true miracle convinces the Saxons to genu-
  inely convert and accept the True Faith. In that case, the new

leftColumn:
converts can be given plots of lands as settlers, and they may even
      fight alongside the Franks. Otherwise, they just pay lip service
      to the new god and wait for an occasion to revert to their pagan
      habits. They leave the village if the church burns down, the priest
      is killed, or the relics disappear.
        If the missionary disappears, the knights can abandon
      the village without loss of Honor, as their mission was to pro-
      tect him. Or they can stand their ground and fight. Defeating
      a Saxon war lord in single combat prevents further Saxon at-
      tacks. Negotiating peace with their enemy is not a viable option,
      as the Saxons will certainly renounce their oaths at the first
      opportunity.
        Conclusion: If the church and the inhabitants all survive
      this adventure, the village is granted as an immunity to a Player-
      knight by the bishop who sent the missionary in the first place.
        Glory: 50 for building a church; +25 per year for maintain-
      ing a Christian outpost in Saxony.
      Adventure: The  Noble Hostage
        Your lord puts you in charge of a foreign noble hostage (a
      Saxon chief, a Saracen prince, or a Moorish knight), whom you
      must lodge and guard.
        Setting: A Player-knight’s manor.

        Characters: A foreign noble hostage (Proud, Chivalrous);
      the Player-knight’s lord; worried peasants.
        Problem: Since the hostage arrived, a series of strange and
      disturbing things have happened around the manor: the chap-
      el was destroyed by lightning, a baby was born with no arms, a
      plague of stinking red flies poisoned the pond, or other disas-
      ters and portents. The local population is getting worried. The
      Player-knights are invited to come and see the sites where the
      strange events took place. The populace then asks for a local as-
      sembly, where the mallus formally accuses the hostage of being
      the cause of all the recent harm, claiming the pagan is a sorcerer,
      or just an insult to God, who shows his wrath by punishing the
      hosts.
        Secrets: What causes all the trouble? Is it sheer coinci-
      dence? Is the hostage indeed a sorcerer? Is there a vengeful
      Faerie? Some great shameful collective sin which must be atoned
      for?
        Actions: Although knights who Hate the hostage may
      feel inclined to agree with the commoners, the Player-knight’s
      Honor dictates obedience to the lord’s orders, so they’ll have
      to protect their hostage (and possibly themselves!) against the
      wrath of the population. In any case, tensions on the domain
      slowly rise: a foreign merchant is molested, the manor retinue is
      publicly threatened, the chapel is desecrated, or a manorial barn
      goes up in flames.
        If the knights take the accusations seriously, they probably
      search the hostage’s room and luggage, spy on him at night, etc.
      This should be done delicately (searching while he is not there,
      for example), since otherwise the haughty hostage will surely feel
rightColumn:
insulted. He can challenge the offenders or threaten their lord
  with some sort of painful retaliation.
     Solutions: Since the hostage is not a Christian, he cannot
  prove his innocence by a traditional trial, though a knight may
  take his place. Submitting successfully to such a trial proves the
  hostage’s innocence. If strange events continue to occur, the pop-
  ulation finds a new scapegoat and everything starts all over again.
     An unusually happy event or a miracle may end the series of
  bad omens and convince the population of the Player-knights’ righ-
  teousness and the hostage’s innocence. Converting the hostage may
  satisfy everybody as well, if the enigmatic events then stop.
     Conclusion: If the players give in and let the locals have it
  their way, the hostage is hanged. While this gains them popu-
  larity among the commoners (raise the Player-knights’ Standing
  [commoners]), the Player-knights will have to face their lord’s
  fury (reduce their Honor and Standing [lord]).
     If the knights protect their hostage but fail to appease the
  peasants, the risk of rebellion becomes real. On a failed standing
  roll, a large band of hot-headed commoners comes to the manor
  with torches and pitchforks in order to take justice into their
  own hands.
     If the knights dutifully protect the hostage, clear him of sus-
  picion, and keep the peace at the manor, the lord is very satisfied
  (raise his standing by 1), while the grateful noble hostage himself
  gives his hosts a precious gift (worth their Glory/£1,000) and
  his friendship.
     An additional complication can occur if the hostage’s kin
  breaks their oaths. The lord will order his execution, but will
  the Player-knights obey if they know their hostage to be an hon-
  orable, or even Chivalrous, man (like young Ogier or Sancho
  Lupus) ? If they do kill him, no doubt his kin swear vengeance,
  or an idealistic paladin may even come to claim justice for the
  wanton slaughter of a chivalrous comrade-in-arms, even though
  he is the son of a treacherous enemy!
     Glory: 50 for protecting the hostage; 75 for keeping the
  peace.

     A desperate pagan lady is betrayed by her Frankish lover
  and calls on the Player-knights for aid.
     Setting: A Saxon court in Phase 2 or later.
     Characters: Gudrun, a Saxon lady (APP 14, Honor 14,
  Chaste 14, Amor/Hate [Gervold] 14); Sir Gervold, her Frankish
  lover (Honor 11, Axe 17, 5d6 damage; best available armor);
  Lord Harvech and his daughter Theudilda; Father Ermoldus,
  the bishop.

  has now been without news from him for over half a year, and
  she fears something bad has happened to him. This is why she

  and calls on the Player-knights for aid.
     Setting: A Saxon court in Phase 2 or later.
     Characters: Gudrun, a Saxon lady (APP 14, Honor 14,
  Chaste 14, Amor/Hate [Gervold] 14); Sir Gervold, her Frankish
  lover (Honor 11, Axe 17, 5d6 damage; best available armor);
  Lord Harvech and his daughter Theudilda; Father Ermoldus,
  the bishop.
     Problem: Lady Gudrun helped her lover, Sir Gervold, to
  escape her father’s prison in return for his promise to baptize and
  marry her. Ever since Sir Gervold rode back to Frankland in free-
  dom, Lady Gudrun has awaited the return of her lover. Alas, she
  has now been without news from him for over half a year, and
  she fears something bad has happened to him. This is why she
  secretly requests the Player-knights (of whom at least one should

title: Adventure: The Pagan Prison
leftColumn:
be famous for his romantic behavior, his current fin’amor affair,
      or his Romance skill) for help.
        Secrets: None, but this might be some devious Saxon trap;
      have everyone roll Suspicious.
        Actions: The Player-knights may want to meet Lady
      Gudrun in secret at her father’s court. Getting into enemy terri-
      tory unseen needs a successful Hunting roll. On a critical, they
      arrive at Lady Gudrun’s village unnoticed. A success means they
      arrived and talk to Lady Gudrun, but are spotted and manage to
      get away before the Saxons attack, while a failure indicates they
      talk with Lady Gudrun, but did not get away in time and have
      to fight their way out of Saxony. On a fumble, some bloodthirsty
      Saxon warriors ambush them on their way to the lady, in unfa-
      vorable terrain like a steep valley or a river ford.
        If the Player-knights succeed in meeting Lady Gudrun in
      secret (any Hunting result but a fumble), she implores their help
      and agrees to almost anything honorable to assist the Frankish
      knights herself. But she threatens them with a full-scale war if
      they refuse to take her to Frankland soon, so that she can be fi-
      nally united with her lover. Her father does not take kindly to
      Frankish suitors!
        If the Player-knights know of Sir Gervold’s betrayal (see
      below) and inform Gudrun of it, she refuses to believe them at
      first. If they find a way to convince her (rolls in Honest, Honor,
      or Eloquence may be in order), Lady Gudrun goes almost mad
      with grief. Her former Amor passion turns into Hate (note that
      this now leaves the possibility for the Player-knights to court her
      themselves…).
        The Player-knights might try to find Sir Gervold. Unless
      the Gamemaster wishes to add a twist to this scenario, the
      Frankish knight broke his promise to Lady Gudrun, and has
      started to court Lord Harvech’s only daughter, whom he wishes
      to marry instead of Lady Gudrun.
        After some possible detours via Gervold’s manor (roll
      Standing [commoners] to learn more about Sir Gervold’s no-
      table character traits), his lord’s court (roll Courtesy to obtain
      more information on Gervold’s ambitions and current schemes),
      and a forest where he is said to have been seen for the last time
      (untrue; roll Hunting to realize this), the Player-knights finally
      meet Sir Gervold at Lord Harvech’s court (successful Intrigue
      needed to locate him). If they inform him of his Saxon lover’s
      insistent demand, he falsely claims that, to his great sorrow, his
      family patriarch ordered him to marry another lady and for-
      bade him to see his Saxon lover ever again. Roll Recognize and
      Suspicious to see through this blatant lie. A successful Intrigue
      roll reveals his recent courtship of Lord Harvech’s daughter.
        If the Player-knights confront Sir Gervold with his own
      falsehood, he laughingly defends himself by claiming that his
      insincere promise to a pagan has no value in the eyes of God.
      If a Player-knight wishes to challenge him in the name of True
      Love, Sir Gervold grimly accepts, but only if the fight is for con-
      quest. Should he be defeated, he agrees to marry Lady Gudrun.
      If the lady has already heard of Gervold’s infidelity, her Amor
      has turned into Hate and she will do anything to get him killed,
rightColumn:
which possibly includes betraying the Player-knights into her
  father’s vengeful hands. If he survives to marry her, he will not
  have a happy life!
     Instead of challenging Sir Gervold, the Player-knights may
  explain the situation to Lord Harvech and inform him of the
  grave political implications this affair may have, rekindling war
  with the Saxons! To sway Lord Harvech, he may ask the Player-
  knights to perform some kind of small quest for him, or sim-
  ply have the Player-knights make some rolls in Honest (if the
  Player-knight is telling the truth), Prudent (“better not provoke
  the Saxons”), Honor (Gervold should be forced to respect his
  promise), or Eloquence (be convincing).
     Even if the Player-knights manage to convince Lord
  Harvech that Gervold is not a good match for his daughter,
  and that he should therefore forbid the union of his daughter
  Theudilda and Sir Gervold, the latter still doesn’t feel bound to
  keep his vow. Instead, he will seek another bride. Only if his own
  lord or some other authority commands him to do so will he
  agree to wed Lady Gudrun.
     As an ultimate recourse, the Player-knights may seek the
  support from Gervold’s lord (rolls in Eloquence, Just or Romance
  may be appropriate), or from his bishop (roll Religion and Love
  [God]). These two magnates have the power to impose right and
  proper behavior on Sir Gervold. If all fails, the Player-knights
  may be challenged to uphold the rightness of their request in a
  duel for love with the lord’s or bishop’s champion.
     Solutions: Sir Gervold must be forced to keep his given
  word and marry Lady Gudrun, or the lady must be comforted
  and successfully wooed to make her forget her former, faithless,
  lover.
     Conclusion: If the Player-knights do not succeed in bring-
  ing this adventure to a conclusion that is satisfying to Lady
  Gudrun, she convinces her father to launch a feud against either
  Sir Gervold or the Player-knights, if not both.
     Accomplishing this adventure in a romantic manner gains
  the Player-knights checks in Honor and Romance, and possibly
  the favor of a Saxon lady. This counts as a successful Lover’s Task
  for the year (see the Romance solo scenario) for all Player-knights
  currently involved in fin’amor.
     Glory: 50 for successfully aiding Lady Gudrun’s to ful-
  fill her passion; 75 for having prevented another war with the
  Saxons; 25 for a stealthy visit to a virtuous pagan lady in hostile
  territory.
  Adventure:  The  Pagan  Prison
     This is a scenario designed for Player-knights who were
  captured by a pagan lord in their previous adventure. They were
  thrown into a dark and damp prison cell and all their equipment
  (armor, weapons, personal gear) taken from them. Characters
  who were captured while Inspired will be in a state of Shock (one
  roll on Table 10–1: Aging). Due to the harsh treatment, all pris-
  oners are Impoverished and must succeed at a CON roll or lose
  a point of CON (as per Winter Phase).

        Secrets: None, but this might be some devious Saxon trap;
      have everyone roll Suspicious.
        Actions: The Player-knights may want to meet Lady
      Gudrun in secret at her father’s court. Getting into enemy terri-
      tory unseen needs a successful Hunting roll. On a critical, they
      arrive at Lady Gudrun’s village unnoticed. A success means they
      arrived and talk to Lady Gudrun, but are spotted and manage to
      get away before the Saxons attack, while a failure indicates they
      talk with Lady Gudrun, but did not get away in time and have
      to fight their way out of Saxony. On a fumble, some bloodthirsty
      Saxon warriors ambush them on their way to the lady, in unfa-
      vorable terrain like a steep valley or a river ford.
        If the Player-knights succeed in meeting Lady Gudrun in
      secret (any Hunting result but a fumble), she implores their help
      and agrees to almost anything honorable to assist the Frankish
      knights herself. But she threatens them with a full-scale war if
      they refuse to take her to Frankland soon, so that she can be fi-
      nally united with her lover. Her father does not take kindly to
      Frankish suitors!
        If the Player-knights know of Sir Gervold’s betrayal (see
      below) and inform Gudrun of it, she refuses to believe them at
      first. If they find a way to convince her (rolls in Honest, Honor,
      or Eloquence may be in order), Lady Gudrun goes almost mad
      with grief. Her former Amor passion turns into Hate (note that
      this now leaves the possibility for the Player-knights to court her
      themselves…).
        The Player-knights might try to find Sir Gervold. Unless
      the Gamemaster wishes to add a twist to this scenario, the
      Frankish knight broke his promise to Lady Gudrun, and has
      started to court Lord Harvech’s only daughter, whom he wishes
      to marry instead of Lady Gudrun.
        After some possible detours via Gervold’s manor (roll
      Standing [commoners] to learn more about Sir Gervold’s no-
      table character traits), his lord’s court (roll Courtesy to obtain
      more information on Gervold’s ambitions and current schemes),
      and a forest where he is said to have been seen for the last time
      (untrue; roll Hunting to realize this), the Player-knights finally
      meet Sir Gervold at Lord Harvech’s court (successful Intrigue
      needed to locate him). If they inform him of his Saxon lover’s
      insistent demand, he falsely claims that, to his great sorrow, his
      family patriarch ordered him to marry another lady and for-
      bade him to see his Saxon lover ever again. Roll Recognize and
      Suspicious to see through this blatant lie. A successful Intrigue
      roll reveals his recent courtship of Lord Harvech’s daughter.
        If the Player-knights confront Sir Gervold with his own
      falsehood, he laughingly defends himself by claiming that his
      insincere promise to a pagan has no value in the eyes of God.
      If a Player-knight wishes to challenge him in the name of True
      Love, Sir Gervold grimly accepts, but only if the fight is for con-
      quest. Should he be defeated, he agrees to marry Lady Gudrun.
      If the lady has already heard of Gervold’s infidelity, her Amor
      has turned into Hate and she will do anything to get him killed,

which possibly includes betraying the Player-knights into her
  father’s vengeful hands. If he survives to marry her, he will not
  have a happy life!
     Instead of challenging Sir Gervold, the Player-knights may
  explain the situation to Lord Harvech and inform him of the
  grave political implications this affair may have, rekindling war
  with the Saxons! To sway Lord Harvech, he may ask the Player-
  knights to perform some kind of small quest for him, or sim-
  ply have the Player-knights make some rolls in Honest (if the
  Player-knight is telling the truth), Prudent (“better not provoke
  the Saxons”), Honor (Gervold should be forced to respect his
  promise), or Eloquence (be convincing).
     Even if the Player-knights manage to convince Lord
  Harvech that Gervold is not a good match for his daughter,
  and that he should therefore forbid the union of his daughter
  Theudilda and Sir Gervold, the latter still doesn’t feel bound to
  keep his vow. Instead, he will seek another bride. Only if his own
  lord or some other authority commands him to do so will he
  agree to wed Lady Gudrun.
     As an ultimate recourse, the Player-knights may seek the
  support from Gervold’s lord (rolls in Eloquence, Just or Romance
  may be appropriate), or from his bishop (roll Religion and Love
  [God]). These two magnates have the power to impose right and
  proper behavior on Sir Gervold. If all fails, the Player-knights
  may be challenged to uphold the rightness of their request in a
  duel for love with the lord’s or bishop’s champion.
     Solutions: Sir Gervold must be forced to keep his given
  word and marry Lady Gudrun, or the lady must be comforted
  and successfully wooed to make her forget her former, faithless,
  lover.
     Conclusion: If the Player-knights do not succeed in bring-
  ing this adventure to a conclusion that is satisfying to Lady
  Gudrun, she convinces her father to launch a feud against either
  Sir Gervold or the Player-knights, if not both.
     Accomplishing this adventure in a romantic manner gains
  the Player-knights checks in Honor and Romance, and possibly
  the favor of a Saxon lady. This counts as a successful Lover’s Task
  for the year (see the Romance solo scenario) for all Player-knights
  currently involved in fin’amor.
     Glory: 50 for successfully aiding Lady Gudrun’s to ful-
  fill her passion; 75 for having prevented another war with the
  Saxons; 25 for a stealthy visit to a virtuous pagan lady in hostile
  territory.
  Adventure:  The  Pagan  Prison
     This is a scenario designed for Player-knights who were
  captured by a pagan lord in their previous adventure. They were
  thrown into a dark and damp prison cell and all their equipment
  (armor, weapons, personal gear) taken from them. Characters
  who were captured while Inspired will be in a state of Shock (one
  roll on Table 10–1: Aging). Due to the harsh treatment, all pris-
  oners are Impoverished and must succeed at a CON roll or lose
  a point of CON (as per Winter Phase).

title: Adventure: The Rebellious Baron
leftColumn:
Setting: An enemy tower or castle in a pagan land.
        Characters: A pagan lord; a jailor; a pagan giant; a pa-
      gan princess (APP 19, Honor 15, Chaste 10, potential Amor
      [knight]).
        Problem: How to get out?
        Secrets: If you want to help the Player-knights, you can
      give them a riddle (a message, a painting) the solution to which
      is an indication to a secret escape tunnel.
        Solutions: The knights may act as the lord’s champion and
      defeat a giant, send a message for help, dig a tunnel, or hope for
      the princess to fall in love with one of them.
        Actions:
        Challenge: At one point, the local lord is challenged by a
      neighboring giant, who defies him to single combat. The lord
      asks his own knights to defend his honor, but apparently the
      reputation of the giant is so terrifying that no pagan knight steps
      forward. If the prisoners themselves don’t volunteer, the pagan
      knights propose that one of them be the lord’s champion in re-
      turn for their freedom. If the Player-knights have the favor of
      the princess, she may help them by giving them a useful magic
      object (a ring, a potion, a sword), especially if the giant cannot
      be defeated by normal means.
      A Saracen chooses a valorous Frankish prisoner as his cham-
      pion when defied by an enemy:
       “Knight, listen to me. Do you see the Giant over there,
       ready to fight? He has challenged me to a combat, and
       none of my warriors is valorous enough to dare accept be-
       ing my champion. I ask you to take on my enemy for me.
       If you defeat this Turk, I will let you return to your coun-
       try, I will accompany you all the way to Acre; likewise, all
       other Franks in my prison shall I set free because of you.
         Furthermore, I will find a solid charger and load him
       with gold; you will present it to your emperor Charlem-
       agne, and as long as I live I will send him the same gift
       every year, as a tribute in return for the lands I will hold
       from him. Finally, if Charlemagne is at war and calls me
       to arms, I will come to his aid with a hundred thousand
       warriors.
         Such a trophy can you win from me, because I prefer
       to be a freed slave in Frankland rather than pay a trib-
       ute of four silver pieces to the monster down there in the
       field. And if you prefer to stay at my court, I will offer
       you my daughter’s hand and you will rule over half my
       kingdom.”
           — Huon of Bordeaux, LXIV
        Call for Aid: The Player-knights may look for a way to
      call for help. They have to bribe a visitor or the jailor with the
      promise of future wealth, or convince the princess to give their
      coded message to an honorable merchant. If help arrives, their
      friends and family will besiege their prison. Meanwhile, the gen-
      tle princess keeps the Player-knights hidden in her own room,
      where they have to fight off pagan intruders who come looking
      for them.
rightColumn:
Tunnel: The Player-knights may simply dig a secret tunnel
  from their prison leading out to a nearby forest or dry well. This
  should be hard work (Energetic for all knights) and difficult to
  conceal (Siege for a single knight).
     Love of a Princess: If all else fails, the GM should pick
  a Player-knight to be the object of the young lady’s affections.
  Alternatively, he may roll each Knight’s APP against the lady’s
  Chaste. The princess becomes infatuated with the knight with-
  out him knowing it. Generate an Amor [Knight] for the lady at
  1d6+15.
     One night the princess visits the prison and discretely de-
  clares her love to her chosen knight. She wishes him to tell her
  romantic stories of the paladins and Charlemagne’s wonderful
  court. The chosen knight should act with caution and treat the
  princess strictly according to the rules of romance. If the Player-
  knight accepts the princess’ proposition, she gives him three ro-
  mantic tests to pass. For example: write her a simple love poem
  (test Eloquence or Languages), not abjuring their Faith when
  threatened with torture (test Valorous and Love [God]), and
  refusing her heinous plan in which she suggests slaying her own
  father (a test of Honor). If the knight successfully completes all
  three challenges, she will help the prisoners escape, on the con-
  dition that the knight baptize and marry her when they return
  to Frankland.
     Conclusion: If they managed to kill the giant as the lord’s
  champion(s), if they were ransomed by friends or liberated after
  a siege, or if they simply dug a tunnel, then the Player-knights
  can return home safely. If they escape thanks to the help of the
  princess, she demands to be baptized and married as soon as they
  are in Frankland. If the knights do not manage to escape this
  year, they can try again next year.
     Glory: 100 for escaping the pagan prison; 250 for defeating
  the giant lord; 500 for marrying the pagan princess.
  Adventure:  The Rebellious Baron
     The Player-knights are sent as envoys to the court of a re-
  fractory noble to deliver an ultimatum (a renewed demand for
  homage or fealty, a list of humbling peace conditions). The hos-
  tile noble can be their lord’s vassal, an arrogant count, a rebel-
  lious lord (Gerard of Vienne, Aymon of Dordon), or a disobedi-
  ent paladin like Renaud of Montauban or Ogier the Dane.

  courteously, but firmly, without offending or provoking their host.

over their weapons and armor, which the Player-knights have the

        While the knight escorts the guests to his lord’s castle, a
      Player-knight may try to feel him out about the lord’s reputation

      at +5 for all subsequent trait rolls, while Reckless knights suffer
      a –5 penalty.

      mocking comments on the Player-knights’ clothes, honor, or
      family to provoke them. A failed Courtesy roll indicates a knight
      loses his temper and gives a sharp reply. One of the court knights
      takes insult and tries to grab the insolent knight by the throat.

      violently to this attack.

      fers an attack with a dagger (unopposed on a failed Awareness,
      otherwise opposed by his DEX; no armor). The next round his

      coldly apologizes for “this regretful incident” and proposes med-
      ical aid, if necessary.

surrounded by hostile knights. First, all Player-knights must roll
  Courtesy to see if they do not inadvertently commit a faux pas.
  A failed roll adds –5 to the next player’s roll, a critical adds +5.
  If a fumble is rolled, the lord of the castle orders his knights to

  Player-knight must roll Eloquence. On any fumble, the lord of the
  castle haughtily sneers and leaves without giving them an answer.
  Otherwise, he dictates his reply to a clerk and give the Player-knights
  a sealed letter for their lord. Unless they politely request it, the hos-
  tile noble does not offer an escort back to the border.

  manage to reach the hostile noble’s castle and successfully deliv-
  er their message (Valorous), without bloodshed (Honor), before
  safely returning to their lord’s castle with an answer (Standing
  [lord]).

  answer.
  Adventure:  The  Small Knight
     Old, grumpy Count Hugo of La Roche organizes an old-
  styled, very unromantic tournament. All contenders must use war
  lances and other non-rebated weapons. The winner will receive
  the hand of his only granddaughter, the magnificent Bertha!
     Setting: La Roche castle, sometime in Phase 2.
     Characters: Count Hugo of La Roche; Lady Bertha of La
  Roche (APP 19); Sir Galeran (Cruel, Proud, Lustful); the Small
  Knight/Lady Alix of Salm (Vengeful).
     Problem: Everybody knows that Sir Galeran is the best
  warrior in the duchy. He is also an honorless creep. Will our
  good knights allow this monster to seize “their” gentle and in-
  nocent Lady Bertha?

  trothed to the not-quite-so-beautiful Lady Alix of Salm, who
  does not take Sir Galeran’s treason lightly. She makes a pact with
  the Devil, and plans to enter the tournament disguised as the
  Small Knight and take her vengeance on both the treacherous
  Sir Galeran and Bertha, her rival.
     Actions: Knowing Sir Galeran’s bloodthirsty reputation, few
  participants show up. Lady Bertha is horrified when she learns of
  Sir Galeran’s participation. Unmarried Player-knights can either
  simply enter the tournament and see what happens, or they can
  try to find out Sir Galeran’s weakness. If they discover Galeran’s
  prior engagement to Lady Alix, the knights may try to convince
  him not to compete. It is almost certain, however, that the proud
  and lustful knight will refuse their demand, so they will have to
  formally challenge his participation. If the knights don’t, the Small
  Knight will. One way or another, Galeran will oppose either a
  Player-knight or the Small Knight in a judicial duel.

title: Adventure: The Wrathful Lord
leftColumn:
Solutions: If the Player-knight wins this duel, he may mar-
      ry Lady Bertha. However, the knights must then find a way to
      reconcile the proud Sir Galeran and Lady Alix. For Galeran,
      they may obtain his promise to do so by granting him mercy
      in the duel. The vengeful Lady Alix, though, is still in a terrible
      state. To calm her down, the Player-knights need strong spiritual
      support, as the lady has made a pact with the Devil. This can be
      the beginning of next year’s adventure.
        If the Player-knight loses, the ridiculous Small Knight
      comes forward to insult Lady Bertha. Count Hugo challenges
      the Small Knight who, surprisingly, defeats and kills the count’s
      acting champion, Sir Galeran. Without revealing her identity,
      the Small Knight then marries Bertha, and during the night she
      commits suicide by leaping out of the tower window, together
      with the newlywed bride.
        Conclusion: If Lady Alix kills herself and Bertha, the lat-
      ter’s ghost returns to La Roche castle, where she aimlessly haunts
      the ramparts during stormy nights.
        Glory: Normal Glory for any ordinary opponents defeated
      in the bloody tournament; 100 for defending Lady Alix’s honor
      in a judicial duel; 75 for defeating Sir Galeran; 250 for marrying
      Lady Bertha; 100 for appeasing Lady Alix’s desire for vengeance
      and liberating her from the Devil’s pact.
      Adventure: The  Wrathful Lord
        A powerful lord (the Player-knight’s liege, the lord’s wife,
      the family patriarch, the bishop, a Frankish princess or the
      queen), personally entrusts the Player-knights with a secret and
      dishonorable mission: they must slay the hated Sir Hardouin.
      This despicable knight was recently condemned to go on a long
      pilgrimage to repent for his bloody sins and seal the peace be-
      tween two feuding houses.
        Setting: Any.
        Characters: A powerful lord (or lady); the intended vic-
      tims: Sir Hardouin (notable knight; Arbitrary 18, Cruel 16,
      Suspicious 17, Honor 6) and his companions (ordinary knights);
      vengeful pursuers (ordinary knights).
        Problem: Will the Player-knights shamelessly obey the
      iniquitous order, or can they find an alternative solution which
      preserves their honor?
        Secrets: The order may in fact be a twisted test of Chivalry.
      Or not.
        Actions: If the Player-knights accept (check Arbitrary)
      or pretend to accept (check Just and Deceitful) the lord’s com-
      mand, they may proceed to following their target.
rightColumn:
If the Player-knights refuse to obey, the lord goes mad with
  frustration and anger. In a state of blind fury, he insults them and
  eventually cries out his hate against the Player-knights, declaring
  them outlaws and his personal enemies. He attacks them with
  his dinner knife and must be restrained by his servants.
     Player-knights who are attacked by the lord must make
  an appropriate passion roll (Honor or Love [family]) to see if
  they can handle the Shock (see Passions in Chapter 3) of being
  betrayed by a social better. Only Player-knights who fail their
  passion roll avoid being shocked. Those who succeeded at their
  passion must roll on Table 10–1: Aging.
     The Player-knights must now either track the victim, or es-
  cape the knights whom their wrathful lords sends after them!
  This step takes the form of a Chase (see Chases and Pursuits,
  below). To gain some advantages, the Player-knights may come
  up with several ideas or subterfuges. Among others, the follow-
  ing rolls may be particularly appropriate: Standing [Church,
  commoners] (receive help along the road from local farmers or
  clergy), Awareness (spot signs of the opponents’ presence), Folk
  Lore (find a short cut through the countryside), Horsemanship
  (pure speed); Hunting (allows pursuers to know Sir Hardouin’s
  intended destination and the road he will be taking, or give flee-
  ing Player-knights a means to find an escape route), Recognize
  (did Sir Hardouin pass by this road; did the pursuers ask around
  for the Player-knights here?), or Swimming (to cross a river).
     For the final confrontation, the Player-knights may either
  challenge (check Honor) or ambush (check Deceitful, lose a
  point in Honor) their opponents.
     Solutions: Instead of wanton bloodshed and the possible
  rekindling of a feud, the Player-knights may persuade their op-
  ponents to join their side. Pursuers must be convinced that their
  lord is a cruel and dishonorable traitor who does not deserve
  their loyalty (win an opposed passion roll).
     As for Sir Hardouin, once informed of the situation, he
  may accept the Player-knights’ protection against possible retal-
  iatory acts from the wrathful lord, and speak up for them later.
  However, Sir Hardouin is a nasty piece of work. He will not eas-
  ily trust the Player-knights and may try to double-cross them at
  the first occasion!
     Conclusion: There is probably little chance of a satisfying
  outcome to this adventure. Either the Player-knights obey their
  lord and commit a deed which stains their honor, or their dis-
  obey their lord’s shameful command and so attract his wrath.
     Glory: 100 for finding a peaceful solution.

      tims: Sir Hardouin (notable knight; Arbitrary 18, Cruel 16,
      Suspicious 17, Honor 6) and his companions (ordinary knights);
      vengeful pursuers (ordinary knights).
        Problem: Will the Player-knights shamelessly obey the
      iniquitous order, or can they find an alternative solution which
      preserves their honor?
        Secrets: The order may in fact be a twisted test of Chivalry.
      Or not.
        Actions: If the Player-knights accept (check Arbitrary)
      or pretend to accept (check Just and Deceitful) the lord’s com-
      mand, they may proceed to following their target.

If the Player-knights refuse to obey, the lord goes mad with
  frustration and anger. In a state of blind fury, he insults them and
  eventually cries out his hate against the Player-knights, declaring
  them outlaws and his personal enemies. He attacks them with
  his dinner knife and must be restrained by his servants.
     Player-knights who are attacked by the lord must make
  an appropriate passion roll (Honor or Love [family]) to see if
  they can handle the Shock (see Passions in Chapter 3) of being
  betrayed by a social better. Only Player-knights who fail their
  passion roll avoid being shocked. Those who succeeded at their
  passion must roll on Table 10–1: Aging.
     The Player-knights must now either track the victim, or es-
  cape the knights whom their wrathful lords sends after them!
  This step takes the form of a Chase (see Chases and Pursuits,
  below). To gain some advantages, the Player-knights may come
  up with several ideas or subterfuges. Among others, the follow-
  ing rolls may be particularly appropriate: Standing [Church,
  commoners] (receive help along the road from local farmers or
  clergy), Awareness (spot signs of the opponents’ presence), Folk
  Lore (find a short cut through the countryside), Horsemanship
  (pure speed); Hunting (allows pursuers to know Sir Hardouin’s
  intended destination and the road he will be taking, or give flee-
  ing Player-knights a means to find an escape route), Recognize
  (did Sir Hardouin pass by this road; did the pursuers ask around
  for the Player-knights here?), or Swimming (to cross a river).
     For the final confrontation, the Player-knights may either
  challenge (check Honor) or ambush (check Deceitful, lose a
  point in Honor) their opponents.
     Solutions: Instead of wanton bloodshed and the possible
  rekindling of a feud, the Player-knights may persuade their op-
  ponents to join their side. Pursuers must be convinced that their
  lord is a cruel and dishonorable traitor who does not deserve
  their loyalty (win an opposed passion roll).
     As for Sir Hardouin, once informed of the situation, he
  may accept the Player-knights’ protection against possible retal-
  iatory acts from the wrathful lord, and speak up for them later.
  However, Sir Hardouin is a nasty piece of work. He will not eas-
  ily trust the Player-knights and may try to double-cross them at
  the first occasion!
     Conclusion: There is probably little chance of a satisfying
  outcome to this adventure. Either the Player-knights obey their
  lord and commit a deed which stains their honor, or their dis-
  obey their lord’s shameful command and so attract his wrath.
     Glory: 100 for finding a peaceful solution.

title: The Hunt
leftColumn:
The   H

      K
         nights hunt for a number of reasons: to get meat for the
         table, to eliminate predators, and for recreation.
         Preparation

        A hunt is normally divided into segments of about an hour
      in length. A single day allows up to 6 segments in winter, 8 in
      spring and autumn, and 10 in summer. Once the segments have
      elapsed, the hunt is over for the day.
        During each hunting segment the hunters engage in many activ-
      ities: mostly searching for tracks, finding the best way to ride through
      the brush, listening for sounds of the chase, and so on. Tracks and
      trails are fairly easily found and pursued with the help of dogs and
      peasants. All of these things are represented by the Hunting skill.
        Some characters may not have much faith in their Hunting
      ability. They can choose to just follow someone else with a better
      Hunting value. These followers do not make Hunting rolls, but
      then they will not mislead the others, either, and will probably
      arrive in time for the kill.

title: Chases and Pursuits
leftColumn:
Surprise Attack
        Once hunters have caught up to the quarry, the first char-
      acter on the scene may make one free attack, as long as he can
      close to melee distance or has a missile weapon with adequate
      range; alternately, he can choose to stay near the creature until
      reinforcements arrive to attack it in normal melee.
        If more than one character arrives on the same segment, any
      character with Glory or rank significantly higher than the others
      should be allowed the first attack. Otherwise, whoever has the high-
      est Movement Rate (or, if tied, DEX score) gets the first attack.
        The surprise attack is an opposed roll pitting the hunter’s
      weapon skill roll against the prey’s Avoidance roll. Check the re-
      sult on the Table 19–12.
      The Rush

        If the quarry lives after a surprise attack, as many as three
      characters with melee weapons (plus any number of ranged at-
      tackers) may attempt another attack, if possible, while the beast
      tries to either escape or close with its attackers. The prey still uses
      its Avoidance value to oppose attacks during the rush, rather
      than an opposed combat roll.
                           Chases    and

      S
         ometimes two characters chase each other on foot or on
         horse, or a creature is chased by several characters (or vice
         versa!). Chases should be fast, thrilling and spectacular,
      involving riotous movement, interesting terrain or obstacles, and
      danger, and they should advance the plot.
        The hunting procedure may be used for chases. For every
      step, instead of opposing a modified Hunting roll to the prey’s
      Avoidance, use the relative speeds of the pursuer and the pursued.
      Speed and  Movement
        First, break down the chase into stages. On the average, you
      should have no more than ten stages per chase. Decide who partic-
      ipates and the base speed of the groups (try to keep things simple).
        Then, decide the unit of measurement (the scale) you want
      to use for the chase. This can be anything from yards to miles,
      or even days of travel. Finally, determine the initial distance (in
      units of measurement) that separates the two chasing groups.
        At each stage of the race, roll 1d6 for both groups, and ap-
      ply the following Modifiers:
       n
        Each unit of speed difference: +/–1;
       n
        Each clever delaying tactic: +1 or +2;
       n
        Each obstacle: –1 or –2.
        Compare the two rolls. The group with the higher modified
      roll gains one unit for every point of difference the roll is higher.
        The chase ends when one group is stopped, when the chas-
      ing group catches up, or when the fleeing group reaches its objec-
      tive or gets out of reach (Gamemaster’s decision).

  Normal Combat
     If the creature survives the rush and attacks, the hunt enters
  normal melee combat at this point. Otherwise, if the creature
  flees, the hunt resumes as a pursuit.

nd Pursuits

  Terrain and  Obstacles

     Obstacles are added encounters meant to delay the Player-
  knights, spicing up an otherwise ordinary chase. You shouldn’t
  add more than one obstacle for every two stages. Either use Table
  19–10: Hunting Obstacles, or add some of your own invention.
  Some ideas for obstacles are:
   n
     A simple obstruction of the path (a fallen tree, a col-
     lapsed bridge, enemy soldiers, a monster);
   n
     Difficult terrain (crossing water, a swamp, on
     rooftops);
   n
     A particular circumstance that needs resolution be-
     fore continuing the chase (a horse collapses, an in-
     jured comrade, starvation or suffocation, people call-
     ing on the Player-knights for help).
  Setting and Danger
     Chases should be conducted in very important situations,
  when the stakes are high. Be sure to have a working plot device
  to involve the knights in the chase. Once this is done and the
  chase has begun, take sufficient time to carefully describe each
  stage: the general scene, the noises, and the weird sensation of
  confusion and speed. Allow the “unengaged” Player-knights one
  of the following actions:
   n
     Can the Player-knight see his pursuers? [Awareness]
   n
     Can he spot a short cut or other advantageous route?
     [Awareness or Hunting]

segments.text:
Surprise Attack
        Once hunters have caught up to the quarry, the first char-
      acter on the scene may make one free attack, as long as he can
      close to melee distance or has a missile weapon with adequate
      range; alternately, he can choose to stay near the creature until
      reinforcements arrive to attack it in normal melee.
        If more than one character arrives on the same segment, any
      character with Glory or rank significantly higher than the others
      should be allowed the first attack. Otherwise, whoever has the high-
      est Movement Rate (or, if tied, DEX score) gets the first attack.
        The surprise attack is an opposed roll pitting the hunter’s
      weapon skill roll against the prey’s Avoidance roll. Check the re-
      sult on the Table 19–12.
      The Rush

If the quarry lives after a surprise attack, as many as three
      characters with melee weapons (plus any number of ranged at-
      tackers) may attempt another attack, if possible, while the beast
      tries to either escape or close with its attackers. The prey still uses
      its Avoidance value to oppose attacks during the rush, rather
      than an opposed combat roll.
                           Chases    and

S
         ometimes two characters chase each other on foot or on
         horse, or a creature is chased by several characters (or vice
         versa!). Chases should be fast, thrilling and spectacular,
      involving riotous movement, interesting terrain or obstacles, and
      danger, and they should advance the plot.
        The hunting procedure may be used for chases. For every
      step, instead of opposing a modified Hunting roll to the prey’s
      Avoidance, use the relative speeds of the pursuer and the pursued.
      Speed and  Movement
        First, break down the chase into stages. On the average, you
      should have no more than ten stages per chase. Decide who partic-
      ipates and the base speed of the groups (try to keep things simple).
        Then, decide the unit of measurement (the scale) you want
      to use for the chase. This can be anything from yards to miles,
      or even days of travel. Finally, determine the initial distance (in
      units of measurement) that separates the two chasing groups.
        At each stage of the race, roll 1d6 for both groups, and ap-
      ply the following Modifiers:
       n
        Each unit of speed difference: +/–1;
       n
        Each clever delaying tactic: +1 or +2;
       n
        Each obstacle: –1 or –2.
        Compare the two rolls. The group with the higher modified
      roll gains one unit for every point of difference the roll is higher.
        The chase ends when one group is stopped, when the chas-
      ing group catches up, or when the fleeing group reaches its objec-
      tive or gets out of reach (Gamemaster’s decision).
