If several people attack, the beast must divide its Avoidance
  value among them just as it would its combat skill in normal
  combat (see Multiple Attackers in Chapter 7).
  Normal Combat
     If the creature survives the rush and attacks, the hunt enters
  normal melee combat at this point. Otherwise, if the creature
  flees, the hunt resumes as a pursuit.
Terrain and  Obstacles

Obstacles are added encounters meant to delay the Player-
  knights, spicing up an otherwise ordinary chase. You shouldn’t
  add more than one obstacle for every two stages. Either use Table
  19–10: Hunting Obstacles, or add some of your own invention.
  Some ideas for obstacles are:
   n
     A simple obstruction of the path (a fallen tree, a col-
     lapsed bridge, enemy soldiers, a monster);
   n
     Difficult terrain (crossing water, a swamp, on
     rooftops);
   n
     A particular circumstance that needs resolution be-
     fore continuing the chase (a horse collapses, an in-
     jured comrade, starvation or suffocation, people call-
     ing on the Player-knights for help).
  Setting and Danger
     Chases should be conducted in very important situations,
  when the stakes are high. Be sure to have a working plot device
  to involve the knights in the chase. Once this is done and the
  chase has begun, take sufficient time to carefully describe each
  stage: the general scene, the noises, and the weird sensation of
  confusion and speed. Allow the “unengaged” Player-knights one
  of the following actions:
   n
     Can the Player-knight see his pursuers? [Awareness]
   n
     Can he spot a short cut or other advantageous route?

        Such actions and their results add player interest and a

        Another element that needs attention is the Player-knights’
      retinue: squires, surplus horses, and so on. In general, they
      should not be part of a chase, unless the Gamemaster wants to
      slow down the Player-knights, because they considerably com-
      plicate the chase encounter.
        Example of A Chase: Sir Adalhart and his companions are
      at a castle and need to get out, and fast! The lord wants to capture
      them and has sent his men after them. The Player-knights’ goal is
      the forest where their lord’s lands begin.
        The initial distance is 1, the unit of measure is 10 yards.
        Stage 1, Inside the castle: Show the players a map of the
      castle and let them chose a way to get out. Prepare some obstacles
      (soldiers, closed doors, missing ladders, etc.).
        If they succeed, they get to their horses and ride out of the
      castle. The Player-knights have better horses, giving them +2 per
      stage for the rest of the chase.
                              Solo   Sce
      S
         olos provide relatively painless ways to try to get expe-
         rience checks for traits or skills. Maybe your character
         missed a couple of games and you want to learn what he
      did while he was gone. Or your character might have chosen not
      to participate in an event or adventure, and is “out of the story.”
      These scenarios offer something for the player and character to
      do while the rest of the game continues. Finally, some things are
      done primarily in private — specifically the practice of Romance.
        At the end of a solo adventure a Gamemaster may assign
      Glory for the accomplished actions and goals, as usual.
      Challenges
        Late Carolingian stories feature encounters with knights
      who are waiting at a road crossing, ford, or bridge to joust with a
      specific opponent, or just with any and all passers-by. This duty
      is often self-imposed, to gain the knight some Glory. Sometimes
      it is dictated by a lady.
      Crossroad Encounters
        First, select the type of road where the knight is waiting,
      for it determines the amount of traffic, and thus the number of
      possible encounters each month.

     Stage 2, In the cleared land around the castle: In this
  stage, pure (horse) speed is all that counts. Hopefully, this allows
  the players to build up a lead. The lord blows his horn, alerting his
  men at the village.
     Stage 3, In the village: To get to the forest, the Player-
  knights have to pass through a small village. Obstacles in the
  village include the peasants, their children, chickens and cattle.
  Ignoring these obstacles deserves a Cruel check and may cause
  accidents, angering the local population. If so, they start throwing
  stones at the Player-knights, or worse!
     Stage 4, Detour: The lord’s soldiers at the village (at least
  three spearmen per Player-knight) have taken refuge behind a hay
  cart, blocking the way to the bridge. Trying to pass the cart is al-
  most suicidal, and the pursuers will probably catch up to them, but
  they may try if they wish. Or they may turn around and go back.
     Stage 5, Over the forest bridge: The last stage is like num-
  ber 2. Speed is essential to bring the character knights safely to the
  bridge. Enemy archers try to shoot at them.

      sPecial eNcouNters
        Personal Enemy: This knight is a personal foe; the
      Gamemaster should determine who. He fights to capture for
      ransom, or to the death if Inspired.
        Bandits: Bandits attack to capture the knight for ransom.
      If captured, they can be sold into serfdom (£1 each). If this en-
      counter occurs after a personal challenge, this means your enemy
      hired some brigands to capture you, instead of fighting himself.
        Foreign Christian Knight: A knight from an exotic land,
      but a (converted) Christian, who is now on an errand for his
      lord, or simply looking for adventure. He accepts any non-lethal
      challenge.
        Pagan Knight: This visitor is peacefully traveling through
      Frankland to learn the customs of chivalry, or to acquire Glory.
      He fights “for love,” if possible.
        Paladin: Paladins only fight in a chivalrous manner, but
      otherwise accept any kind of challenge.
      The Jousts

        For each fight, the solitaire player must make the Lance
      rolls for both his character and the opponent. Each opponent is
      fought separately and successively. If the Player-knight is wound-
      ed, captured, or loses all his horses then the rest of the month is
      affected.
        Each week spent healing subtracts 5 from the number of
      knights not yet encountered. For instance, a character on a roy-
      al road rolls a 4, expecting to fight 12 enemies that month. But
      if the first one wounds him badly enough to require 2 weeks
      healing, the player must subtract 10 from 12. After recovery he
      would then encounter only 1 more opponent (since he has al-
      ready fought one).
        Victorious jousters who release their opponents for ran-
      som collect the money in 2d6 months. Characters may keep
      their defeated opponents’ warhorse, armor, and weapons if they
      wish, without incurring a Selfish check. However, returning the
      equipment at least half the time gets a Generous Check.
        If the Player-knight loses to an unchivalrous knight, roll
      Forgiving. On a failure, roll Vengeful. The Player-knight might
      develop a Hate [opponent] of 5+ the value of a successful
      Vengeful roll.
      The Feud
        A feud is a private war against another noble house. A
      feuding Player-knight must start by mustering his kin to sup-
      port him in a punitive expedition against the hated enemy. The

      sPecial eNcouNters
        Personal Enemy: This knight is a personal foe; the
      Gamemaster should determine who. He fights to capture for
      ransom, or to the death if Inspired.
        Bandits: Bandits attack to capture the knight for ransom.
      If captured, they can be sold into serfdom (£1 each). If this en-
      counter occurs after a personal challenge, this means your enemy
      hired some brigands to capture you, instead of fighting himself.
        Foreign Christian Knight: A knight from an exotic land,
      but a (converted) Christian, who is now on an errand for his
      lord, or simply looking for adventure. He accepts any non-lethal
      challenge.
        Pagan Knight: This visitor is peacefully traveling through
      Frankland to learn the customs of chivalry, or to acquire Glory.
      He fights “for love,” if possible.
        Paladin: Paladins only fight in a chivalrous manner, but
      otherwise accept any kind of challenge.
      The Jousts

For each fight, the solitaire player must make the Lance
      rolls for both his character and the opponent. Each opponent is
      fought separately and successively. If the Player-knight is wound-
      ed, captured, or loses all his horses then the rest of the month is
      affected.
        Each week spent healing subtracts 5 from the number of
      knights not yet encountered. For instance, a character on a roy-
      al road rolls a 4, expecting to fight 12 enemies that month. But
      if the first one wounds him badly enough to require 2 weeks
      healing, the player must subtract 10 from 12. After recovery he
      would then encounter only 1 more opponent (since he has al-
      ready fought one).
        Victorious jousters who release their opponents for ran-
      som collect the money in 2d6 months. Characters may keep
      their defeated opponents’ warhorse, armor, and weapons if they
      wish, without incurring a Selfish check. However, returning the
      equipment at least half the time gets a Generous Check.
        If the Player-knight loses to an unchivalrous knight, roll
      Forgiving. On a failure, roll Vengeful. The Player-knight might
      develop a Hate [opponent] of 5+ the value of a successful
      Vengeful roll.
      The Feud
        A feud is a private war against another noble house. A
      feuding Player-knight must start by mustering his kin to sup-
      port him in a punitive expedition against the hated enemy. The

recruitment of mercenaries is optional, and earns a check in
  Cruel.
  Exhort Your Kin
     As the leader of his war band, the player should explain why
  he is engaging in or pursuing the family feud, and gain a possible
  check in Eloquence in addition to checks in Proud, Vengeful,
  Standing [family] and an appropriate passion (Honor, Love
  [family], Love, or Amor, for example).
  Reconnaissance

The next step in a feud is to gather information about the
  enemy. The Player-knight may roll Intrigue to find out about the
  strength of possible opponents. If the roll is a critical, the Player-
  knight gains a check and a –1 to the Feuding Enemies table. If he
  fumbles, the Player-knight is surprised himself. Roll Awareness.
  A failed roll indicates the Player-knight was ambushed (auto-
  matic roll of 6 on the Feuding Enemies table), otherwise he gets
  +1 on the table.

        Most of Frankland is wooded. This table can be used as a
      guide to wandering in unknown forests. It can also be used as a
      Winter Phase Solo adventure. Characters often find themselves
      departing the company of the other characters and going off on
      their own, out of the game.

      til a 20 is rolled, whereupon the character finds his way home
      again. Each roll is one day of wandering.

eNcouNters

     Bandits: Fight against 1d6 bandits. They are desperate
  and foolish, and attack with intent to capture. The knight must
  fight them. The bandits fight until half of them have been killed
  or made unconscious. This constitutes a successful encounter
  against them. If successful, the knight gets 1d20 pence.
     If unsuccessful, the knight is captured and can be ransomed.
  He is stripped of all equipment and held prisoner until winter.
  On a successful Standing [lord] roll, his liege will pay his ran-
  som. After collecting the ransom, the bandits take him to the
  nearest road and let him go.
     If the lord does not pay, the Player-knight remains captive
  for another year, and the Player-knight will be allowed a new
  Standing [lord], or Standing [Family] –5, roll to see if someone
  pays his ransom.
     Paladin: A Player-knight may attempt to cure a melan-
  cholic paladin. Unless the Player-knight decides to flee (check
  Prudent), an encounter with a mad paladin results in a fight
  against an unarmored hero (check Reckless; the paladin fights
  with a club), in which the knight should attempt to subdue the
  paladin without killing him. Slaying a mad paladin costs 10
  Standing [Charlemagne] and 5 Honor points.
     Wild Animal: These are all hostile beasts that will attack
  the knight. Yes, even the deer!
     Manor Encounters: These are generic encounters. In a solo
  game you may wish to elaborate upon these individuals, making
  friends or enemies for the future.

      The Holy  Lands

        A Player-knight may travel to visit Jerusalem as a pilgrim or
      as a crusader. For the sake of simplicity, this solo does not distin-
      guish between roles. The knight may undertake his voyage with
      the lord’s approval (roll standing), as a penance for a deadly sin,
      or as a punishment pronounced by the knight’s lord — or even
      by Charlemagne himself.
        If all goes well, this solo lasts at least two years, as traveling
      to or from the Holy Lands takes a year.
      The Voyage
        First, a pilgrim or crusader must buy passage on a ship to
      take him to Jerusalem. The voyage costs £4 for just the knight
      himself, plus £1 per horse or squire. This includes the cost of
      the return voyage, which is paid in advance. Roll once on Table
      19–18: Holy Lands Travel.

title: Missus Dominicus
leftColumn:
Oath-Givers
        Now the two opposing knight bring forward their support-
      ing witnesses, or “oath-givers.” These men (no women allowed)
      support their version of the story and agree to share in the pun-
      ishment should the knight they supported be sentenced. Roll
      once on Table 19–23.
             table 19–23: oatH-givers

      1d6 Result Oath-Givers
         1   The plaintiff brings forward more oath-givers.
         2   The accused brings forward more oath-givers.
        3–5  Both knights have an equal number of oath-givers.
         6   Neither knight produces any oath-givers.
      Bribes

        Now see if either, or both, knights offer bribes to influence
      the Player-knight’s judgment. If the Player-knight accepts the
      bribes, he must check Selfish and Deceitful. Roll once on Table
      19–24.
            table 19–24: offered bribes
      1d6 Result Offered Bribes

         1   The plaintiff offers a bribe of £1.
         2   The plaintiff offers a bribe of £1d).
         3   The accused offers a bribe of £1.
         4   The accused offers a bribe of 1d6£.
         5   Both knights each offer a bribe of 1d6£.
         6   Neither knight offers a bribe.
      Sentencing

        Now that the knight has heard the plaintiff and the accused, as
      well as the support brought by their oath-givers, the time has come
      to deliver a judgment. For this, the Player-knight may either chose
      a side (check Arbitrary), or roll Just (at –5 if he accepted bribes).
        A successful Just roll (check Just) means he sentences law-
      fully and according to his own conviction of guilt. If he con-
      demns the knight who presented more oath-givers, he must
      check Suspicious.
        If he fails the Just roll, he must roll Arbitrary. A success indicates
      he deliberately pronounces a preferential judgment, instead of one
      based on his conviction and the law (check Arbitrary and Cruel).
        A failed Arbitrary roll leaves the player a choice. He
      may support the knight with most oath-givers, if any (check
      Arbitrary and Trusting), and condemn the other to the payment
      of a compensation equal to his heribannum. Or he may suspend
      his judgment and demand a trial by combat (check Suspicious).
        If the Player-knight’s sentence goes against a knight from
      whom he accepted bribes, he must check Deceitful.
      Missus  Dominicus
        If a Player-knight is given the position of missus domini-
      cus, he is obliged to perform this solo whenever Charlemagne
rightColumn:
(the Gamemaster) demands it (see the sections on Missus
  Dominicus in Chapter 11 for more information on their duties
  and prerogatives).
     It is assumed that the Missus is being sent to the court of a
  corrupt count, and that there are grave faults to find. The Player-
  knight is paired with a high-ranking churchman for the mission.
  Either of the missi may make any of the Inspection checks below.
  It is assumed the churchman will make the Religion and Reading
  & Writing tests, though the Player-knight may make them him-
  self if he wishes.
  The Reception
     First, the player missus and his colleague are received by the
  count whose domain they will be inspecting. The player must
  roll Courtesy to see if the missi are received with due honors. A
  successful roll reveals the count’s and his retinue’s hidden ner-
  vousness, which gives the inspecting missus a check on Courtesy
  and +1 to all his future inspection rolls (+2 on a critical, –1 on
  a fumble).
     During the feasting of the honored guests, roll Recognize
  to see if the Player-knight correctly observes his host’s notable
  character traits. If he does, he gains a check and a +1 bonus (+2
  for a critical, –1 on a fumble) to all his inspection rolls.
  The Inspection
     The actual inspection of the county is a test of several skills,
  serving to determine the current state of affairs in the county.
  Successful rolls earn checks to the missi who made them.
     Roll Folk Lore to hear the complaints of the commoners.
  Success allows the missus to discover that the free men are ex-
  ploited, forced to sell their land in return for the count’s protec-
  tion, or obliged to assart new lands for the count instead of for
  themselves.
     A successful roll in Stewardship reveals serious practices of
  corruption, unlawful collection of taxes and tolls, or confisca-
  tion of income from royal fiscs.
     A successful Awareness roll allows the missus to observe
  general errors in the application of the capitularies, the course of
  justice, and the military procedures.
     A Religion roll serves to evaluate the educational level of
  the priests, and to find out if any widespread pagan practices per-
  sist among the commoners.
     Success in Reading & Writing discovers the existence of
  corrupted bibles and other liturgical books.
     A successful Intrigue roll reveals that that the count made
  some serious threats against any court members who aided the
  missi in their tasks — a very serious crime!
  The Report

     The missi must now report their conclusions about the
  county’s administration to Charlemagne. To determine the
  Inspection Score, a missus gains 2 points for every critical suc-
  cess, 1 for a normal success, 0 for a failed roll, and –1 for a fumble.

             resources nor the peace and happiness our people deserve.”
        4–5  Reprimand: “We regretfully note the count’s irrespon-
             sible and arbitrary practices, which are harmful to his
             authority and honor, as well as to your glory.”
       6 or more Degradation: “A thoroughly corrupt and brutal count,
             who is a disgrace to our people and to your royal dignity.
             We have temporarily suspended him from his functions,
             pending a trial at your glorious court.”
        If the result is unfavorable (Inspection Score of 4 or high-
      er), the count offers each missus a bribe of 2d20£ value to get
      a positive report. If the player missus accepts, he checks Selfish
      and Deceitful and loses a point in Love [Charlemagne]. He may
      make a positive recommendation to Charlemagne. If he refuses,
      he may check Just.
        At the conclusion of his royal mission, the Player-knight
      earns checks in Energetic, Suspicious/Trusting, and Standing
      [Charlemagne].
      The Pilgrimage
        A pilgrimage is a spiritual journey to an important Christian
      site of worship in Frankland, often one where some major relics
      are preserved. The knight may perform this spiritual journey ei-
      ther of his own free will, or as a penance imposed by his bishop.
      Mortification
        To accentuate their humility, pilgrims often travel in partic-
      ular conditions, such as going barefooted, wearing a rough hair
      shirt or bearing a wooden cross. Roll Modest. A success means
      the Player-knight imposed himself a mortification. He earns a
      point in Modest.
      Religious Donation
        To stress the sincerity of his pilgrimage, a Player-knight
      may voluntarily donate one year’s income to the Church. Check
      Generous.
      Encounters

        Now roll on the Pilgrimage Encounter table twice (once on
      the way to the shrine, and once on the way back) to see what
      happened during the voyage.

title: Chapter Nineteen: Adventures
leftColumn:
well-known Gamemaster character, perhaps an heiress or maybe
      even a princess!
        The Gamemaster should generate a Potential Amor for the
      Lady using the same guidelines as for the knight. If her Amor is
      less than 10, she will never give in to him, though she’ll enjoy
      his gifts and attention. Her Reluctance is infinite. If the Amor is
      10–15, she is interested in him, and will entertain the notion of
      falling in love with him. If the Amor is 16 or more, she will play
      the game, but never has any intention of not following it through
      to the essai. The Gamemaster should keep the lady’s Potential
      Amor secret from the player.
      Virtuous Rejection by the Lady
        The object of Amor is always reluctant. Figure her
      Reluctance, which is the length of time that she is willing
      to resist, even if she has been favorably impressed. The base
      Reluctance score is 20 minus her Potential Amor for him, if any,
      plus any Chaste points over 15.
      Wooing
        From this point on it is a matter of chipping away at her re-
      luctance through flattery, gifts, and performing deeds. Each win-
      ter, when the knight and his lover are together (or if they spent
      considerable time, perhaps non-played time, together during the
      year) the wooing may proceed.
        Gift and Approach: Each winter, the knight must give the
      lady a gift worth at least £1, and make a successful Romance roll
      to get her attention. Failure at this roll ends the attempt and no
      further action in romance may be attempted this year. If success-
      ful, she imposes a Task.
        Lover’s Tasks: Roll 1d20 on Table 19–28: Lover’s Task
      Table, +1 for each task successfully completed so far.
        For each task successfully completed, subtract 1 from the
      knight’s skill or trait, if applicable, and attempt a d20 roll (unless
      noted otherwise, like for jewelry, jousts, tournaments or fights).
      Success indicates that he satisfied her. For each successful at-
      tempt, the Gamemaster should lower her Reluctance by 1 point
      (2 on a critical success).
        If you decide that you will attempt the task, you’re still not
      done: To defy your lord or assassinate her father, roll Amor vs.
      Honor. Amor must win in order for you to make the attempt.
        These tests reduce Reluctance by 2 points if performed
      successfully.
        The Gamemaster is encouraged to add other tasks to this list.
        A knight may impose tasks on himself even if his lover does
      not know of his love for her — each successful task adds +1 to
      the lady’s Potential Amor roll when he finally meets and declares
      his love for her.
        Increased Familiarity: At successive stages of success the
      lady allows her lover more liberties: to address her affectionately;
      kiss the hem of her dress, her hand, her arm; receive a hug; give
      him a little kiss on his forehead; rest his head on her lap; and so
      on. When the last point of resistance is overcome, she may allow

     1d20 Result
    +1 per task already Task
      performed (skill or trait, modified for Difficulty)
       1–2     Bring her a valuable piece of jewelry (1d6 £).
       3–4     Sit around, sighing and looking moon-
               struck (Amor).
       5–6     Make her smile (APP).
       7–8     Get some fresh flowers from far away
               (Horsemanship).
       9–10    Sing a pleasant song, surprising her in the
               garden (Singing).
       11–12   Recite a traditional love poem at court
               (Eloquence).
       13–14   Be seen pacing the ramparts late at night
               (Energetic or Amor).
       15–16   Enter a tournament, and fight in every
               event (Lance and best melee weapon).
       17–18   Recite a love poem addressed to the lover,
               but disguised (Eloquence or Romance).
       19–20   Joust with all strangers for a month (Go to
               the Challenges solo).
       21–22   Fight a boar, without armor (Play out
               combat).
       23–24   Carry her favor at a tournament and win a
               prize of champion (Go to the Tournament
               solo).
       25–26   Defy your lord to prove your love.*
               (Deliberately defy your lord).
       27–28   Kill her husband/father/guardian* (Fight
               a combat to the death against a notable
               knight).
     *These might be straight requests, or may be tests of Honor. As they have
  grave consequences on the campaign and your character, you should consult the
  Gamemaster, who will determine if she actually means for you to do the deed, or
  to refrain. A successful Romance roll will indicate her true motives. An unsuc-
  cessful Romance means you should decide for yourself whether she is serious or
  not, and whether you should attempt the deed or not.
  her lover a soulful, lip-to-lip kiss. Her Reluctance is known only
  to the Gamemaster, so your knight will not know exactly how
  far along he is except by the increased attention she allows the
  knight to pay her.
     When the Gamemaster tells you that her Reluctance
  has been eliminated, proceed to The Essai (for Amor), or
  Consummation (for mundane wooing).
  The Essai
     The lovers must lie naked in bed for a night, without
  touching each other. Roll Chaste. If the Player-knight suc-
  ceeds, the lady falls in love with him. Her Amor turns to Love
  at the same value, and the two proceed to Consummation at the
  next Winter Phase.

       27–28   Kill her husband/father/guardian* (Fight
               a combat to the death against a notable
               knight).
     *These might be straight requests, or may be tests of Honor. As they have
  grave consequences on the campaign and your character, you should consult the
  Gamemaster, who will determine if she actually means for you to do the deed, or
  to refrain. A successful Romance roll will indicate her true motives. An unsuc-
  cessful Romance means you should decide for yourself whether she is serious or
  not, and whether you should attempt the deed or not.
  her lover a soulful, lip-to-lip kiss. Her Reluctance is known only
  to the Gamemaster, so your knight will not know exactly how
  far along he is except by the increased attention she allows the
  knight to pay her.
     When the Gamemaster tells you that her Reluctance
  has been eliminated, proceed to The Essai (for Amor), or
  Consummation (for mundane wooing).
  The Essai
     The lovers must lie naked in bed for a night, without
  touching each other. Roll Chaste. If the Player-knight suc-
  ceeds, the lady falls in love with him. Her Amor turns to Love
  at the same value, and the two proceed to Consummation at the
  next Winter Phase.

title: Solo Scenarios
leftColumn:
If he fails, he disappoints his Amor, who gains 5 Reluctance
      points. A disappointing knight must also fail a subsequent
      Lustful roll, otherwise he has not only disappointed, but he has
      dishonored his lady. The knight loses 3 points of Honor and is
      definitively rejected by his Amor. She may develop a Hate pas-
      sion equal to the previous Amor, and she will most likely stir up
      her family against the knight. He loses his Amor passion and
      may never develop another.
      Consummation
        If this has been a wooing, the lady agrees to marry her suit-
      or. The Romance ends here and a wedding takes place in the
      next year. The Gamemaster may determine if Love occurs be-
      tween the two.
        If this has been Amor, the lady sees the light. Ah, sweet suc-
      cess, bliss and pleasure. The lovers are joined on all planes. The
      passion changes from Amor [person] to Love [Amor]. It is still
      secret. Continue to the next step.
      Subterfuge and Troubles

        Now that the lovers are in accord, they must keep their
      burning desire a secret. This is not easy, since their natural desire
      is to be together and the woman is married, as often as not.
        Determine Discovery Factor: The Discovery Factor is
      equal to 1d6+the husband’s Suspicious or Romance, +1 for each
      year for which the affair has gone on. If the lady is not married,
      use her father’s or guardian’s Suspicious or Romance.

  knight.

     17   Spiteful maids expose their knowledge.

  Exposure and Shame
     The lovers have been discovered (e.g. the Amor was beat-
  en by the Discovery Factor), exposed, or otherwise caught. Roll
  1d20 to find the husband’s reaction:

        table 19–30: eXPosure results
   1d20 Result Husband’s Reaction
      1   He and his family start a feud.
      2   He wants to fight to the death.
     3–5  He publicly shames the knight and repudiates his de-
          nounced wife.
     6–10 He seeks to exile the knight and beats his wife.
    11–18 He privately threatens the knight and repudiates his
          wife.
     19   He privately threatens the knight and forgives his wife.

     20   He does nothing. He doesn’t like women anyway.
  Possible Pregnancy
     After consummation, be sure to check whether the lady
  becomes pregnant during each Winter Phase (see Chapter 10).
  Her resultant child may be her lover’s or her husband’s. Oh, what
  tangled webs love and genetics weave!
  Conclusion

     Where all of this leads is up to the players, Gamemaster, and
  flavor of the campaign. It is possible that the lover, his beloved,
  and her husband all neatly forget it now that it is over. Perhaps
  the husband harbors a grudge. Maybe she doesn’t really want to
  end it. There is no end to the intrigue.

title: The Royal Court
leftColumn:
The Royal  Court

        Many knights dream of being admitted to Charlemagne’s
      court and sharing in its glory. Roll Standing [Charlemagne], +1
      per Glory/1,000 (max. +10). If successful, the Player-knight is
      accepted at court, where he may spend some months in the stim-
      ulating company of the royal family, paladins, high nobles and
      learned scholars.
      Gifts
        Charlemagne’s guests must present their sovereign a gift
      according to their status (typically one-tenth of their heriban-
      num value). To see what the Player-knight gets in return from
      Charlemagne, roll Standing [Charlemagne]. On a critical, the
      king presents a gift worth five times the value of the received
      gift; twice its value for a success; of equal value for a failure; and
      half its value on a fumble.
      Court Life
        During his stay, the player attends many courtly events, in-
      cluding weddings, dubbings, and other feasting activities. For
      this, he may check Temperate/Indulgent, and 3 of the following
      skills (player choice): Courtesy, Recognize, Dancing, Gaming,
      Heraldry, Play Instruments, Singing.
      Politics

        The Player-knight dines in the hall in the presence of offi-
      cers, dukes, bishops and other important people, with whom he
      shares the latest news and gossip. Check Intrigue.
      Romance

        Roll 4d6. If the result is 10 or more, and the knight does not
      already have an existing Amor or Love [Amor] passion then the
      Player-knight falls in love with a princess (Frankish or foreign).
      If he decides to secretly woo her, he may check Romance and
      perform the Romance solo adventure next year.
      Contests
        Charlemagne loves to challenge his guests to various types
      of manly competitions. The Player-knight may participate in
      three contests, choosing from falconry, horsemanship, hunting,
      swimming, jousting, or a melee weapon.
        For each challenge, roll the appropriate skill. A critical success
      means he defeated Charlemagne, who congratulates the knight.
      This gains him a check and double Glory (40 instead of the nor-
      mal 20 for a critical skill success). A normal success earns normal
      Glory and a check, a failure is without any consequences, while a

  The  Tournament

     After Phase 1, knights may participate in regional tourna-
  ments. A classic tournament consists of three contests: the joust,
  the challenges, and the melee. A Player-knight is not obliged to
  participate in all three contests.
  The Helm Show
     First, a Player-knight may check Gaming for participating
  in the presentation of the shields and the helm show. Heralds an-
  nounce the tournament rules and conditions, for example if the
  contests are “for love” (the winner gains only glory), “for gear”
  (the winner takes the loser’s equipment), “for gear and steed”
  (the winner also gains the loser’s horse), or, very rarely, “for con-
  quest” (the winner may ransom the loser). The tournament may
  be fought with rebated weapons (à plaisance), or sharp weapons,
  with the normal chance of injury (à outrance), with an attendant
  difference in Glory.
  The Joust

     For each jousting round, pair up the Player-knight with a
  random opponent.
              table 19–32:
       tourNaMeNt JoustiNg oPPoNeNts
   1d6 Result+RN* Opponent Lance Skill Damage
      2–3   Young knight 9+RN* 5d6
      4–5   Ordinary knight 11+RN* 6d6

      6–7   Ordinary knight 13+RN* 6d6
      8–9   Notable knight 15+RN* 7d6
     10–11  Famous knight 17+RN* 7d6
      12+   Paladin   19+RN*   8d6
     * RN is the Round Number.
     For each opponent, make an opposed Lance roll. If the
  Player-knight wins, he goes to the next round. If his oppo-
  nent rolled a partial success, the Player-knight must check for
  Knockdown and suffer possible damage from a fall (1d6; 2d6 on
  a fumbled Horsemanship roll). If he is knocked down, he loses;
  if he stays on his horse, he wins.
     If the Player-knight loses a joust, he is out of the jousting
  tournament. He collects combat Glory (one-tenth if using rebat-
  ed weapons) for all defeated opponents.

title: Vassal Service
leftColumn:
A knight may forfeit a joust. If he still has more than half
      his Total Hit Points, he must check Cowardly. If he is severely
      injured, he checks Prudent. He may be compelled to forfeit by
      his amor, as a test of his love…
        If he wins all the rounds, he wins the joust and is crowned
      Champion of Lances.
        In any case, the Player-knight checks Horsemanship, Lance
      and Gaming.
      Challenges
        If he so desires, a Player-knight may participate in the in-
      dividual challenges. Each should be a single opposed resolution
      only, for love or first blood (not to the death), with certain type
      of weapon, mounted or not, with rebated weapons or not. Win
      or lose, the Player-knight gains a check in the weapon he uses.
      The Melee

        The melee is like a real battle between two opposing sides.
      Each round, roll up a different opponent. Roll your weapon
      once against this knight to determine the outcome of the round
      of combat.
                  table 19–33:
           tourNaMeNt Melee oPPoNeNts

      1d6 Result Opponent Sword Skill Damage
         1   Young knight 10      3d6
         2   Ordinary knight 13   4d6
         3   Ordinary knight 16   5d6
         4   Notable knight 19    6d6
         5   Famous knight 22     7d6
         6   Paladin     25       8d6

        On a critical victory, he captures his opponent and receives
      a ransom. On a fumble, the Player-knight is captured and must
      pay his own ransom.
        After each melee round, a Player-knight may retire to the
      neutral zone behind the palisade to rest or recover from injuries.
      As for jousts, severely injured knights may check Prudent, while
      those who are not check Cowardly.
        After the last melee round, roll 1d6. If the result is lower
      than the number of his critical victories, the Player-knight is
      crowned Champion of the Melee.
        For his participation in this event, a Player-knight may
      check Battle and a melee weapon.
      Court Life
        A major part of a knight’s life is spending time at his lord’s
      court, giving advice, meeting important people, or romancing
      the ladies.
        All participating knights gain checks in Courtesy and
      Heraldry, plus two courtly skills from the following list (play-
      er’s choice): Dancing, Falconry, Gaming, Play Instruments,
      Romance, Singing.
rightColumn:

title: Your Manor
leftColumn:
a fumble the knight wrongfully “recognizes” a band of honest
      pilgrims as spies. He accuses and imprisons them, which costs
      him a point of Honor.
      Your Manor

        Knights who own land must spend time on it, doing all of
      the things which landlords and farmers do. Each year perform
      each of the tasks below.
      Lord Visits
        The lord invites himself to the Player-knight’s manor, to
      check if everything is going well and to reaffirm his power. The
      lord talks politics and discusses news and rumors with his vassal.
      Check Intrigue.

      Estate Review
        Together with the steward, the Player-knight evaluates the
      state of the population and the lands, and supervises the works
      going on at his domain. Check Folk Lore and Stewardship.
      Judgment

        The knight must listen to the complaints of his peasants.
      Two peasants bring a case before him.
        First find out who are the two contestants in the argu-
      ment. Roll twice: first for the plaintiff who makes the com-
      plaint, and then for the defendant, who must defend himself
      against the claim. Roll on the Table 19–36 to find out what
      they are arguing about.
       table 19–35: coMMoN court ParticiPaNts
       2d6 Result
       2  A rich farmer, who offers you £2 to settle for him.
       3  The village priest.
       4  A rich farmer, who offers you £1 to settle for him.

       5  A poor old widow.
       6  A peddler.
       7–8 A farmer.
       9  A tradesman (blacksmith, cooper, carpenter, miller, tanner).
       10 A poor farmer.
       11 An attractive and flirtatious widow.
       12 A childhood friend, who offers you £1 “to help you think.”

table 19–36: disPutes
    1d20 Result Dispute
      1    The ownership of a cow.
      2    The ownership of a pig.
      3    The ownership of an ox.
      4    Time to use the plow.

      5    An unpaid debt.
      6–8  An exchange of verbal insults.
     9–12  A brawl.
      13   A knifing.
     14–15 Theft of petty property.
     16–17 Theft of real property.
      18   Something about a wife...
      19   Something about a daughter...

      20   A killing
     Now you can attempt a Just roll (and gain a check in the
  trait), or simply choose a party and decide in their favor. In this
  case you collect the promised bribe, if any, and get an Arbitrary
  check.
  A Hunt
     To alleviate boredom, the Player-knight does some routine
  pleasure hunting. Roll 1d6. On 1–4 check Horsemanship and
  Hunting, on 5–6 he was visited by some noble companions or
  ladies; check Courtesy and Falconry instead.
  Superstitions

     Someone reports that peasants are practicing pagan rituals.
  Roll Faerie Lore to gain accurate information about the rituals
  performed. A critical gains a check and indicates the actual pres-
  ence of a faerie creature. A fumble does the same, but the Player-
  knight mistakes it for a demonic presence.
     If the Player-knight takes no action, he gains a point in
  Standing [commoners], but loses one in Standing [Church].
     If the Player-knight destroys the site and has a priest erect
  and bless a stone cross on the site, he may check Standing
  [Church] and Love [God]. However, he loses a point in Standing
  [commoners], unless he finds a solution to satisfy the locals by
  means of a success in Religion.
     If the Player-knight attacked an enchanted site, he attracts
  the wrath of the faerie inhabitants and provokes subsequent bad
  harvests and cattle plagues until he makes amends.
